Provisional Agenda Item 12
Consideration of funding
proposals – Addendum VI
Funding proposal package for FP211
Summary
This addendum contains the following fix parts:
a) A funding proposal summary titled “Hardest-to-Reach” submitted by Acumen Fund. Inc.;
b) No-objection letters issued by the national designated authorities or focal point(s);
c) Environmental and Social report(s) disclosure;
d) Independent Technical Advisory Panel’s assessment;
e) Response from the accredited entity to the independent Technical Advisory Panel’s
assessment; and
f) Gender documentation of the funding proposal.
These documents are presented as submitted by the accredited entity and the national designated
authority(ies) or focal point(s), respectively. Pursuant to the Comprehensive Information Disclosure
Policy of the Fund, the funding proposal titled titled “Hardest-to-Reach” submitted by Acumen Fund.
Inc. is being circulated on a limited distribution basis only to Board Members and Alternate Board
Members to ensure confidentiality of certain proprietary, legally privileged or commercially sensitive
information of the entity.

Note to Accredited Entities on the use of the funding proposal template
● Accredited Entities should provide summary information in the proposal with cross-
reference to annexes such as feasibility studies, gender action plan, term sheet, etc.
● Accredited Entities should ensure that annexes provided are consistent with the details
provided in the funding proposal. Updates to the funding proposal and/or annexes must be
reflected in all relevant documents.
● The total number of pages for the funding proposal (excluding annexes) should not
exceed 60. Proposals exceeding the prescribed length will not be assessed within the usual
service standard time.
● The recommended font is Arial, size 11.
● Under the GCF Information Disclosure Policy, project and programme funding proposals will
be disclosed on the GCF website, simultaneous with the submission to the Board, subject to
the redaction of any information that may not be disclosed pursuant to the IDP. Accredited
Entities are asked to fill out information on disclosure in section G.4.
Please submit the completed proposal to:

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 6
A
Provide an executive summary of the project/programme including:
1. Climate change problem 2. Proposed interventions 3. Climate results/benefits
Acumen is establishing a $250m inclusive, innovative and multi-country investment initiative to deploy
impact-focused capital and targeted technical assistance to off-grid-solar companies. The goal of ‘Hardest-
to-Reach’ is to develop the off-grid solar (OGS) sector in countries where it is currently nascent or far
below the capacity required to address the energy access challenge. The initiative will focus on least
developed countries (LDCs) in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly with electrification rates at-or-below the
sub-Saharan African average and high rates of poverty (45% or above), where investors have not been
willing to enter at sufficient scale to meet the energy access and climate resilience needs of underserved
segments.
Climate change problem
Across the 16 eligible Hardest-to-Reach (H2R) geographies, there are around 54 million African
households that do not have access to modern electricity services. Even compared to their sub-Saharan
African peers, these countries are being ‘left behind’ on energy access and are not on track to achieve
Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7). On average, 78% of the population in these countries lives
below the lower-middle-income poverty line,4 and these communities are both fast-growing sources of new
energy demand and are residing in acutely climate vulnerable contexts – in contexts of worsening heat
stress, more frequent droughts, more intense floods, and extreme weather events including tropical
cyclones. Nearly half of the bottom-twenty countries listed in the ND-Gain Climate Vulnerability Index5 are
Hardest-to-Reach countries, with H2R countries (for which there is available data) obtaining an average
index score of 36.6, compared to a global average of 59.8. Maplecroft’s Climate Vulnerability Index6 Fig 1
(below) displays the disproportionate incidence of climate vulnerability across Africa, where population
growth is also at its highest.
Fig 1: Maplecroft Climate Vulnerability Index (2018)
4 World Bank PovCal (n.d)
5 The ND-GAIN Country Index summarizes a country's vulnerability to climate change and other global challenges in
combination with its readiness to improve resilience. Higher index scores are given to less climate vulnerable countries.
6 The Maplecroft Climate Change Vulnerability Index provides a single figure rating for climate change exposure, sensitivity
and adaptive capacity, helping companies calculate risks from future climate change. It combines exposure to climate
extremes and change with the current human sensitivity to those climate stressors and the capacity of the country to adapt
to the impacts of climate change. Higher index scores are given to less climate vulnerable countries.

=== PAGE 11 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 7
A
In the face of escalating climate variability and change, the delivery of climate-resilient energy access
infrastructure and services is now more critical and urgent. The most recent data from the IEA Africa
Energy Outlook projects that, for every person in sub-Saharan Africa to have access to electricity by 2030,
thus achieving SDG 7, 6% of the current total population or 90 million people, including a significant
proportion from rural areas, would need to gain power access each year from 2022.7 Without energy that is
both clean and climate resilient, households in Africa’s LDCs will face the climate future with increasing
uncertainty and risk to their livelihoods, health and wellbeing.
The interplay of several factors points to the need for an energy access solution that puts climate
adaptation and resilience at the forefront.
Inadequacy of existing infrastructure
The past decade of climate trends and events has displayed the fragility of existing network
infrastructure against extreme weather shocks, with the significant damage and long periods
without repair being frequent, leading to severe and underappreciated consequences. Along with
power outages come disruptions to household routines, diminished public safety, and halted
economic activity, while the regularity of these incidents mean that households and small
businesses are forced to invest in inefficient coping measures, ranging from the purchase of water
tanks and diesel generators, to keeping expensive back-up inventories.8
Vulnerability of people without access
7 IEA Africa Energy Outlook (2022)
8 World Bank Policy Research - Underutilized Potential: The business costs of unreliable infrastructure in developing
countries (2019)

=== PAGE 12 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 8
A
Households without any electricity access, meanwhile, are trapped in climate vulnerability, as they
lack the social, technological, and financial resources that are enabled and multiplied by energy
access, such as early warning and post-disaster public notifications. For these households, energy
access will likely be the springboard for climate resilient sustainable development. For example,
addressing the energy access challenge through OGS products can have a transformational impact
on economic activity, which can boost economic resilience to climate shocks. Around a third of the
solar home systems (SHS) in East Africa were purchased with the intent to extend the working day
or boost enterprise. Usage of SHS in East Africa boosted monthly earnings by US$ 46 a month,
around 14% increase on average income.9
Dependency on nature
Research from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)10 has
pointed to the disproportionate dependence of the poorest and most marginalized on environmental
resources to meet their basic needs, such as forests (for energy, materials and food), land (for
farming) and water (for drinking, household use and farming). This is a reminder that the pathways
of electrification that investors and developers deploy in low-income communities, should be the
least nature-intensive, the most climate resilient, and the most supportive of community norms,
even as the benefits of economic development unfold.
Inequitable distribution of climate burden
On these considerations alone, entry-level distributed residential solar compares favorably to other
alternatives, separate from its mitigation and energy security benefits. And though the continent has
contributed to less than 4% of global emissions,11 the burden of climate change on least developed
countries and livelihoods across the continent is disproportionately high.12 Such climate injustice
already threatens to undermine development gains and inflict additional economic costs and social
disruption. Adaptation alone is projected to cost the continent at least $500 billion annually by 2050.
The African Development Bank’s African Economic Outlook summarizes several dynamics at play in the
continent’s potential low-carbon transition out of energy poverty:13
● Low-carbon transitions in Africa will vary by country, but they could be transformational. These
variations reflect differing ecological zones, climates, settlement patterns, economic structures,
resource bases, and governance systems;
● Africa is generously endowed with renewable energy resources, such solar irradiation, which
present significant opportunities for the green transition;
● With Africa’s limited lock-in to fossil-based energy technologies, renewable energy technology
opportunities could help the continent build a climate-resilient and integrated sustainable energy
sector;

DFID Literature Review on Energy Access and Adaptation to Climate Change (2015)
11 Carbon Disclosure Project CDP Africa Report (2020)
12 AfDB Climate Resilience and a Just Energy Transition in Africa (2022)

=== PAGE 13 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 9
A
● Interventions to achieve climate resilience and a just energy transition in the continent should be
inclusive, “leaving no one behind.”
Africa needs a decade of highly adaptive and resilience-promoting infrastructure investment to deliver on
the promise of sustainable development by 2030 and in this century. Yet, across the African continent, only
a small number of countries have seen strong growth in electrification in the past decade, in particular
Kenya, Senegal,and Ghana, as well as Ethiopia and Rwanda where there is still significant scope for
development. A substantial scale-up of investment is needed throughout sub-Saharan Africa, as it totals
two-thirds of the required additional global investment in electricity access. In terms of the emissions
mitigation pathway, the lesson from across the globe, historically, is that in a business-as-usual
environment, electricity and heat generation have been the greatest contributor to anthropogenic drivers of
greenhouse gas emissions, sometimes twice as large as the second most-contributing economic sector.
Still, today, power generation remains the largest GHG-emitting sector in developed economies across
Europe14 and the second-largest in the US,15 suggesting that the carbon-intensity of power generation and
economic development trajectories is highly material for mitigation outcomes, and showing that the
established pathways of electrification are inconsistent with net zero objectives and climate targets of the
United Nations SDGs and the Paris Accord. A similar fossil-fuelled trajectory in sub-Saharan Africa would
be catastrophic for our climate; if African emissions per person were to rise to only the current global
average, the continent would emit 12.5 billion tonnes of greenhouse gasses per year by 2050 — roughly
equivalent to all emissions from China and India today.1617
Proposed intervention
Acumen’s Hardest-to-Reach energy access initiative seeks to mobilize a blend of institutional and donor
finance to deliver much-needed investment into the region, to contribute to closing the energy access gap
in sub-Saharan Africa towards achieving SDG 7 by providing more than 60 million people with clean,
climate-resilient, off-grid solar energy products. Hardest-to-Reach (H2R) will establish two separate
financing facilities with different investment risk profiles, and invest with different forms of capital to match
the needs of off-grid solar companies and markets. This is designed to help off-grid solar companies to
expand in H2R countries and extend their reach to underserved segments, thus achieving sustainable and
inclusive scale with cross-cutting climate impacts. The first facility, the $50M grant-funded Market Support
Facility (MSF), intends to deploy debt, equity, and grants using a patient capital approach that is consistent
with Acumen’s core investment experience. The principal work of the MSF is to prove an approach in a
new market with a range of capital investment options and technical assistance accompaniment. A second
vehicle, the $200M blended finance Market Expansion Facility (MEF), intends to extend impact-linked debt
to OGS players, with the objective of responsibly expanding the reach and impact of OGS technologies,
while achieving high levels of inclusion and sustainability. To this end, H2R seeks to support companies
with technical assistance and invest in ecosystem development to ensure the sustainability of the
intervention and its impacts beyond the life of the fund.

Climate results/benefits
By the end of the program, investments developed, financed, and accompanied by H2R will be able to
provide:
● ~72.4M people with year-round access to clean, affordable, reliable and modern off-grid solar
energy.
● ~120 MW of newly-installed, decentralized solar energy generating capacity across H2R
geographies.
● ~54.3M people with first time energy access and improved climate resilience through decentralized
solar power delivery.
● ~5.4M people with improved climate resilience through diversified income sources enabled by first-
time access to a solar powered product.
● 5.1M tCO2e in emissions reduced or avoided (excl. black carbon mitigation impact).
● In addition, some 13,922 clean energy jobs, with 4,641 as sources of employment for women.
18 GOGLA Consumer Protection Code consists of a set of principles and an assessment framework to enable companies to
measure, demonstrate and improve their practices, and provide investors and other stakeholders with a framework to
promote good consumer protection (CP) practice. The code establishes the de facto industry standard for CP that adds
value to off-grid solar companies, investors and other stakeholders.

B. PROJECT/PROGRAMME INFORMATION
B.1. Climate context (max. 1000 words, approximately 2 pages)
Climate change problem: Describe the climate change problem the proposal is expected to address. Describe the mitigation needs
(GHG emissions profile) and/or adaptation needs (climate hazards and associated risks based on impacts, exposure, and
vulnerabilities) that the proposed interventions are expected to address. Also describe the most likely scenario (prevailing
conditions or other alternative) that would remain or continue in the absence of the proposed interventions. Include baseline
information. The methodologies used to derive such information, including the mitigation and adaptation needs, should be included
in the feasibility study.
Context: In describing the mitigation and/or adaptation needs, briefly describe the target region/area of the proposed interventions
including information on the demographics, economy, topography, etc.
Related projects/interventions: Also describe any recent or ongoing projects/interventions that are related to the proposal from
other domestic or international sources of funding, such as the Global Environment Facility, Adaptation Fund, Climate Investment
Funds, etc., and how they will be complemented by this project/programme (e.g. scaling up, replication, etc.). Please identify
current gaps and barriers regarding recent or ongoing projects and elaborate further how this project/programme complements or
addresses these.
Africa is the most vulnerable continent to climate change impacts under all climate scenarios above 1.5
degrees Celsius.19 Exponential collateral damage in the face of climate change poses systemic risks to the
continent’s economies, infrastructure investments, water and food systems, public health, agriculture, and
livelihoods, threatening to undo its modest development gains and slip into higher levels of extreme
poverty. There are substantial disparities across Africa, with many countries in sub-Saharan Africa being
the most vulnerable and exposed to the impacts of climate change. Many of these form the group of
Hardest-to-Reach target countries. All are highly vulnerable, and least ready, under the NDI-GAIN
indexation, with ranks reaching from 1st – 56th most vulnerable to, and 127th to 176th most ready to cope
with, adaptation challenges.
Constraints to the supply and demand of electricity drive the energy access problem. Two drivers -
household poverty, which limits a household’s ability to pay for electricity, and the lack of physical access
to electricity, due to costly, weak or non-existent coverage of grid electricity outside urban areas - are
particularly harmful to climate vulnerable populations. Accordingly, the baseline context can be presented
through two key indicators: poverty rate and electrification rates. At least half of all sub-Saharan Africans
have no access to electricity at all,20 and two-thirds of the global extreme poor population reside in this
region,21 with more than three quarters living below the $3.65/day poverty line across H2R program
countries on average.22 Acumen’s Hardest-to-Reach energy access initiative is seeking to contribute
towards closing the energy access gap in sub-Saharan Africa’s least developed countries (LDCs).

This vulnerability has recently been confirmed by a large-scale climate survey of thousands of people
across six sub-Saharan African countries. The survey found that 88% of people feel that climate change is
already having an impact on their everyday lives, that 63% of people consider climate change and
environmental degradation to affect their income and source of livelihood, and 57% of people have already
incurred losses due to climate change.25 These findings demonstrate that climate change is no longer only
a future threat, but a reality that many vulnerable people in Africa are living with already.
Climate Adaptation Context
The IPCC sixth assessment report shows that most regions in Africa have experienced a gradual increase
in temperatures in the past 40 years which has led to an increase in the frequency of annual heatwaves.26
Rainfall trends in the continent have higher degrees of uncertainty and only a few regions show statistically
significant historical rainfall trends. Projections indicate that both mean temperatures and temperature
extremes will increase over most of the continent, while mean annual rainfall is likely to increase over the
eastern Sahel, and eastern and central Africa.27 The frequency and severity of heavy rainfall events are
projected to increase throughout Africa, except in the northern and southwestern regions.28 Conversely,

The number of observed climate-related hazard events in sub-Saharan Africa has also increased in recent
years (Fig 2) and at a faster pace than the rest of the world.30 Given the high poverty levels and
dependence of most rural households on agriculture, climate events exacerbate the vulnerability of the
region. As seen in Fig 3, climate-related epidemics, floods and storms have been the most common
climate-related disasters faced by the continent’s fragile states.31 An increase in the frequency and
intensity of natural disasters has also been observed, which has been accompanied by an increase in the
number of people being affected by these events. Six times more people were affected by droughts in
2010-2019 relative to 1970-1979, while flooding impacted eight times more people over the same period.32
Perhaps unsurprisingly, the Hardest-to-Reach countries rank as the top 15% most vulnerable countries in
the world on the ND-Gain index.

Regional vulnerability to the changing climate and increasing climate hazards is exacerbated by non-
climate drivers such as high poverty levels, weak
infrastructure systems, a lack of emergency response
capabilities, and fragile grid electricity and
telecommunications networks. In particular, a lack of
access to modern energy sources heightens Africa's
climate vulnerability. The region’s energy systems
have been compromised both by extreme and slow-
onset climate events, with resulting economic losses,
disruptions of services and impacts to wellbeing.
Accordingly, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate
Change’s (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report (AR6)
considers decentralized energy generation to be an
important component of the systems transition of
energy, where adaptation, mitigation and development
solutions are pursued together to exploit synergies
and reduce trade-offs within the sector.33 Within
energy system transitions, the most feasible adaptation options support infrastructure resilience, reliable
power systems and efficient water use: “Energy generation diversification, including with renewable energy
resources and generation that can be decentralized depending on context (e.g., wind, solar, small scale
hydroelectric)...can reduce vulnerabilities to climate change, especially in rural populations (high
confidence)”.34
33 IPCC Sixth Assessment Report Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability (2022)
34 Ibid Chapter 9: Africa (2022)

It is now well understood that extreme weather events induced by climate change are a major source of
vulnerability.35 While these impacts are well tracked in developing countries, extreme weather events and
their impacts tend to be underreported when they happen in Africa, meaning that we have a much lower
level of understanding of their effects on peoples’ lives.36 This is closely linked to a lack of effective
hydrometeorological systems in particular in the North and Central African regions.37 Furthermore, even
where events are registered internationally, they often are those affecting the more population-dense, and
better connected urban locations, while similar events in rural regions simply go unnoticed.
With this being the case, it is likely that the vulnerability profile of African countries understates the levels of
exposure of the rural poor, who are least able to implement measures to protect themselves from this. EM-
DAT provides a detailed look at extreme weather events impacting Africa in 2022 (see Figure 4 below).
Figure 4: Extreme Weather Events in Africa, 202238
The energy access-climate-rural poverty context
Today’s climate change impacts are felt most acutely in developing economies. In sub-Saharan Africa,
where 70% of the world’s LDCs are located, climate hazards such as floods, rising temperatures, aridity
and droughts, storms, among others, are real and present threats to lives and livelihoods, inflicting tangible
35 https://unfccc.int/topics/resilience/resources/climate-related-risks-and-extreme-events
36 https://www.preventionweb.net/news/analysis-africas-unreported-extreme-weather-2022-and-climate-change
37 https://www.ctvnews.ca/climate-and-environment/africa-needs-better-weather-warning-systems-urge-experts-1.5934651
38 https://www.preventionweb.net/news/analysis-africas-unreported-extreme-weather-2022-and-climate-change data from

collateral damage and physical risks to infrastructure investments, water and food systems, public health
and agriculture.39 The economies and livelihoods of most sub-Saharan African nations are driven by rain-
fed agriculture and pastoralism. FAO reported that agriculture alone provided jobs for almost 50% of the
total labor force of these countries.40
At the same time, rural poverty is widespread in the target countries of H2R, and considerably exceeds the
rate of urban poverty (see Figure 5 below). As mentioned, all H2R countries are LDCs with a high
incidence of both poverty and climate vulnerability among the millions of smallholder farmers and the
communities that dwell in rural, often informal, settlements with low access to the basic services
sometimes available in cities. In addition, as the Global Center for Adaptation (GCA) ‘State and Trends in
Adaptation Report 2021’ notes, large swathes of Africa, and especially the drylands areas that cover 60
percent of the continent, are warming at a rate twice the global average, putting half a billion people at
risk.41
Rural poverty is also exacerbated by the lack of access to basic services provided by electricity. This
explains why spatial and temporal variations in rainfall and recurrent drought episodes have severe
impacts on the livelihood of people living throughout the continent.42

Up until now the continent has seen adaptation interventions that are primarily reactive rather than
proactive, such as efforts focused on disaster relief or reconstruction and recovery following severe floods
or a pandemic. The Africa-Led Consultative Dialogue Report on adaptation highlights the complementary
need for a hazard and risk-oriented approach to adaptation, which considers it holistically across factors
such as vulnerability, exposure, and adaptive capacity. The risk approach to adaptation can potentially
“enable preparedness to not just address the climate risks but also the various shocks such as natural
disasters…that are either exacerbated by climate change or exacerbate climatic impacts.“44
The GAC 2021 report points to new research which considers interlinkages between climate, conflict and
energy.45 In the face of increasing climate stressors, there is the risk that certain energy systems are
potentially maladaptive and could play a contributory role in increasing the risk of conflict. The disruption of
energy flows at the local, national, regional and global scale can increase the risk of conflict, and energy
sources can also become the target of sabotage or attacks, particularly by non-state armed groups.
Additionally, there is a close link between energy and food security. Restricted energy access and
increased energy prices can have significant impacts on overall food security, contributing to drivers of
conflict. Though the research in this area is nascent, it points to the need to develop energy systems that
are the most resilient and least vulnerable to the physical and human dimensions of climate risk. By many
of these adaptation-based criteria, the case for decentralized solar power, particularly residential solar, as
a prominent part of the electricity mix, has become a compelling one.
44 ARIN & UKRI Adaptation Research in Africa: Progress and Gaps Insights from the COP26 Africa-Led Consultative
Workshops (2021)
45 Ibid.

The ultimate measure of the effects of energy access on climate resilience will be the extent to which off-
grid residential solar electrification can be associated with reducing sensitivity and exposure, and
increasing adaptive capacity during adverse effects of shocks and stresses related to climate (see Figure
2). Some examples of this impact pathway can be seen in Table 3 below. Energy access which, for
example, supports early warning systems can prevent human and economic losses in case of extreme
events, while extending rural electrification can enable adaptation and mitigate climate vulnerability. If
based on a diversified and decentralized network of energy sources, it can reduce the vulnerability of
energy supply.46 As a review of NAPs and NDCs highlights47, low levels of energy access are considered
to reduce resilience, while measures to increase resilience and adaptability are often leading to higher
energy needs, risking increased emissions. It is therefore important for energy access measures to
capitalize on the opportunities of energy transition. For example, modern energy access in drylands
reduces reliance on biomass fuels, leading to less wood extraction and charcoal use - which currently
exceeds tree production, and increases resilience against the climactic trend of soil depletion and tree loss
(roughly three million hectares of forest are lost annually48). At the same time, lack of reliable access
affects the ability of people to access important health, or early warning information in the context of
disaster preparedness - both of these are areas highlighted for improvements in NDCs and NAPs49, but the
impact of this improvement will be limited without basic access. Per capita energy consumption is also
strongly correlated to economic output. At higher levels of energy consumption and through productive
uses of energy, we observe how clean energy can power adaptation through value-added agro-systems
that unlock socioeconomic opportunities.50 Adaptation impacts are also unlocked when we understand and
capture the potential synergistic links among actions and technologies, for example household entry-level
energy access alongside mobile telecommunications, TV or radio to enable early hazard warning.
Socio-economic development is one of the foremost strategies to reduce community vulnerability,51 and
access to clean energy is a cornerstone of sustainable socio-economic development. Energy access as a
whole is thus linked to community climate resilience and adaptation, and OGS have an important role to
play in providing the stepping stone towards wider access. Therefore, delivering enhanced, even basic
energy access has the potential to unlock a wide range of adaptation-linked socio-economic development
outcomes that drive resilience of the population.52 53 54 55
At a practical level, lighting, cooking, heating, cooling, communication and information access services are
derived from energy. A community’s basic needs, economic activities and institutions (schools, health
centers, government buildings) are substantially enhanced through access to these energy services. For
these reasons, long-term access to reliable energy builds self-resilience and adaptive capacity within

households and local communities. Specific benefits of enhanced access include (see also Table 3 for
examples):
● Enhancing energy, food and water security by improving self-reliance in the face of increasing
climate-induced risks;
● Providing easier and lower-cost access to information and digital services which may enhance
disaster planning and response to climate-driven events such as EWE;
● Improving the health of households and communities by e.g. enabling access to health-information,
providing clean lighting without accompanying indoor air quality degradation, thus reducing climate-
induced health risks (e.g. vector borne diseases) while utilizing mitigation measures to improve
health and living standards;
● Diversifying jobs, particularly for women who can expand their opportunities as a result of time-
saving achieved through greater household productivity, thus increasing their resilience to slow-
onset climate events; and
● Diversifying livelihoods and the local economy by boosting incomes, savings, and productivity of
households and enterprises, also increasing their resilience to slow-onset events.
There is also a moderately strong link between rural poverty and access to electricity, with a correlation
factor of 0.74.56 While there are some countries that see lower levels of rural poverty on the MPI index,
there is a clear clustering around combined high levels of rural MPI and low levels of rural electricity
access, as shown in Figure 6 below.

Emissions Context
Sub-Saharan Africa currently accounts for less than 4% of cumulative historical global greenhouse gas
(GHG) emissions.76 However, the region’s economies and populations are growing rapidly and emissions
have been rising steadily. Between 1950 to 2016, Africa’s CO2 emissions increased by a factor of 14.
Today, Africa is home to 1.3 billion people; this number is projected to grow to 3 billion by 2060.77 More
than half of today’s population currently has no access to electricity. For a significant share of peri-urban
and rural households, access to electricity services is made possible through local kiosks which provide
cell phone charging, refrigeration and other electricity-driven services. In off-grid areas, these kiosks and
other local infrastructure such as clinics are primarily supplied by diesel generators or hybrid mini-grids and
people’s periodic access to these service points constrains their electricity usage. As a result, off-grid
communities are experiencing suppressed energy demand, and current household energy consumption
does not reflect the real demand for energy services.
Due to the low base of current energy use on the continent, and particularly in H2R program countries, and
the rapidly growing and youthful populations, the continent’s future energy trajectory has real implications
for global net zero targets and the safety of our planet. In one scenario, an African transition out of energy
poverty that relies on fossil fuels, could result in increased CO2 emissions that would offset a 20 percent
cut in the emissions of China, the United States, India, Russia, Japan, and Germany combined.78
Currently, the majority of rural households rely on emission-intensive kerosene and biomass as their
primary energy source for lighting, cooking, heating etc.79 Across the region, the percentage of total wood
harvested used as fuelwood varies from 90% in Africa, 62% in Asia, 50% in South America to less than
20% in Europe, North America and Oceania.80 Under current projections, electrification can play a role in
alleviating the pressure on native forests, while also reducing the share of agriculture, forestry and land

77 Wilson Center, The Battle for Earth's Climate Will Be Fought in Africa (2021)
78 Wilson Center, The Battle for Earth's Climate Will Be Fought in Africa (2021)
79 World Health Organization Household air pollution fact sheet (2022)
80 IPCC Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Uses (AFOLU) (2022)

use (AFOLU) activities in the region's emissions of dangerous greenhouse gasses such as methane (CH4)
and nitrous oxide.81 Currently, sub-Saharan Africa’s AFOLU activities account for 60% of CH4 emissions.82
To mitigate and adapt to an increasingly warming planet, it is critical that all countries transition to
renewable energy willand, even where energy consumption is currently low, embark on clean energy
pathways. The energy pathways and resource dependencies developed across the continent today will
have profound climate impacts in the medium and long term. Data shows that developing economies
(excluding China) now account for roughly 45% of carbon emissions and will propel almost all the growth
going forward.83 Providing first-time electricity access via a low carbon trajectory avoids approximately 268
million tonnes of CO eq emissions, with a technology mix that is 45% decentralized renewables.84
2
54 countries in Africa signed the Paris Agreement and submitted ambitious Nationally Determined
Contributions (NDCs). Most African NDCs incorporated two targets: an unconditional target that was
designed to be met by African countries with their own resources (about 15%), and a conditional target,
subject to financial support from the international community (about 85%). Each country’s specific NDC
adaptation and emission targets as well as climate policies have been assessed and documented in the
accompanying country reports. Acumen’s objectives through Hardest-to-Reach are directly aligned to
National climate priorities, including National Adaptation Plans, National Climate Change Action Plans, and
NDC’s (see Section D.5).
Complementarity & Coherence
B.2 (a). Theory of change narrative and diagram (max. 1500 words, approximately 3 pages plus
diagram)
Present the theory of change (ToC) that contains a goal statement and describes how the proposed project/programme will
contribute towards the goal statement by using results chain links from activities, outputs, to outcomes. By referring to the sample
ToC diagram template available in the guidance note, present a ToC diagram (approximately 1 page) which visually represents the
same logic in the narrative description. The ToC diagram and narrative may include a wide range of co-benefits85 as applicable in
the context of the project/programme.
Note all co-benefits will need to be further elaborated in section D.3 (sustainable development potential) and correspondent co-
benefit indicators should be provided under section E.5 (project/programme specific indicators).
The theory of change should also include any relevant barriers (social, gender, fiscal, regulatory, technological, financial,
ecological, institutional, etc.) that need to be addressed as well as risks and assumptions. Note that the assumptions can be
elaborated further in sections E.3 (GCF outcome level: reduced emissions and increased resilience) and E.5 (project/programme
specific indicators) for each relevant indicator, as appropriate.

Theory of Change Narrative |  | 

=== PAGE 39 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 35
B
In 2020, 733 million people were still living without access to (affordable, clean) electricity, of which 298
million people were in nascent off-grid solar (OGS) markets where there is little commercial OGS activity.86
Approximately 70% of this number have the ability to pay but live in areas deemed too remote or too risky
to be served by traditional grid extensions and business as usual approaches in these markets. However, if
the appropriate investment capital and technical assistance is provided to OGS companies, then they will
likely be able to deliver clean energy access and adaptive capacity to low-income, underserved people and
build sustainable markets. This will happen because they will be adequately incentivized and capacitated,
through an enabling environment, to operate and grow in currently untested, ‘Hardest-to-Reach’ (H2R)
areas.
There are however multiple barriers that prevent access to alternative forms of energy access, such as
OGS. There is a funding gap, as the OGS market for the most deprived customers is considered highly
risky, with the potential customers often the poorest populations in a country, and there are few track
records due to market fragmentation. OGS companies themselves struggle to grow, or even survive, due
to a lack of internal capacity and inability to access finance. Markets are often either unregulated, or the
regulation is not appropriate for the types of products on offer. Taken together, these barriers lead to a lack
of access to capital, in turn leading to OGS companies being underfunded, and to markets stagnating,
rather than growing rapidly in response to the clear needs of the rural populations where energy access is
lowest.
The Hardest-to-Reach energy access initiative aims to deliver energy access to 72.4M low-income
customers in least developed and climate-vulnerable countries in sub-Saharan Africa, 54.3M of whom will
be accessing energy for the first time. It will do so by engaging with stakeholders, including financing
partners, governments and donors, to establish two new funds, H2R MSF and H2R MEF, which will
provide early-stage and scaled-up funding to OGS companies. The engagement will also seek to lower
barriers where these relate to e.g. regulation or a lack of shared knowledge. H2R MSF/MEF will then
provide impact-linked capital and technical assistance to incentivize off-grid solar companies (OGS) to
expand into new, under-reached markets, to build sustainable business platforms and to scale up, and for
new OGS to be established. Investee OGS companies can then provide more off-grid solar energy
products such as solar home systems to low-income customers via Pay-as-you-go mechanisms, providing
many people with first-time access to modern energy.
H2R will be focused on learning how our interventions are able to drive impact at the household, enterprise
and market level through a range of different measurement techniques, including feedback from customers
(project beneficiaries) through lean data surveys. Furthermore, we will aim to disseminate the learnings to
all stakeholders.The sharing of knowledge will be supported through our partnerships with industry,
government, civil society and private sector, creating the long-lasting impact of a demonstration effect and
the blueprint for other investors to follow.
Hardest-to-Reach focuses on creating impact at the sector, enterprise and household levels in fledgling
markets, and thus will seek to deliver a number of outputs by scaling the OGS markets in the participating
countries:
86 GOGLA Market Trends Report: State of the Sector (2022)

=== PAGE 40 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 36
B
● Through the establishment of H2R MSF/MEF achieve greater provision of climate-resilient clean
energy and greater installed renewable energy capacity across energy sectors of participating
countries;
● Through engagement at AE/EE level deliver new partnerships to enable last-mile energy access for
the poorest;
● Support the creation/growth of new and fledgling OGS businesses through H2R MSF finance and
support to allow them to become sustainable, inclusive, and investable, and providing clean energy
access to low-income people in hard-to-reach areas;
● Enable the scaling up of existing OGS businesses through H2R MEF finance and support to allow
them to reach new clients to whom they can provide clean energy access to low-income people in
hard-to-reach areas;
● Achieve sales of OGS systems to 13.3M households, benefiting 72.4M people;
● Deliver 120 MW of new renewable energy capacity.
Taken together, these outputs will seek to deliver substantial adaptation, mitigation and enabling
environment outcomes, specifically:
● The advancement of the OGS sector in hardest-to-reach countries
● The establishment and growth of OGS companies in sustainable and gender- and poverty-inclusive
ways in H2R countries;
● Creation of new jobs in the green economy, including employment women;
● OGS customers and their households benefit from enhanced energy security;
● OGS customers and their households are able to more securely access information including
extreme weather event and health warnings, health information, and market data for e.g.
agricultural produce;
● OGS customers and their households benefit from reduced harmful emissions from fossil fuels
through reductions in indoor air pollution;
● OGS customers and their households benefit from increased and/or diversified income sources;
● Emissions of 5.1MtCO2eq over the lifetime of the fund are avoided.
Beyond adaptation and resilience benefits, H2R plans to deliver mitigation benefits. By reducing the need
to rely on kerosene and other dirty fuels for lighting, through the provision of renewable energy
technologies, the programme is expected to reduce over 5MtCo2 over its lifetime, about equal to the total
annual fossil-fuel driven emissions of Burkina Faso in 202287.

Sector-level: Advancement of the OGS section in H2R countries, and increasing provision of climate-
resilient, clean energy across the energy sector of Program Host Nations through market creation, blended
finance, partnerships
Challenge
There is a significant investment gap in the sector due to the perception of the high risk and low return of
underdeveloped OGS markets. Current OGS stakeholder efforts are fragmented, resulting in overlapping
and uncoordinated efforts and missed opportunities for greater impact through collaboration. The use of

=== PAGE 42 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 38
B
blended finance to crowd in climate finance is constrained in part because the industry does not yet have a
clearly defined narrative on how OGS products and services contribute to adaptation and resilience. In
addition, the scale of many proposed initiatives in this space has been too small to attract commercial
investors.
Activities and Outputs
Acumen will establish the H2R blended finance structure to crowd in investors with different risk appetites.
Acumen also will develop partnerships that convene different financiers, TA providers, policy advocates,
government, and OGS company investees in an effort to jumpstart the OGS market in H2R areas, support
the creation of an enabling environment for other investors and businesses and share knowledge within
the OGS sector. Specifically:
● Activities 1.1 and 2.1 comprise of fundraising and the establishment of the two funds that facilitates
the investments, discussions and interest in the H2R regions.
● Activity 1.2 intends to drive partnership development designed to crowd in new investors, improve
the level of knowledge sharing in the sector, coordinate the actions of various stakeholders, and
make the initiative's impact sustainable.
Furthermore, the H2R initiative encourages more investment by improving the risk-return profile and track
record of these markets. It does so by providing new market entrants with concessional finance and
targeted technical assistance, and supporting the development of local networks and capacity. It intends to
also increase the capacity of local distributors to become reliable partners to suppliers expanding in the
region, and spur inclusive market development with a range of actors.
Outcome
H2R markets are developed and scaled with greater engagement towards an improved enabling
environment and market conditions. Markets are shown to be viable, with the right approach, providing
incentives and conditions to sustainably attract OGS companies, local participants and investors
(philanthropic, development and private capital). The building blocks for OGS market advancement - such
as the creation of market intelligence studies, capacity building for off-grid solar manufacturers and local
distributors, consumer awareness efforts, policy engagement, access to finance and risk mitigation, and
consumer subsidies, where needed - are developed in H2R countries.

=== PAGE 43 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 39
B
This leads to increased capital inflows (philanthropic, development, private) and to a better-coordinated
OGS sector in H2R geographies through blended finance solutions. Investment in the OGS sector will
likely lead to clean, climate-resilient energy access for vulnerable people and increased installed capacity
across the energy sectors of Program Host Nations.
The impact of OGS on climate change (mitigation and adaptation), and demonstration effect of the
intervention, including replicable aspects, will also be better established through the generation and
sharing of expert insights and empirical evidence.
Enterprise-level: Fostering the sustainable and inclusive growth of OGS businesses
Challenge
OGS companies struggle to serve the poorest and most vulnerable in H2R areas due mainly to the lack of
flexible funding and the concentration of investment in a small number of large players, operating in a
handful of well-understood markets. Companies also have limited capacity to serve riskier customers in
new markets that lack distribution channels.
Activities and Outputs
Acumen intends to manage the Hardest-to-Reach initiative combining two facilities with $250M under
management. $50 million of market support capital is available via the philanthropically-backed Market
Support Facility, to de-risk H2R markets by building local management and distribution capacity, as well as
increasing awareness of OGS products. In addition, the Market Expansion Facility provides companies
with $200 million of impact-indexed loans, providing targeted concessional capital. This impact-linked
capital intends to also incentivize companies to retain a focus on entry-level solar products for lower-
income customers and prevent mission-drift.
The provision of TA alongside investment aims to also help companies develop capacity in the areas of
consumer protection, business development, gender and ESG. Per activity 1.3, 2.3 and 1.5, H2R
emphasizes the support (financial and via TA) of enterprises at different stages, in particular to ensure
sustainability and impact of the investments.
Outcomes

=== PAGE 44 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 40
B
As a result of the market development activities, H2R countries benefit from the sustainable and inclusive
growth of OGS businesses, able to reach and impact the Hardest-to-Reach. The H2R initiative will seek to
help new companies to enter the OGS market, help fledgling companies to grow to critical mass to be able
to survive and continue to grow, and finance existing companies to scale up sales of OGS systems.
Demonstration and validation of climate-positive business models in these challenging contexts, through
the support of the mechanisms within the Market Support Facility, allows for replication and scale of impact
achieved through the Market Expansion Facility. Strengthened local management capacity and distribution
networks dynamize the sector, encouraging participation by other players in the market, while increased
awareness of OGS solutions and positive customer experiences serve to build trust and stimulate demand.
OGS solutions become more widespread, affordable, and cost effective.
In addition, jobs are created and sustained in the clean energy economy, with a significant portion of jobs
being a source of employment for women.
Household level: Delivering 13.3M sales of off-grid solar projects and increasing the resilience and
adaptive capacity of 54.3M people in Hardest-to-Reach areas and avoidance of 5.1M tCO2.
Challenge
In H2R areas, many people are climate-vulnerable because they are located in areas that are highly
exposed to the impacts of climate change and their sources of income are tied to activities which are
weather dependent, such as agriculture, while access to basic energy services is both costly and time-
consuming, impacting on household incomes. Their incomes can therefore be intermittent and they
typically lack access to credit on reasonable terms.
Furthermore, these people are often living in unelectrified areas with no grid connection. As a result of their
low asset bases, inconsistent incomes and lack of supporting infrastructure, people in H2R areas may be
unable to adapt to the effects of climate change. The result is that many people living in H2R areas have to
rely on fossil fuels to power their day-to-day activities, such as light, charging and cooking. Fossil fuels
such as kerosene and diesel are harmful to those using them, harmful to the environment through the
carbon emitted, and are notoriously expensive and unreliable. They are also made more vulnerable by not
having assured access to communication tools to keep abreast of weather, health and market information.

=== PAGE 45 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 41
B
Finally, women and children are likely to be disproportionately affected as they often spend more time at
home with the harmful and emissions-intensive fossil fuel source which can lead to respiratory illnesses, or
with candles which can lead to fires and burns.
Activities and Outputs
All fund activities contribute to seeing impact at the household level. Critically, products and services
supplied through H2R investments intend to support household resilience/adaptation. (See B.1). Acumen
incentivizes and facilitates OGS companies to set-up, and market and sell solar energy products via
PAYGo financing to low-income people in H2R areas. This means that unelectrified people are able to
access clean energy sources, many for the first time, and are able to afford them thanks to longer-term
payment plans. Furthermore, after a payment period of 12-36 months, households should own their SHS
outright for the remaining lifetime of 24-48 months. Companies are expected to monitor impact by
collecting gender-disaggregated sales data as well as representative sampling on product accessibility,
use and benefits.
Outcomes
Clean energy pathways are created for 72.4M people in H2R areas. This leads to increased resilience and
adaptive capacity of the 54.3M beneficiaries accessing energy for the first time, including through improved
energy security, income diversification and access to climate information. Data shows that a portion of
customers will be able to diversify their sources of income, making their livelihoods more resilient to climate
change . Beneficiaries will also be able to readily access climate-related information through the use of
ICTs such as mobile phones and radios, allowing them to prepare for upcoming weather events.
Furthermore, some people should benefit from a safer home and better health due to reduced use of
lighting sources that can cause fires and burns or are harmful to respiratory health (co-benefit).
OGS use can also lead to reduced vulnerability in the context of climate change via a less climate-
vulnerable energy supply. OGS is less vulnerable to weather events than grid-connected energy sources
because they are decentralized. As the owners of a high quality OGS product, in the event of displacement
due to a climate-related natural disaster, a person and their household are more able to retain access to
electricity (with the benefit of it being clean and safe). Furthermore, OGS should take less time to repair or
replace, meaning that people with SHS are able to access energy more quickly following a weather event.
Finally, displacement of emissions-intensive lighting sources is intended to lead to 5.1M tCO2 being
avoided.

people who live in H2R countries without electricity. Using benchmarks from the GOGLA Market Trends
Report 2022, approximately 190M people in H2R countries could afford an entry level off-grid solar
connection, but are at risk of being left behind by business-as-usual market approaches to electrification.88

H2R aims to unlock first-time clean and resilient energy access for these communities. These are
challenging markets with electrification rates at-or-below the sub-Saharan Africa average (48%) where
investors have not been willing to enter to serve low-income segments. Our approach is to incentivize and
accompany companies to enter into and grow in these challenging geographies to serve underserved
segments by mobilizing capital at scale from various investor bases in off-grid solar. This approach is
based on Acumen’s deep knowledge of the energy access challenge, relationships with players in the off-
grid solar sector with an ability to scale, and the experience of deploying innovative, patient capital to
achieve impact.
H2R will target 16 sub-Saharan African countries with electrification rates of 48% or below and high
poverty rates (above 45%). Out of this total, all eligible countries are considered least developed countries
and they hold around 54 million African households that do not have access to modern electricity services.
On average, 78% of the population living in these geographies lives below the lower-middle-income
poverty line.
All 16 H2R countries are eligible countries for Acumen’s H2R program. As part of H2R preparation, in
depth country studies have been conducted across a number of H2R countries. In the first window of the
Market Support Facility (MSF), explained in more detail later, country level research has identified barriers
and guided the development of investment approaches and ensured policy alignment. Ongoing research
and engagement in these countries will help to ensure that H2R achieves complementarity and coherence
with other interventions and investments that donors, DFIs and private investors are doing.
At Acumen our approach is always to use the right kind of capital to tackle the right kind of problem. Hardest-
to-Reach expects to use a diversified approach to inject capital and technical assistance to match the needs
of off-grid energy companies at each stage of development and capacity. To build an off-grid solar market in
these challenging H2R geographies, “start-up to scale-up” or “whole-of-life cycle” financing is needed to
support entrepreneurs to set up in these markets and then scale up their operations, and thereby achieve
their impact. This is why Acumen is structuring two independent financing mechanisms, tailored to the
different stages of operators’ evolution and the different risk appetites of investors.
Components, outcomes, and underlying activities within Hardest-to-Reach.

=== PAGE 50 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 46
B
Component 1: Sustainable Market Creation in H2R countries (Market Support Facility)
A philanthropically-backed Market Support Facility aims to support the development of local players and
regional companies’ expansion into these new challenging markets. This $50 million facility is expected to
support companies with the flexibility to set up operations through grants, equity and debt, and the technical
assistance to enter and navigate unfamiliar territory of high risk countries. The MSF is specifically designed
to provide the right type of financing and accompaniment to enable companies to enter new markets. Set-
up grants are expected to be provided to companies to address the high costs associated with expansion
activities. Equity/equity-like capital, such as convertible notes, simple agreements for future equity (SAFEs)
and recoverable grants, enables companies to innovate and scale up their operations. Concessional debt
lowers the cost of operating in H2R markets compared to business-as-usual. Technical assistance aims to
help reduce the real and perceived risks of entering new markets and build the capacity of companies in key
areas such as management and strategy, credit risk analysis, consumer protection, gender equity and
market studies. The facility aims to also improve the capacity of local distributors to become reliable partners
to suppliers expanding in the region to build a local ecosystem for off-grid solar markets.
Component 2: Sustainable Market Expansion in H2R countries (Market Expansion Facility)
A subsequent blended finance-backed $200 million Market Expansion Facility aims to provide impact-linked
concessionary loans to scale up companies’ operations and settle in H2R countries. A blended finance
structure helps mobilize different types of investors with different risk appetites for the same purpose. The
primary instrument used in the Market Expansion Facility is expected to be impact-indexed loans, an
innovative RBF approach, where we intend to determine interest rates based on the impacts achieved in
terms of first-time energy access and poverty level of the customers. The interest rates should range between
a market rate and a zero percent, depending on the impact performance. The impact-linked incentives are
designed to motivate the companies to provide first-time energy access to low-income customers and
minimize the level of concessionality to the required level for delivering specific impacts. The objective of this
approach is to integrate the impact into our financing structure, therefore into companies’ operations, which
will likely allow us to adapt, strengthen and maximize impacts along the way. Certain KPIs will also be used
to ensure companies manage their growth sustainably and inclusively, disincentivizing sales growth at the
cost of portfolio quality, for example.
MEF also seeks to invest in accounts receivable facilities, which should allow OGS companies to finance
themselves rather than rely on third party investors, making them self-sustaining. Fundraising for the MEF is
ongoing. We are not aware of any investors proposing exclusions or restrictions on their use of proceeds.
Our intention is to deploy loans only to the borrowers for operations in NOL countries. Assuming there are
no exclusions, our intention is to have a single set of criteria when selecting borrowers, and that all investors
will receive returns on loans pro rata to their contributions to MEF. We also seek to ensure that all MEF
investors will participate in each financing transaction entered into by MEF pro rata to their commitments to
MEF.
See sections C.1 and C.2 for a summary of MSF/MEF breakdown by financing source and component.

will then sell off-grid solar products to customers, many of whom will be accessing energy for the first time.

activate and support the development of these H2R OGS markets. By defining these market activating
“tipping points” and demonstrating our impact, we hope to create a blueprint for other impact investors
seeking to make market level changes.

Outcome 2: Establishment and Growth of OGS companies in sustainable and gender- and poverty-
inclusive ways
H2R seeds new ventures and backs existing players in challenging markets, supporting the establishment
and growth of these nascent ventures and markets through partnerships and productive engagements with
government and non-government stakeholders. New sales of OGS products help provide first-time
connections and electrification through clean energy technologies. By supporting stronger and more viable
businesses, creating a local investment history, and incentivizing impact, we hope to create sustainable
and impactful opportunities for companies operating in or seeking to expand into H2R markets.
We seek to demonstrate that OGS companies operating in Hardest-to-Reach markets can build climate
resilient, sustainable, and inclusive businesses with technical assistance. H2R companies will receive
technical assistance across consumer protection, gender, ESG, and enterprise development activities.
Consumer protection activities focus on enhancing consumer protection policies, procedures, and sales
strategies for companies, and monitoring portfolio quality to manage credit risk and consumer protections.
On gender, gender experts will support companies in developing and executing gender action plans,
improving gender policies, and collecting sex disaggregated data. Additionally, technical assistance funds
will be assigned to be used to improve gender equity in the OGS market by training women workers and
raising female customer awareness of OGS products. ESG and climate TA focuses on ESG action plans
for companies, support companies on enhancing e-waste policies and procedures, and building climate
and ESG resources for OGS companies. Enterprise development work focuses on making companies
more investable, supporting talent retention, improving operations, building customer and market
knowledge, and supporting financially distressed companies. We expect companies to more strongly
protect customers and mitigate credit risk, identify and engage with ESG risks, build more equitable and
empowering workplaces and customer experiences, and develop and manage stronger, more talented and
investable OGS companies because of targeted technical support.
Outcome 3: OGS customers (and their households) benefit from enhanced energy security
OGS products reduce the vulnerability of people’s energy supply to climate change. OGS is less
vulnerable to climate-change-related weather phenomena than grid-connected energy sources because
they are decentralized. Furthermore, OGS should take less time to repair or replace, meaning that people
with SHS are able to access energy more quickly following a weather event.

MSF Structure
- MSF is intended to raise grant and repayable grant capital to build capacity for entities to establish
and bolster a market for clean energy access for individuals in least developed countries. Target size is
$50 million, of which a majority has already been raised and for which several pilots are in planning.
- GCF is requested to provide $10 million in the form of a partially repayable grant for MSF. Such
repayable grant shall be used for all activities of the MSF, including expenses, grants and investments; of
such GCF funding toward grants and investments is hereinafter referred to as “GCF Investment Proceeds”.
-
- MSF is expected to provide technical assistance grants and potentially recoverable
grants/convertible notes/equity, engage in joint ventures and provide impact indexed loans to incentivize
established solar home systems manufacturers and distributors to enter LDC markets, and to bolster
existing distributors in LDCs.
- Any joint ventures are expected to contain mechanisms for ownership to transfer to the counterparty
once the ventures are financially self-sustaining.
Joint venture agreements may incorporate grants to cover set up and other initial costs.
- The operations of MSF are overseen by a management committee consisting of the Chief of
Strategic Initiatives, Chief Financial Officer and General Counsel of the AE. The management committee
seeks to ensure that the operations of the MSF are compliant with GCF requirements, applicable laws,
regulations and policies. Grants and investments made by MSF are subject to review and approval of the
global Investment Committee of the AE
- Members of the AE that will operationalize the MSF include the General Counsel, the Chief Strategic
Officer, the Chief Financial Officer, a Director, an Associate Director, and the Legal Counsel of the AE.
- MSF is expected to build capacity within entities to be a viable pipeline for MEF borrowers. MSF will
take the risk during the development stage of LDC operations for these potential borrowers with its high
risk grant and repayable grant capital, reducing the risk for MEF.
- MSF expects to have an investment period of 7 years.
-

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 61
B
MEF Structure
- MEF is intended to bring together senior, mezzanine and junior equity capital to incentivize
investors with different risk profiles to provide clean energy access for individuals living off-grid in
the least developed countries. MEF also intends to raise grant capital to enable further interest rate
adjustments payable by borrowers as a reward for first-time energy access, among other metrics,
which grant capital is intended to be swept to the operating account of MEF and made available for
fees, expenses and deployment, as an offset for such adjustments.
- MEF is designed to make loans for working capital to borrowers providing clean energy
access in H2R countries, with incentives to borrowers to enable first time clean energy access for
their customers, with interest rate adjustments to the extent of such access.
- MEF is expected to use performance incentives within the loan structure to incentivize
businesses to achieve specific impact targets, in the form of interest rate adjustments to the extent
of achieving impact, to essentially provide a partial offset to interest.
- Borrowers may receive impact adjustments based on certain predetermined metrics. Such
metrics will be collected and analyzed annually (using 3rd party verification of certain metrics, such
as lean data studies), and result in an impact index score that will be aligned with an interest
adjustment.
- In addition to impact adjusted loans, the MEF expects to lend to accounts receivable
financing facilities, to support cash and inventory management of OGS companies operating in our
target geographies. Current facilities under review have 4 year terms.
- Target MEF size is $200 million, with indicative allocations across layers as follows: senior –
$60 million; mezzanine – $60 million; junior – $60 million; and grant – $20 million. This proposal
requests GCF to provide $50 million for junior equity and $5 million for non-repayable grant capital.
-
- The above structure is designed to incentivize capital with different risk tolerance, noting that
mission oriented and concessionary capital is expected to provide the mezzanine, junior and grant capital,
while more commercially oriented capital is expected to provide senior capital.
- MEF is expected to have a 7 year investment period, which may be extended for up to two one-year
periods
- Investment decisions for MEF will be made by an investment committee designated by the GP
- MSF is expected to provide pipeline borrowers to MEF. To mitigate conflicts of interest that may be
perceived to bias MEF decisionmakers, 1) underwriting criteria has been developed to vet the viability of

=== PAGE 66 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 62
B
the prospective borrowers, and 2) the investment committee and LPAC will be apprised of borrowers that
have also received MSF funding for transparency and the opportunity to discuss any concerns.
- The non-reimbursable grant will flow from GCF to the AE via the FAA entered into between the AE
and GCF. The money in turn will flow to the MEF via a subsidiary agreement to be entered into between
the MEF and the AE. No additional money will flow to the borrowers; they benefit by virtue of an interest
rate adjustment, so pay less to the MEF. The MEF retains the grant capital and is able to use it for
operating purposes to the extent of the adjustment offset.
Track Record
Acumen is an AE that has three funding proposals in implementation. The first program is KawiSafi
Ventures, a venture capital fund focused on creating clean energy access in East Africa, and is at the end
of its investment period, having successfully deployed approximately $42 million in investments that as of
end of Q3 2022, impacted 110 million low income individuals and offset 24 million metric tons of carbon
dioxide and kerosene. The second program is Acumen resilient Agriculture Fund, a venture capital fund
focused on building climate resilience for smallholder farmers in West and East Africa, and is in the middle
of its investment period, having successfully deployed $20.2 million in investments that as of end of Q3
2022, impacted almost 1.6 million low income individuals. The third program is Energy Access Relief Fund,
a debt fund focused on providing concessional capital to support businesses in the solar home system
sector survive the impacts of COVID, and is in the middle of its investment period, having successfully
deployed approximately $49 million in loans. In addition, for over 20 years, Acumen has been directly
investing in small and medium-sized enterprises that serve low-income communities in developing
countries across South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Latin America, with the goal of changing the way the
world tackles poverty. As of the end of 2021, Acumen had deployed approximately $146 million into 151
companies, impacting approximately 443 million lives. A significant sector of focus for Acumen has been
the off-grid energy sector, and Acumen contributes to many sectoral initiatives, including with GOGLA.
Capacity Assessment
Manager, as executing entity, is expected to be a wholly owned subsidiary of Acumen. Such an entity will
be formed with policies and procedures directed by the AE, and with staff screened for experience in debt
investing, the OGS sector and our target host country markets. We are in discussions with certain service
providers to potentially engage for discrete functions, such as back office and support in risk assessments,
but not to be decision makers for the Manager or MEF.

Why H2R needs GCF
Addressing the unelectrified populations requires affordable solutions, which themselves require
affordable, abundant capital. Yet the perceived risk and small size of these markets means that capital
there is both scarce and expensive. Blended finance, anchored by the most influential concessional
investor focused on climate change adaptation (GCF) is the only way to overcome this impasse and bring
energy to people who are vulnerable to climate change.
GCF’s involvement in this project is critical. GCF’s concessional capital will play a catalytic role to mobilize
capital at scale and channel it toward serving low income and climate vulnerable customers in LDCs.
Public and private capital directed to the energy access sector has been concentrated in a few lower-risk
markets in Africa and has avoided the regions with the lowest electrification rates. Between 2012 and
2019, western, central and southern Africa accounted for 71 percent of SSA’s unelectrified population, yet
received just 24 percent of cumulative off-grid solar investment.91 Research shows that even when
investment dollars are directed to low-income regions, they are not always directed where the need is
greatest. Most investors only operate in markets that are lower risk or proven to yield financial returns. For
this reason, progress has been contained to a few investor-ready countries.
According to IEA research, the affordability of clean energy transitions will depend on reducing the cost
and improving the availability of capital.92 Addressing the remaining unelectrified population demands a
