=== PAGE 68 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 64
B
shift towards more challenging market environments and thus keeping financing costs low will be vital to
enabling clean energy transitions while keeping them inclusive and affordable. However, capital is
substantially more costly in emerging and developing economies than in advanced economies. Nominal
financing costs are up to seven times higher than in the United States and Europe, with higher levels in
riskier segments.93 This points to a relatively high bar for projects to raise debt finance and offer sufficient
returns on equity.
OGS companies have therefore not been able to expand into these riskier markets, because their cost of
financing is too high, financing doesn’t exist, or they don’t have the capacity to expand into nascent
markets. Sales of off-grid solar products are very low or non-existent in many of these geographies, even
though the technology has been proven as an effective means of providing energy access for low-income
communities. For example, OGS sales in Burundi over the last 3 years were less than 0.1 percent of total
sales in East Africa across the same period. Furthermore, sales growth in Sierra Leone over the last 3
years has been four times lower than the average across West Africa. What’s more, sales of OGS
products in DRC over the last 3 years were 1.6 percent of the total SSA sales, despite the country making
up over 8 percent of the population of sub-Saharan Africa. The business-as-usual approach is not serving
low-income communities in Hardest-to-Reach geographies, even though they have a significant need for
energy access.
The GCF will enable H2R initiatives to channel much needed financing and technical assistance to OGS
companies to support them to enter riskier markets and grow sustainably. The concessional component
provided by GCF is vital because it means that Acumen can issue financing with lower interest rates and
longer tenors. Companies will therefore be able to access affordable capital and should not suffer from
over-indebtedness. Furthermore, they will be able to pass the concessionality onto customers in the form
of cheaper products. Without a concessional component, OGS companies would have to charge
potentially prohibitively high prices to their customers, many of whom will be earning below $3.20 a day. If
this were to happen, the H2R initiative would not be able to have an impact on the people who need
energy access most.
GCF’s financing package
H2R is creating a paradigm shift in African energy markets by unlocking finance from investors that would
otherwise find these markets too risky. GCF’s catalytic capital will be vital in providing companies with
concessional financing and mobilizing different types of investors with different risk appetites at scale to
tackle the aforementioned problem. Each type of financing will likely provide unique benefits:
● Reimbursable grant: GCF’s $10 million reimbursable grant to MSF, together with a target $40
million grant from other partners, is needed for the Market Support Facility to help develop markets
that are currently too underdeveloped or risky for most investors to enter. This concessional
93 IEA Financing clean energy transitions in emerging and developing economies (2021)

=== PAGE 69 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 65
B
financing will allow Acumen to provide a range of financial instruments to meet the needs of
companies entering risky markets, including start-up grants and technical assistance.
● Junior equity: GCF’s $50 million investment of junior equity, along with a target $10 junior equity
from other financiers, is needed to create the Market Expansion Facility’s blended finance structure,
which is designed to mobilize an additional target $120 million from investors with different risk
appetites at scale. GCF’s risk-taking capital in this structure will seek to mobilize financing from
private sector investors, thereby crowding mainstream investors into a market that has mostly
received financing from foundations, risk-supportive DFIs and impact-focused investors. This will
allow the H2R initiative to reach significant scale and maximize its impact.
● Grant: GCF’s $5m in grant funding will be used to provide performance incentives to investee
companies based on the performance of impact targets particularly targeting low-income customers
with first-time energy access - sustainably and inclusively.
The 1:1:1 structure is intended to match the risk appetite of the investors with the incentive needed by
companies to expand into H2R markets. Concessional financing is needed by companies to go to hardest-
to-reach markets and thus the cost of capital has to be low enough to incentivize the companies to do so.
At the same time Acumen would like to attract private investors into the sector. This tiered structure
provides a de-facto guarantee for senior investors, despite high risk, low return investments.
Without GCF’s $10 million repayable grant to MSF, this intervention would not be able to innovate and
bolster the LDC markets in which H2R seeks to operate. Without GCF’s $55 million anchor investment in
the Market Expansion Facility, Hardest-to-Reach would not be able to crowd in other investors and would
not be able to reach sufficient scale to have a significant impact in the region. With GCF’s investment,
Hardest-to-Reach aims to shift the paradigm and develop a new frontier for energy investment by creating
new markets that have the potential to thrive beyond the lifetime of the initiative.
What GCF brings to H2R
The GCF is the world’s largest dedicated climate fund, and as such brings significant credibility to the
Hardest-to-Reach initiative. In addition to the direct investment into the initiative, GCF’s involvement will
have the following benefits:
● Provide a framework for mobilizing support from relevant governments, with nationally designated
authorities as touch points for continued engagement and alignment
● Mobilize investors by enhancing both the risk profile and reputability of the H2R initiative
● Enhance stakeholder engagement with the initiative through its dedication to country ownership
● Strengthen the climate rationale of the initiative through its robust investment criteria and integrated
results management framework
● Have strong signaling effects to the market of the importance of energy access in increasing the
adaptive capacity of beneficiaries
Uniqueness of H2R

=== PAGE 70 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 66
B
There are a handful of other funds and facilities that invest in energy access in SSA, such as the Energy
Access Fund, Access to Clean Power Fund, Facility for Energy Inclusion Off-Grid Energy Access Fund,
and Africa Go Green Fund . However, none of these funds have a specific objective to support off-grid
solar energy companies’ expansion into riskier, hardest-to-reach markets with low electrification rates.
Hardest-to-Reach plugs that funding gap by delivering capital to the markets most often overlooked by
investors.
H2R is also unique in its two-stage approach. Through the Market Support Facility, H2R can provide a
flexible blend of capital to meet companies’ financing needs in these riskier markets. This includes grants
for companies to cover the start-up costs of expanding into a new market, which is a differentiating feature.
Through the Market Expansion Facility, H2R expects to provide impact-linked debt that incentivizes a focus
on sales to first-time energy access customers. This distinguishes H2R’s approach from others as
particularly high-impact. H2R intends to furthermore provide TA support to companies as needed through
both facilities in order to build capacity and strengthen markets for the long term.
B.6. Exit strategy (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
Explain how the project/programme will successfully exit once implementation is completed, including how results and benefits will
continue beyond the project/programme period and how the contribution to paradigm shift will be maintained.
Include information pertaining to the longer-term ownership, project/programme exit strategy, operations and maintenance of
investments (e.g. key infrastructure, assets, contractual arrangements). In case of private sector, please describe the GCF’s
financial exit strategy through Initial Public Offerings, trade sales, etc.
Provide information on additional actions to be undertaken by public and private sector or civil society as part of the
project/programme to ensure sustainability of the results attained.
By investing in nascent off-grid markets with few to no examples of off-grid solar players operating at scale,
the Hardest-to-Reach initiative seeks to be a pioneer in untested markets, making operating companies
more attractive to other investors and more sustainable beyond the life of the initiative. H2R will seek to
achieve a paradigm shift by building OGS company capacity and scale through technical assistance and
investment, demonstrating the viability of these markets and replicability of the investment approach, and
ensuring the long-term interest of beneficiaries, companies, investors, and the public sector.
Sustainability
The initiative intends to provide investees with targeted accompaniment in the areas of consumer
protection, enterprise development, gender and ESG. Technical assistance supports capacity building, can
act as a risk management approach, and should enable companies to embed best practices that sustain
responsible growth over the long term. Additionally, in order to develop a sustainable off-grid solar market
in underserved geographies, H2R aims to boost the capacity of local distributors and companies and help
establish local distribution networks.. H2R aims to source and invest in eligible local entities, with the
objective being to ensure that local businesses also receive the concessionary capital and the technical
assistance needed to operate in high-risk markets. By providing accompaniment to companies and local

both facilities in order to build capacity and strengthen markets for the long term. |  | 
 |  | 
 | B.6. Exit strategy (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page) | 
 |  | 
Explain how the project/programme will successfully exit once implementation is completed, including how results and benefits will
continue beyond the project/programme period and how the contribution to paradigm shift will be maintained.
Include information pertaining to the longer-term ownership, project/programme exit strategy, operations and maintenance of
investments (e.g. key infrastructure, assets, contractual arrangements). In case of private sector, please describe the GCF’s
financial exit strategy through Initial Public Offerings, trade sales, etc.
Provide information on additional actions to be undertaken by public and private sector or civil society as part of the
project/programme to ensure sustainability of the results attained.
By investing in nascent off-grid markets with few to no examples of off-grid solar players operating at scale,
the Hardest-to-Reach initiative seeks to be a pioneer in untested markets, making operating companies
more attractive to other investors and more sustainable beyond the life of the initiative. H2R will seek to
achieve a paradigm shift by building OGS company capacity and scale through technical assistance and
investment, demonstrating the viability of these markets and replicability of the investment approach, and
ensuring the long-term interest of beneficiaries, companies, investors, and the public sector.
Sustainability
The initiative intends to provide investees with targeted accompaniment in the areas of consumer
protection, enterprise development, gender and ESG. Technical assistance supports capacity building, can
act as a risk management approach, and should enable companies to embed best practices that sustain
responsible growth over the long term. Additionally, in order to develop a sustainable off-grid solar market
in underserved geographies, H2R aims to boost the capacity of local distributors and companies and help
establish local distribution networks.. H2R aims to source and invest in eligible local entities, with the
objective being to ensure that local businesses also receive the concessionary capital and the technical
assistance needed to operate in high-risk markets. By providing accompaniment to companies and local |  | 

=== PAGE 71 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 67
B
distributors, the initiative aims to develop robust off-grid solar sectors in key H2R countries, which will
enable markets to self-sustain their growth and become more attractive to investors.
Replicability
The proposed approach has replicability in-built. Two separate financing facilities are proposed with
different investment risk profiles, and will invest with different capital blends to match the needs of the
company and market, as scale is achieved. The Market Support Facility (MSF) expects to extend debt,
equity/equity-like capital, and grants using a patient capital approach that is consistent with Acumen’s core
investment experience. While the MSF seeks to prove an approach in a new market with a range of
capital, the Market Expansion Facility (MEF) deploys impact-linked debt that aim to help responsibly
expand the reach of investees in the long-term. As H2R will share lessons-learned and insights widely,
successful expansions into new markets can be replicated by that company in another eligible geography
or the playbook can be copied by another investor. For example, other investors can apply impact-indexed
loans to target incentives or utilize flexible patient capital to support companies in the so-called ‘pioneer
gap’ - the stage of enterprise development where businesses face real challenges raising capital to
validate and prepare their business models for growth and build out the systems and infrastructure that are
expected to enable them to scale effectively and responsibly.

=== PAGE 72 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 68
B
Demonstration effect
High-risk investments made via the Market Support Facility provide the right balance of incentives and
support to help companies weather the first-mover disadvantage, educate customers, test market and
product approaches, and ultimately demonstrate the viability of these markets. By sharing insights and
results from the initiative, valuable lessons can be passed on to other investors and OGS enterprises. The
demonstration effect is key to unlocking other investments from broader sources of capital and sustaining
the growth of these markets in the long term.
Policy alignment
Investments at the operational level will be aligned with long-term national policy, such as integrated energy
planning and rural electrification strategies, to meet the needs of the recipient and prevent avoidable
competing interests and inefficiencies, which are a threat to business sustainability. Section D5 specifies the
context and policies of countries relevant to the initiative. These complementary efforts will help to ensure
long-term interest in the project. The broader enabling environment is also critical to reducing market barriers
and ensuring the long-term viability and attractiveness of Hardest-to-Reach markets and companies. By
ensuring policy alignment, investees may also benefit from lowered duties and taxes, and the sharing of

=== PAGE 73 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 69
B
public data, among other benefits, to cut the cost and timeline of business set-up and improve the accuracy
of customer targeting. In addition, reporting and engagement with government entities will give us
opportunities to share how they can support this work. Furthermore, H2R intends to only invest in countries
in which it has received a no-objection letter from the National Designated Authority, thus ensuring country
ownership of investments and supporting an enabling environment for off-grid solar.

If the project/programme is expected to support capacity building and technology development/transfer, please provide a

N/A
The H2R intervention seeks to provide capacity building activities in the form of technical assistance
to investee companies and ecosystem development to strengthen the off-grid solar markets in Host
Nations. A Technical Assistance Facility (TAF) is expected to be established as part of the Market
Support Facility. By integrating capacity building into the initiative through the TAF, H2R aims to
develop more resilient and impactful business models that can scale their operations sustainably in
H2R markets. As a result, these markets should become stronger and more competitive, paving the
way for other OGS businesses to thrive even beyond the life of the initiative.
TA will be provided for four main areas: Consumer Protection; Enterprise Development; ESG; and
Gender. In particular, Hardest-to-Reach aims to support investees to navigate the business
challenges, risks and barriers of delivering energy solutions to underserved segments; to grow
sustainably and inclusively, with an eye on protecting consumers; to access capacity building for
better financial performance; to enhance commercial and leadership capabilities for greater
business sustainability, particularly for locally-owned and managed companies; to identify and
mitigate environmental, social and governance risks; and understand and address the inequities
women face in energy, as users, entrepreneurs and members of the workforce. H2R aims to also
support the development of off-grid solar markets with a gender equity lens by providing training for
female professionals and community members, and by uplifting women in OGS markets, as
leaders, entrepreneurs, valued workforce and consumers. Similarly, H2R aims to strengthen ESG

women face in energy, as users, entrepreneurs and members of the workforce. H2R aims to also
support the development of off-grid solar markets with a gender equity lens by providing training for
female professionals and community members, and by uplifting women in OGS markets, as
leaders, entrepreneurs, valued workforce and consumers. Similarly, H2R aims to strengthen ESG |  |  |  |

global population will live in the region, and energy demand will rise significantly.96 To mitigate and adapt to
an increasingly warming planet, it is critical that all countries transition to low carbon-intensity and
affordable modern energy and, even where energy consumption is currently low, embark on clean energy
pathways. The energy pathways and resource dependencies developed across the continent today will
have profound climate impacts in the medium and long term. Data shows that developing economies

(excluding China) now account for roughly 40 percent of carbon emissions,97 and will propel almost all the
growth going forward.
Sub-Saharan Africa produces, on average, only 0.8 tonnes of CO2eq per person per year - compared to a
global average of 4.8 tonnes.98 However, highly developed and coal-dependent South Africa (85 percent
electrified) produces nearly ten times that per person - an extreme example and a cause for some concern
if large nations such as Mozambique (29% electrified), DRC (19%), and Uganda (29%) were to only
partially follow suit. These are all countries with electrification rates below the regional average of just over
48 percent,99 which is the primary selection criteria for Hardest-to-Reach target countries. Predictive
modeling illustrates Africa’s low-carbon SDG 7 scenarios and their correlation to SDG 13 as the region
electrifies.100 Providing first-time electricity access via a low carbon trajectory avoids approximately 268
million tonnes of CO2eq emissions, with a technology mix that is 45 percent decentralized renewables.101 If
African emissions per person were to rise even to the current global average, the continent would emit 12.5
billion tonnes of greenhouse gasses per year by 2050 — roughly equivalent to all emissions from China
and India today.102
The H2R initiative seeks to contribute to SSA’s low-emissions sustainable development pathway. By
providing people with first-time energy access through low-emissions energy sources, such as solar home
systems, customers gain trust and familiarity in the technology and payment models and opt to use similar
technologies in the future, even as their energy consumption grows. This aligns with the idea of low-carbon
development pathways, where economic development is decoupled from increasing carbon emissions.

- Impact Potential (vii): anticipatory, absorptive and adaptive resilience for households via OGS
characteristics (see below)
Energy System Resilience through decentralized solar
Access to electricity is considered a key part of adaptive capacity; one of the three principal factors which
determine climate change vulnerability in a region, along with sensitivity and exposure to hazards and
impacts. Adaptive capacity, the characteristic which allows people to cope with these hazards and impacts,
includes elements such as social networks, livelihood diversity, asset diversity, innovation and access to
financial services. Anticipatory capacity, the characteristic which allows people to plan for and invest and/or
change behavior and habits in advance of events, includes disaster preparedness, including access and the
ability to respond to weather forecasts and warnings of hazards. Electricity access is the thread linking all of
these, as it plays a key role in enabling all these components. As such it plays a significant role in making
livelihoods less vulnerable in H2R target countries.103
Limited power access in turn threatens livelihoods which rely on agriculture for a number of reasons. First
and foremost, the inability to access power means the inability to reliably access information and to
communicate. This is a crucial weakness during natural disasters, which are expected to continue to increase
in frequency and intensity as a result of climate change. In terms of enabling anticipatory capacity, energy
access can contribute to increasing household income by increasing working hours through access to light
and increasing opportunities for home based business, while direct access to power reduces the cost and
time investment in keeping a mobile phone charged, or of keeping a kerosene lamp fueled.
Energy systems have been compromised both by extreme and slow-onset climate events, with resulting
economic losses, disruptions of services and impacts to wellbeing. The threat to the reliable provision of
energy is exacerbated by the centralization of power generation and where distribution is interconnected,
including across regional power pools. Centralized energy systems across sub-Saharan Africa are already
facing the strain of climate change. For example, following low rainfall and droughts in 2015-16 in southern
Africa, power generation reduced by 75 percent at the Kariba dam in Zambia, and by 66 percent at the
Cahora Bassa dam in Mozambique due to insufficient water resources, with widespread impact on
electricity supplies across neighboring countries. As a result, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe all
experienced widespread and prolonged load shedding. The impact was felt throughout the regional
economy and reflected in reduced GDP growth.104 Furthermore, in 2019 Cyclone Idai caused significant
damages to Mozambique’s energy sector, and resulted in an estimated loss of $47.9 million. The cyclone
damaged or destroyed 1,345 km of transmission lines, 10,216 km of distribution lines, two 90 MW
generation plants, 30 sub-stations, 4,000 transformers.105 Similarly, Malawi lost 30% of its electricity to
Tropical Storm Ana in February 2022 because of damage to the 130 MW Kapichira hydropower plant.106
The World Bank approved a loan of $45M to restore the power plant, which is set to reopen in May 2023,
leaving the country at 2/3 of its energy generation capacity for over a year.107 These examples

demonstrate some of the ways in which traditional utility scale energy systems are vulnerable to the effects
of climate change.
The IPCC has therefore recognised the role that decentralized renewable energy can play in increasing the
resilience of energy systems, as it helps to diversify energy supplies and reduce pressure on the grid.108
Decentralized energy also has a role in reducing the vulnerability of rural populations to climate change. In
fact, evidence suggests that solar home system usage is considered as a coping mechanism against
natural disaster-induced electricity disruption by households in climate vulnerable areas. The research
points in particular to the attributes that make distributed renewable energy easier to be rebuilt (where
necessary), reconnected, and fully functioning in a shorter period.109 By diversifying energy sources,
increasing the distribution of energy solutions and adopting technical improvements to reduce systems’
climate vulnerability, we are able to see more adapted and resilient energy systems in H2R countries.110
Anticipatory, absorptive and adaptive capacity for households through characteristics of OGS
Energy access impacts the ability to anticipate, avoid, plan for, cope with, recover from and adapt to
(climate related) shocks and stresses’.111 Three dimensions or capacities of climate resilience can be
improved through off-grid solar: adaptation (adaptive capacity), anticipation (anticipatory capacity), and
absorption (absorptive capacity). By enabling the sale of climate resilient, affordable and reliable OGS
products to underserved communities, Hardest-to-Reach contributes to all three. Firstly, OGS energy
products are durable and portable, meaning that they are able to withstand climate-change related
phenomena, and can be moved and safely stored in the event of extreme weather events.112 They are also
repairable, enabling a resumption of energy provision following product damage. Thirdly, they lead to a
more diversified energy system and take pressure off the grid, which can reduce systemic climate
vulnerability. As described, distributed renewable energy (DRE) reduces vulnerability to climate impacts by
increasing the resilience of energy provision in the face of natural disasters and climate shocks, which are
increasingly frequent and intense in these geographies.113 Each solar home system is an important
independent energy source that can continue to provide a household with energy even if the grid has been
compromised because of increased demand or damage caused by an extreme weather event. Recent data
show that an estimated 775 million people worldwide are connected to weak grids, undermining the
potential social and economic development of access to electricity. Off-grid solar can play an important role
in improving the quality of electricity access here as well as deliver significant climate mitigation and
adaptation benefits; Diesel generators used to provide grid back-up emit more than 100 megatons of CO2

ARA 2: Health, wellbeing, food and water security

Improved health, wellbeing and quality of life through energy access
In least developed country contexts, in particular, energy access is an enabler for poverty reduction that is
crucial for enhancing people’s livelihoods and wellbeing. According to the IPCC and research by the UK’s
Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (formerly DFID) there is growing evidence of the role of
DRE in reducing people’s overall vulnerability, especially in underserved populations, through more well lit
private land and assets, less hazardous household lighting, such as via open flames, and cleaner air in the
absence of black carbon emitted from kerosene lanterns.115 Energy access can also reduce the impact of
climate hazards. Without electricity, for example, households cannot receive SMS, radio or TV news to
receive early warning messages or public safety announcements before and after a climate event. Thus,
across sub-Saharan Africa, where 33 of the world's 46 LDCs are situated, delivering energy access to
enable specific applications such as information communication technologies, and by driving socio-
economic development (i.e, improving incomes, health outcomes and access to education), is highly
impactful for quality of life perceptions, health and overall well being. The 60 Decibels Energy Benchmark,
a Lean Data survey of off-grid energy customers in developing economies, found that 51% of people felt
that their quality of life had improved significantly after buying an off-grid product in general, compared to
68% for solar-powered off-grid products in particular.116 Acumen’s PEII portfolio companies scored high on
this metric, where 60 Decibels surveys of PEII portfolio customers found that 64% of off-grid energy
customers felt their quality of life had improved substantially. Whilst this measure is subjective and could
incorporate a number of different factors, it indicates how significant an impact energy access has on
people’s lives. Finally, residential solar PV requires neither water nor additional land to generate electricity,
meaning OGS products reduce stress on land use and water systems, with broader positive impacts on
food security and biodiversity.
Even though it can be concluded that the impact of energy access through SHS on livelihood resilience in
SSA is conditional and limited, solar lamps and SHS are nevertheless an important milestone on the route
to initial last-mile electrification in rural areas of sub-Saharan Africa. In countries where grid expansion is

too costly and time-consuming, it is ultimately not realistic in many regions. Even the introduction of larger

D.2. Paradigm shift potential (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
Paradigm shift potential is defined as ‘degree to which the proposed activity can catalyse impact beyond a one-off project or
programme investment’. In this section, elaborate on the contribution to paradigm shift and how the proposed project/programme
aims to contribute towards it based on the theory of change described in section B2(a). Also describe how and to what extent the
project/programme will be able to promote or contribute to paradigm shift through the below.
● Potential for scaling up and replication
● Potential for knowledge sharing and learning
● Contribution to the creation of an enabling environment
● Contribution to the regulatory framework and policies
● Overall contribution to climate-resilient development pathways consistent with relevant national climate change adaptation
strategies and plans
Paradigm Shift
The H2R initiative will deliver a paradigm shift by:
I. Nurturing and developing companies to serve underserved off-grid solar markets; and by
II. Unlocking the provision of - and investment in - clean, climate-resilient decentralized solar, that will
III. Power low-carbon economic development for the long-term.
One of the key aims of Hardest-to-Reach is to transform the African energy sector by building (and
eventually scaling up) off-grid markets where there currently are none or they are fledgling. The initiative
will focus on LDCs in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly with electrification rates at-or-below the regional
average, where investors have not been willing to enter. H2R’s blended finance structure is
transformational in its design as it will crowd-in investors that would otherwise find the markets too nascent
or risky. The initiative intends to de-risk these markets by providing new market entrants with impact-linked
concessional finance and targeted technical assistance, and seeks to support the development of local
networks and capacity. By proving the OGS business model in untested markets, companies can also
crowd in additional capital to achieve scale in these markets. In the scale phase, H2R’s impact-linked debt
financing aspires to incentivize OGS companies to maintain their focus on low-income, first-time energy
access customers.
A blend of capital is needed to achieve this. Data from Shell shows that approximately $11 billion will be
required in debt into SHS enterprises towards SDG 7 in non-established markets.118 A further $2.8 billion of

debt is required in established markets. Equity and equity-like capital is critical as fledgling and latent
markets require substantial early-stage, risk tolerant capital in order to be unlocked. H2R’s approach is
based on allocating the right type and size of capital for the stage of the company and development of the
market intending to create an enabling environment in these difficult to operate regions. Last-mile
distributors (LMDs) have a crucial role to play in delivering OGS products to H2R consumers, but capital is
not flowing into the space. Research from the GDC shows that all types of capital - grant, equity and debt -
are needed to unlock the full potential of LMDs, depending on their growth trajectory.119 The MEF allows
a targeted use of loans to established companies seeking to scale.
Technical assistance will play a fundamental role in delivering H2R innovation. By focusing on TA that
overcomes enterprise and market barriers to achieving long-term and inclusive growth, there is a holistic,
whole-of-company-lifecycle approach that represents a paradigm shift compared to current investment
practices and sector interventions. Acumen will also develop partnerships that convene different financiers,
TA providers, policy advocates, government, and OGS companies in an effort to jumpstart the OGS market
in H2R areas. Through Hardest-to-Reach, Acumen is working to form a partnership with the World Bank
Group, Power Africa, and other leading energy access practitioners and financiers to address the
affordability gap through demand side subsidies to expand our reach to the lowest income level customers.
Across the range of partners are those able to help address other market barriers, including developing the
right VAT and duty structures for renewables products and narrowing the affordability gap for low-income
customers. Coordinated efforts like these should reduce inefficient use of resources, create opportunities to
leverage stakeholder experiences and competencies, and minimize distortive risks. This is expected to
lead to a paradigm shift in the investing landscape in H2R areas, and help increase capital inflows and
more coordinated investments on the ground, with multiple stakeholders and government buy-in for climate
resilient off-grid solar. Through H2R’s innovations - not only scaling up innovative business models and
technologies, but also strengthening the entire OGS ecosystem through investing in local distribution
networks, delivering consumer protection and other TA, fostering partnerships and conducting robust
impact monitoring - Acumen intends to use GCF’s much-needed concessional financing to create a
paradigm shift by de-risking OGS markets, creating a commercial track record and crowding-in private
finance to deploy new climate solutions at scale. It is a blueprint that can set a new course for
decentralized and decarbonized electrification in these Hardest-to-Reach markets.
Acumen seeks to develop the knowledge base in the sector by generating and sharing insights and
lessons so that other development partners can learn from the H2R initiative and replicate successful
aspects in their own energy access initiatives. As outlined in the program activities (Sect E.6) and the
program-specific indicators (Section E.5), H2R intends to develop as many as 10 independent thought
pieces to be shared with the wider community of stakeholders, such as white papers, blog posts, insight
studies, toolkits , or playbooks . Subjects may include lessons from our development of more robust
consumer protection practices, studies to deepen the sector’s understanding of household-level impacts of
decentralized solar and how these can be maximized, and what role investors can play.
Acumen is playing a convening role in the sector and through sharing the knowledge and evidence-based
insights gained through H2R, particularly on the impact of energy access and climate resilience, will be
able to increase capital inflows and more coordinated investments on the ground, with the buy-in of
multiple stakeholders and government toward climate resilient off-grid solar. H2R intends to coalesce all
the relevant stakeholders (NDAs, government entities, academics, OGS businesses, industry associations,

indigenous communities, civil society organizations, and women’s groups). Additionally, the team hopes to
report on insights to GOGLA, investors, and other climate financiers as to crowd in climate adaptation
financing for energy access projects. We believe that these efforts will help to bolster H2R''s demonstration
effect of "energy access as adaptation". This aspect should bring positive externalities in unlocking funding
for powering resilience and building a resilient OGS ecosystem.
The 16 target countries for Acumen’s Hardest-to-Reach initiative signed the Paris Agreement and
submitted Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC). All 16 countries have pledged both conditional and
unconditional targets to reduce their GHG emissions by 2030 under the Business-as-Usual (BAU)
scenario. The unconditional targets are targets expected to be met by countries with their own resources
without external support, whilst conditional targets are subject to financial support from the international
community. Two of the 16 countries have set their conditional mitigation targets at over 50% emission
reduction by 2030, namely: Malawi and Togo at (51% and 51%) respectively.120 The lowest conditional
emission reduction targets were from Burundi at 16%. The NDCs further incorporate mitigation and
adaptation actions. For instance, Uganda’s NDC provides 48 priority adaptation actions and 82 indications
with adaptation targets for 2030, one of the targets is to achieve 75% electrification by 2030.121 Acumen’s
objectives through Hardest-to-Reach are directly aligned with national climate priorities, including National
Adaptation Plans, National Climate Change Action Plans, and NDCs. Further details on country
electrification, climate policies and climate adaptation overviews can be found in the country climate
reports .
D.3. Sustainable development (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
Describe the wider benefits and priorities of the project/programme in relation to the Sustainable Development Goals and provide
the potential in terms of:
● Environmental co-benefits
● Social co-benefits including health co-benefit
● Economic co-benefits
● Gender-sensitive development benefit
Sustainable Development
Modern society depends on reliable and affordable energy services to function smoothly and to develop
equitably. Carbon intensive development patterns have historically relied on inexpensive and energy-dense
fossil fuels, which are also the primary source of greenhouse gas emissions contributing to climate change.
Hardest-to-Reach is aligned with SDG 7 (affordable, reliable, modern and sustainable energy for all) and
through the power of energy access will enable broader sustainable development outcomes; good health
and wellbeing (SDG 3), improved educational outcomes (SDG 4), economic savings and income
generation (SDG 1 and SDG 8), and climate action (SDG 13). Acumen’s intervention is also partnership-
focused, envisioning a more coordinated investment ecosystem to transform the prospects for growth in
the off-grid solar sector (consistent with SDG 17).

The H2R initiative has a number of broader sustainable development impacts. Firstly, off-grid solar
products can improve people’s health, safety and wellbeing. For those trapped in energy poverty,
particularly the rural households in H2R target countries, fossil-fuel based energy sources such as
kerosene may be the only available energy source., These traditional lanterns provide low-quality light, are
harmful to people’s health because of household pollutants, and can cause burns and fires. This
disproportionately affects women and children who spend more time at home. Replacing fossil-fuel based
energy sources with clean off-grid solar products can therefore have positive impacts on people’s health
and safety as customers will have access to better quality lighting,122 which can prevent falls at night, help
with security, and allow for cleaner air at home. A 2018 study in Uganda cited the fact that single-wick
lanterns were once responsible for 70 percent of fire incidents and 80 percent of burn injuries in energy
poor households.123 These data points are likely to be less stark in today’s Uganda, thanks in part to some
success of off-grid solar technologies. There is still a task to do to ensure no household has to rely on
these fuels for lighting. Meanwhile, where households have replaced kerosene lanterns with single use dry
cell battery LEDs, these batteries pose a health (and environmental) risk, as they contain heavy metals.124
Additionally, fuel combustion releases hundreds of pollutants into the air, including carbon monoxide,
formaldehyde and benzene, along with a myriad of other damaging particles.Secondly, OGS products can
enable people to generate income through their use.125 This can be directly (use in a business) or indirectly
(task-shifting activities to the evening because of better quality light). This can help increase people’s
economic security. Thirdly, the PAYGo financing structure should enable many people to access mobile
wallets and credit for the first time, leading to the financial inclusion of low-income people and helping to
build their credit scores.126 This is particularly important for women, who are often excluded from accessing
credit because of land-based collateral requirements. Fourthly, the local distribution networks that will be
created and after-sales services provided will be a source of livelihood options and income generation
opportunities, as they should create employment for people in low-income areas.127 The increased income
they receive is expected to be an important contributor to their increased resilience and adaptive capacity.
Lastly, H2R envisions a co-benefit of job creation that is consistent with SDG 8. As OGS companies scale,
they will require additional human capital to support their growth and sustain their level of service. Jobs
include customer service personnel, office and administrators, product sales staff, and technicians for
installations and repair.
Environmental and Social
To ensure strong environmental and social co-benefits, Acumen developed an Environmental and Social
Impact Assessment to better understand the positive impacts, environmental risks, and potential mitigants.
The ESIA informed the development of the H2R Environmental and Social Management System. The H2R
ESMS is also aligned with the GCF Environmental and Social Policy and the Acumen ESMS for GCF-
funded Projects. The ESIA and ESMS are submitted as part of this proposal.
Our Project seeks to support the development of the OGS sector in H2R markets. An important co-benefit
of supporting these nascent markets is building and sustaining green jobs. The H2R program targets the

creation of ~13,900 additional green jobs as a co-benefit of this intervention. An estimated 4,600 of these

Gender
Hardest-to-Reach intends to have significant benefits for women both by creating more opportunities for
women to participate in the OGS industry and ensuring access to electricity for women. As mentioned
previously, H2R expects to improve the health and safety of women and expects to also lead to their
financial inclusion. The initiative will target the industry’s benchmark of having 32% of its customers as
women128 and will aim to support women-led businesses. H2R also seeks to engage companies and the
OGS ecosystem in developing more opportunities for women to work in the OGS system in H2R markets
with the Project Technical Assistance Facility. Additionally, H2R intends to diligence and monitor Sexual
Exploitation, Abuse and Harassment (SEAH) across Investees operations and engagement with
customers. H2R commits to supporting equitable and empowering workplaces for women with Investees.
Investees are expected to address opportunities for growth in their Gender Action Plans, and with the
support of gender experts using technical assistance. Importantly, H2R expects to track gender-
disaggregated data for certain indicators, which improves industry-wide knowledge on how women engage
with energy products and services, and allows for the greater consideration of gender throughout the OGS
industry.
The H2R team developed a gender assessment in accordance with industry best practices, guidance and
support from gender experts, community input, and following the GCF Gender Policy. The gender
assessment informed the Project’s Gender Action Plan and Gender Lens Investing Strategy.
These documents can be found in Annex 8.

The investment deficit is at the root of both the energy access gap and the lack of adaptive capacity faced
by countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Despite the tremendous progress made by off-grid solar companies in
improving energy access in sub-Saharan Africa, a substantial number of financially viable customers in
difficult, hard-to-reach markets will not be catered for by current market-based interventions. OGS
companies were estimated to have cumulatively raised US$1.5 billion129 as of 2019 from an increasingly
diverse investor base as the industry
has matured. However, there is a clear
geographic bias in the flow of funding.
80 percent of the capital raised in the
sector, between 2012-2019, has flowed
to larger and more established, first-
generation, companies whose primary
location and focus is East Africa, with
Kenya attracting the lion’s share of the
capital. Additionally, as OGS start-ups
evolve towards profitability, they have
increasingly focused on entrenching
their market position and attracting
higher margin customers in the most
active markets at the expense of
expanding into the less-active markets
with a higher actual and perceived risk.
As the two Figures show, the regional
disparities in the size and capitalisation
of the OGS sector are largely
incongruent with the distribution of
people without access to electricity. Thus, it is imperative to direct more resources, financial and otherwise,
to where they are needed the most.
The overall level of investment has been adversely affected by the pandemic, with foreign private
investment into Africa falling some 16% in 2020.130 Significant financial commitments are required to close
this gap and governments are unable to carry the fiscal burden alone. One estimate suggests that $35
billion a year is required to reach SDG 7 by 2030. At the same time, the NDCs of 40 African countries
cumulatively show a need for an estimated $331 billion in investment for adaptation through 2030, with
only 20% of this figure coming from public budgets.131 The map shows the dearth of international financing
going to developing economies in support of clean energy, particularly given the size of developing-
economy populations.132 Within sub-Saharan Africa a concentration of investment flows to now-proven
markets risks leaving other countries and regions behind. However, barriers exist, including political
instability, macroeconomic uncertainty (because of inflation and exchange rates), policy and regulatory
issues, institutional weaknesses, and lack of transparency. All these make for a less favorable investment
climate. Underinvested geographies need capital that is willing to bear the risk of proving and scaling off-
grid business models in untested conditions, and bring with it practices that drive the growth of responsible

Benin Country Context
Benin is a low-income country, with a population of more than 13 million people and a population growth
rate of 2,8%.133 The rural electrification rate is 9%. Benin’s current electrification rate stands at 33% which
is below the sub-Saharan African average of 48%, leaving 7.9 million people without access to
electricity.134 This is disaggregated with 58% and 9% urban and rural electrification respectively.135 As the
country develops, the energy demand is anticipated to increase, thus there is a need to match the energy
supply to the growing energy demand.
DRC Country Context
DRC is a low-income country, with a population of more than 96 million people and a population growth
rate of 3.2% per year.136 According to the World Bank Group, poverty in DRC is high and is among the five
poorest nations in the world. The 2019 electrification rate for the DRC stood at 9% relative to the sub-
Saharan African average of 48%, leaving 79 million people without access to electricity.137 19% of the
urban population has access to electricity whereas this figure is less than 1% for the rural population.138 In
2021, DRC had an installed electricity capacity of 2.8 GW comprising 99% hydropower and 1% non-
renewable sources. The national electricity grid powers 19% of the population living in urban areas but only
1% for the population living in rural areas. 139
Burundi Country Context
Burundi is a low-income country, with a population of more than 12.55 million people and a population
growth rate of 2.7%.140 In 2019, Burundi’s national electrification rate stood at 11%, relative to the sub-
Saharan African average of 48%, leaving 11 million people without access to electricity.141 There is a 66%
connection rate in urban areas, but only 2% in rural areas. As of 2019, the total energy supply in Burundi
was sourced from 85% renewables, 14% oil, and 1% coal and others.142 Of the renewables, 98% is
biomass, 0% solar, and 2% hydro. Hydroelectric power alone provides electricity to 9% of the population,
which translates to 75% of those with access to electricity.

Mozambique is a low-income country, with a population of more than 32 million people and a population
growth rate of 2.9%.143 Only 22% of the population in rural areas had access to electricity in 2019.144 This
is comparable to the urban electrification rate of 57%. Mozambique’s national electrification rate stood at
35% in 2019, relative to the sub-Saharan African average of 48%, leaving 21 million people without access
to electricity.145 The country has an installed capacity of 2.9 GW, comprising 90% hydropower and 10%
natural gas. However, only 36% of the produced power is used for domestic consumption, whilst the
remaining 64% is exported to nearby countries.
Zambia Country Context
Zambia is a low-income country, with a population of more than 18 million people and a population growth
rate of 2.9%.146 Zambia’s primary sources of energy include wood fuel, hydropower, coal and solar. In
2019, Zambia’s national electrification rate stood at 37%, relative to the sub-Saharan African average of
48%, leaving 11 million people without access to energy. Its urban electrification rate was 76% and its rural
electrification rate was 6%. Zambia has an installed capacity of 3.3 GW, comprising 80% hydropower, 11%
coal, 4% diesel, 3% heavy fuel oil (HFO) and 3% solar.147
Gender Context
The link between energy access and gender equality is compelling. Energy poverty has a strong gender
dimension, as the lack of access to energy inhibits a woman’s freedom from household drudgery, her
freedom to allocate time, to access economic opportunities, and enjoy improved household living
conditions. Off-grid energy technologies have a direct benefit to women’s health, particularly in terms of
reduced risks of pulmonary and respiratory diseases, caused by long-term proximity to fumes from
kerosene lanterns.148 At the enterprise level, women’s participation and leadership in the OGS sector can
help accelerate the transition to a low-carbon economy by promoting clean energy use and addressing
energy poverty, while also advancing women’s economic empowerment. However, multiple barriers limit
women’s ability to access OGS technologies and to fully participate in OGS value chains as business
leaders, employees and entrepreneurs. These barriers include, but are not limited to, (i) a historically
unequal distribution of economic assets which impacts women’s ability to access OGS products; (ii) the
limited collection and use of sex-disaggregated data to help better understand the needs of women as
energy users, and more broadly as stakeholders in the sector; (iii) a lack of targeted training and
mentorship opportunities for women to enter the workforce and thrive in the clean energy economy.
Overall, evidence shows that women have less access to off-grid electricity than their male counterparts,
and they mostly use pico-solar products and lanterns or other lower-tier technologies.149 SHS customers
are predominantly rural men living under the median poverty line of $3.10.150 In a survey conducted on
35,000 customers of 49 OGS companies in 16 countries, 60 Decibels found that only 32% of customers

Energy Access Companies
Equity investors push for profit margins, creating pressure on energy companies to shift in focus toward
multi-purpose and higher-end SHS and away from entry-level products and first-time access as a result.
Companies are often reluctant to pursue more first-time access customers in unfamiliar territories and have
indicated that entering a market as a second or third mover is far more advantageous. This is due to the
significant hurdles that need to be overcome in a completely new market such as finding good local
management, establishing logistics lines, and understanding the nuances of the local finance and
regulatory system. While the challenges faced by OGS are of a similar nature across Sub-Saharan Africa,
they can be prohibitively more pronounced in some countries, substantially diminishing the attractiveness
of a market as an expansion destination. OGS companies in these countries also face geographical
barriers such as vast distances between the location of targeted customers and the capital city or
warehousing locations, which is exacerbated by poor road networks. These challenges or viability gaps
can be segmented into three broad categories-company-specific constraints, market constraints and
funding constraints-as summarized in the table below. Company-specific viability gaps refer to constraints
which are an outcome of the OGS company’s strategic and market positioning and includes issues with
existing capital structures and lack of management bandwidth. Market constraints on the other hand are
specific to each country and are the result of structural and economic deficiencies such as high poverty
rates, low mobile penetration rates, different fiscal systems and political risk. Finally, funding constraints
refer to lack of bespoke financial products that can be leveraged by OGS to expand into more challenging
markets. These viability gaps are presented in the table.

Hardest-to-Reach’s investment approach enables capacity building of OGS enterprises by addressing key
viability gaps, through patient capital that meets the needs of companies, alongside targeted technical
assistance. The investment approach has the built-in flexibility to support all business models in the OGS
space including vertically integrated companies and pure manufacturers who leverage distribution channel
partnerships, both of whom are set to be the principal beneficiaries of the program. The impact-linked
structure of the Market Expansion Facility loans rewards first-time energy access sales, improving the
economic incentive to serve often more remote and lower-margin customers.Local African founders and
business owners in particular face structural inequities in respect of these challenges, with greater difficulty
to access challenge being a challenge for the majority. Just 6 percent of startups that secured more than
$1 million in Kenya were led by local founders in 2019, while a survey of 70 predominantly local last mile
distributors revealed that three quarters experience access to finance as a key barrier to growth, with 54%
specifically seeking debt finance.152

nascent and challenging emerging markets. In addition, there are those for whom commercial access to
energy access will not be a viable option. Some $4.5 billion is needed just to close the affordability gap to

Payment plan models, such as PAYGo, can enable lower upfront investment and payment over time,
making systems affordable for poor customers. PAYGo increases by 40% the number of people who can
afford an entry-level (Tier I) solar product.154 Even in the short term, the PAYGo model enables customers
living in off-grid regions to transition away from fossil fuel-based energy sources, such as kerosene or
diesel generators, to solar energy, with material GHG emissions avoidance impacts.
In addition, a climate justice component is tied to the needs of communities living in energy poverty. Low-
income people in Hardest-to-Reach regions have contributed the least to climate change, yet they stand to
suffer the most from it and benefit the least from global capital allocated for renewable energy and climate-
friendly investment. Governments and climate investors have bypassed them, particularly in the most
remote and fragile regions, prioritizing the countries that have higher greenhouse gas emissions and offer
better returns on investment. Through Hardest-to-Reach, Acumen will invest where others won’t, to bring
remote, low-income people access to clean, renewable solar energy, helping them adapt to a changing
climate and build the resilience needed to face climate and economic shocks.

According to UNEP (2017), the energy sector is considered a focus area in 45% of the INDCs in all total
Non-Annex 1 countries155. Based on the data from UNEP, the energy sector is the most important sector
for sub-Saharan Africa. The prioritization of the energy sector in most NDCs is likely to reflect both its
relevance as a large emission source and the availability of various cost-effective mitigation measures. All
developing countries include mitigation measures within the energy sector in their NDCs.
In the early part of the investment period, Hardest-to-Reach will seek to work with OGS companies with
different business models (i.e. vertically integrated and pure-play distributors) to enter or expand their
reach in a range of countries, some of which rank among the bottom markets across indicators. The
countries below provide an example. They represent an addressable market of approximately 147 million
people without electricity, roughly 25% of the total unelectrified population of sub-Saharan Africa. The
alignment of these countries to the mission of H2R is strong across existing policies, such as Nationally
Determined Contributions (NDCs), national electrification strategies, and National Adaptation Plans
(NAPs):
● Benin: In Benin, the national electrification rate is 33%. In 2020, the country adopted a new
electricity code that provides for the opening of the electricity market to private investors, who can
now produce, transport, distribute and market electrical energy in the country in the same way as
the national utility.156 Benin contributes 0.06% to global GHG emissions and its Government has
committed to reducing emissions by 20% by 2030 compared to the reference scenario, accounting
for 48.75Mt CO2eq.157 Energy and agriculture are recognized in its NDC as the key reduction
areas. Benin’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP)158 outlines specific measures for improving the
climate resilience of the energy sector. Certain of these measures, including the improvement in the
use and availability of early warning systems, are based on higher levels of energy availability. The
plan also mentions the adoption of quality standards for energy infrastructure and equipment, which
H2R is aligned with.
● Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC): The DRC has a national electrification rate of 9%. The
government aims to reach a target of 65% electrification by 2025. Currently, the DRC contributes
1.39% of global GHG emissions, and its government is committed to reducing emissions by 21% by
2030 compared to the business-as-usual scenario. The sectors targeted for this reduction are
forestry, agriculture, energy, and waste. The DRC’s National Adaptation Plan159 aims to increase

According to UNEP (2017), the energy sector is considered a focus area in 45% of the INDCs in all total
Non-Annex 1 countries155. Based on the data from UNEP, the energy sector is the most important sector
for sub-Saharan Africa. The prioritization of the energy sector in most NDCs is likely to reflect both its
relevance as a large emission source and the availability of various cost-effective mitigation measures. All
developing countries include mitigation measures within the energy sector in their NDCs.
In the early part of the investment period, Hardest-to-Reach will seek to work with OGS companies with
different business models (i.e. vertically integrated and pure-play distributors) to enter or expand their
reach in a range of countries, some of which rank among the bottom markets across indicators. The
countries below provide an example. They represent an addressable market of approximately 147 million
people without electricity, roughly 25% of the total unelectrified population of sub-Saharan Africa. The
alignment of these countries to the mission of H2R is strong across existing policies, such as Nationally
Determined Contributions (NDCs), national electrification strategies, and National Adaptation Plans
(NAPs):
● Benin: In Benin, the national electrification rate is 33%. In 2020, the country adopted a new
electricity code that provides for the opening of the electricity market to private investors, who can
now produce, transport, distribute and market electrical energy in the country in the same way as
the national utility.156 Benin contributes 0.06% to global GHG emissions and its Government has
committed to reducing emissions by 20% by 2030 compared to the reference scenario, accounting
for 48.75Mt CO2eq.157 Energy and agriculture are recognized in its NDC as the key reduction
areas. Benin’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP)158 outlines specific measures for improving the
climate resilience of the energy sector. Certain of these measures, including the improvement in the
use and availability of early warning systems, are based on higher levels of energy availability. The
plan also mentions the adoption of quality standards for energy infrastructure and equipment, which
H2R is aligned with.
● Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC): The DRC has a national electrification rate of 9%. The
government aims to reach a target of 65% electrification by 2025. Currently, the DRC contributes
1.39% of global GHG emissions, and its government is committed to reducing emissions by 21% by
2030 compared to the business-as-usual scenario. The sectors targeted for this reduction are
forestry, agriculture, energy, and waste. The DRC’s National Adaptation Plan159 aims to increase

D
the climate resilience of priority thematic sectors, including energy. Low-carbon energy
development, in particular via solar and other renewable sources, is outlined in the plan.
● Guinea: The national electrification rate in Guinea is 46%. Guinea aims to achieve universal
energy access by 2030.160 There is the potential for off-grid solutions in the country, and one of
Guinea’s strategic priorities is to promote decentralized energy solutions involving local
communities and the private sector at the rural level. In its NDC, Guinea outlined an unconditional
emissions reduction target of 9.7% by 2030 relative to the business-as-usual scenario, and an
emissions target of 17% by 2030 that is conditional on external support. Guinea relies on
hydropower for 58% of total electricity generation, meaning its energy sector is vulnerable to
climate change.161 Reduced rainfall combined with warming is projected to reduce flows in the
Konkouré River in western Guinea by 30–50 percent by 2100.162 This is a major concern, given that
several dams along the river provide much of the country’s hydropower. Water has therefore been
highlighted as a key adaptation area in Guinea’s NDC.
● Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone has a national electrification rate of 26%. The government has a
target to reach a 92% electrification rate by 2030 and recognized that 42% of the population would
be best reached by off-grid stand-alone systems by 2023.163 Sierra Leone contributes to 0.02% of
global GHG emissions and the government has committed in its NDC to reduce emissions by 25%
by 2050 compared to the projected business-as-usual level.164 There is strong alignment between
Sierra Leone’s NAP and H2R.165 It aims at universal access to energy through the promotion of
renewables, in particular promoting off-grid stand-alone solar investments through technical advice
and knowledge sharing. The government has a dedicated Off-grid Solar Energy Strategy (OGSES)
with a strong focus on mobilizing financial institutions to create investment packages and
counterpart funding.
● Uganda: Uganda has a national electrification rate of 29%. Uganda has made huge progress in
closing the energy access gap, as electrification rates grew by 3% per year between 2010 and
2019. Uganda has made electrification a national priority and aims to achieve a national
electrification rate of above 98% by 2030 under the Sustainability Energy For All (SE4All)
Initiative.166 The Government estimates there are potentially 2,906,525 rural households that could
be electrified through the provision of solar home systems and up to 130,000 households that could
be electrified through mini-grids. In its NDC Uganda outlined an emissions reduction target of 22%
by 2030 relative to the business-as-usual scenario, conditional on external support of 70% of the
required financial resources.167 Energy is one of its key sectors of focus for emissions reduction.
The country’s energy sector is also highly vulnerable to climate change as it is dominated by
hydropower. Energy supply is at risk of being disrupted because of extreme weather events, such
as reduced river flows resulting from droughts, and damage to power plants and transmission lines
from floods and landslides.168 Energy is therefore an adaptation priority under Uganda’s NDC.
● Zambia: The national electrification rate in Zambia is 37%. The country is targeting universal
energy access by 2030, which means connecting over 11M people. The Government also aims to
connect 31.6% of the population to SHS by 2030.169 Zambia’s NDC outlined an ambitious
unconditional commitment to reduce GHGs by 25% compared with BAU by 2030, and a
commitment to reduce emissions by 47% compared with BAU based on conditional support.170
Energy is one of its key areas of emissions reductions. The energy sector is also vulnerable to
climate change, as 84% of its electricity generation is from hydropower.171 Energy generation has

The list of countries in which we operate will naturally expand throughout the life of the Market Support
Facility and Market Expansion Facility, and believe this model is also applicable to the following Hardest-to-
Reach markets in sub-Saharan Africa: Burundi, Burkina Faso, Chad, Guinea Bissau, Lesotho, Malawi,
Mozambique, Niger, Somalia and Togo.
In the project development phase, the AE has developed the Hardest-to-Reach Stakeholder Engagement
Plan . The AE has conducted significant desktop research on civil society organizations, and other
relevant stakeholders including NDAs, indigenous groups, women, and other vulnerable groups.
As of April 28, 2023, we received 16 NOLs from Benin, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Chad, DRC, Guinea,
Guinea Bissau, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Niger, Sierra Leone, Somalia, Togo, Uganda, Zambia. The
AE is in advanced discussions with several other countries, including (without limitation) Liberia,
Madagascar and Tanzania. These countries all expressed significant interest in the project, but haven’t
been able to complete their internal sign-off processes for various reasons. Nevertheless, we expect to
receive NOLs from most, if not all, of these countries before the publication deadline. Additional countries
may be added to the programme after initial Board approval, provided they submit an NOL and the addition
is approved by the Board.
Additionally, the AE has begun hosting stakeholder town halls with our first town hall in Sierra Leone. We
engaged 10 different groups in that meeting, received project feedback, and strengthened relationships in
Sierra Leone. We anticipate hosting in-person and virtual stakeholder town halls for stakeholders in each
H2R country.
The AE has developed improved capacity to engage relevant stakeholders as reflected by the H2R
Stakeholder Engagement Plan, Acumen’s Stakeholder Engagement Plan for GCF-Funded Projects, and
Acumen’s recent re-accreditation with GCF.

D.6. Efficiency and effectiveness (max`. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
Describe how the financial structure is adequate and reasonable in order to achieve the proposal’s objectives, including addressing
existing bottlenecks and/or barriers, and providing the minimum concessionality to ensure the project is viable without crowding out
private and other public investments. Refer to section B.5 on the justification of GCF funding requested as necessary.
Please describe the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed project/programme, taking into account the total financing and
mitigation/ adaptation outcome the project/programme aims to achieve, and explain how this compares to an appropriate
benchmark.
Please specify the expected economic rate of return based on a comparison of the scenarios with and without the
project/programme.
IPlease specify the expected financial rate of return with and without the Fund’s support to illustrate the need for GCF funding to
illustrate overall cost effectiveness.
Please explain how best available technologies and practices have been considered and applied. If applicable, specify the
innovations/modifications/adjustments that are made based on industry best practices.
Hardest-to-Reach’s Market Expansion Facility is expected to be funded by capital from a range of
investors, including private sector financiers, Development Finance Institutions (DFIs), governments,
foundations, and corporations. The blended structure with the support of GCF should mobilize different
types of investors with different risk appetites at scale for the same purpose, providing first-time energy
access for low income customers in Hardest-to-Reach geographies. Generally, the initiative’s goal is to
substantially preserve investor capital, not to produce significant returns. The H2R initiative anticipates
providing funding to energy access companies with the intermediate goal of providing sufficient and
appropriate liquidity to firms that are in the pioneer gap. Lack of returns of invested capital (including some
losses) that enable the sector’s preservation or development would be deemed a successful outcome.
Hardest-to-Reach has set a fundraising target of $200 million for the overall MEF, inclusive of the potential
GCF investment. The targeted raise is meant to be sufficient to sustain the operations and impact of a
significant number of energy access companies. Government agencies, DFIs, and even commercial
investors have indicated an interest in layering their capital with first-loss grant capital. In fact, GCF’s $55
million investment into the facility will likely allow Acumen to crowd-in $145 million of co-financing from
other investors, including those from the private sector. GCF is mobilizing nearly three times as much
capital into an LDC-focused initiative that investors would otherwise find too risky.
The Hardest-to-Reach initiative is also very efficient and effective in terms of its impact. The $250m raised
for both the Market Support Facility and Market Expansion Facility is targeting the provision of electricity to
72.4 million people, many of whom live below the poverty line. The initiative intends to provide electricity to
millions of people at a very low-cost, especially when compared with the material impact that electricity
access will have on people’s lives.
As a further marker of efficiency, we note that the total investment amount well exceeds the total H2R
project size through reinvestments. Without GCF’s participation, Hardest-to-Reach may be able to
proceed with an initial raise, but it will likely be unable to meet more than a fraction of the demonstrated
demand for liquidity. If GCF is not able to contribute funding, there is a high risk that many companies will
not maintain operations, as many investor entities consider such firms too risky. The resulting lack of

E. LOGICAL FRAMEWORK
E.1. Project/Programme Focus

F. RISK ASSESSMENT AND MANAGEMENT
F.1. Risk factors and mitigations measures (max. 3 pages)
Please describe financial, technical, operational, macroeconomic/political, money laundering/terrorist financing (ML/TF), sanctions,
prohibited practices, and other risks that might prevent the project/programme objectives from being achieved. Also describe the
proposed risk mitigation measures. Insert additional rows if necessary.
For probability: High has significant probability, Medium has moderate probability, Low has negligible probability
For impact: High has significant impact, Medium has moderate impact, Low has negligible impact
Prohibited practices include abuse, conflict of interest, corruption, retaliation against whistleblowers or witnesses, as well as
fraudulent, coercive, collusive, and obstructive practices
Selected Risk Factor 1: Execution
Category Probability Impact
Technical and Operational High Medium
Description
Energy access companies that are newly entering a volatile market, may not be able to execute on first-
time energy access goals, and may struggle to generate high volumes of quality sales. Last mile
distributors may face difficulties with expanding their operations in H2R markets with immature business
operations,and external market, political, currency, and macro level risks.
Additionally, Acumen is expanding into new markets that the firm has not invested in to date. Inexperience
in the market could expose the project to unexpected political, legal, and other forms of risk. Acumen also
may have some gaps in navigating the market landscape in H2R markets leading to longer due diligence or
missed investment opportunities.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The chief mitigant to execution risk for Investees will be to ensure that companies have the funds and
accompaniment they need to build capacity. The team engaged with many off-grid solar companies about
the right investment instruments, tenors, and loan terms needed to incentivize companies into entering or
scaling in H2R markets. Following the information gathering phase, creating realistic, data-based
projections will be essential, as will combining funding with needed resources such as Technical
Assistance (TA) and market research. The Market Support Facility, with its focus on building capacity and
stable operational foundations, ahead of scale-up, offers calibration to the ambition of the project,
demonstrating an acknowledgement that any expectation of immediately high sales would be unrealistic
and hazardous. That being said, this project is ambitious and high risk (and in our view, necessary for the
world’s poor).

Selected Risk Factor 2: Macro
Category Probability Impact
Other High High
Description
Hardest-to-Reach markets often face significant security risks, political volatility, regulatory inconsistency
and legislative unpredictability. These risks do not exist in isolation, some even have the potential to be
correlated across a given region. A major crisis or series of interlocking risk events could derail progress on
energy access.
Moreover, global trends have been very impactful to volatile markets and unstable political environments.
Inflation, a potential global recession, and the ongoing effects of the Covid-19 pandemic have created even
more instability in H2R markets.
Macro and global risks have had significant impacts on potential offgrid solar customers. Rising inflation
has increased the costs of necessary goods and services making other expenditures less affordable for
people in poverty. Covid-19 created lock downs and supply chain issues that contributed to unemployment
in some markets and harmful shipping delays for OGS companies.
Mitigation Measure(s)
Targeted technical assistance may support legal evaluation to understand risks. Political risk insurance can
be a valuable tool to hedge some of these risks. The team has conducted multiple political risk studies on
H2R markets. The team intends to create political risk assessments for each market . Macro risks for
each investment will be summarized in investment memos and will be shared with the Investment
Committee along with strategies to address the risk aligned to the context of the specific investment. It’s
also worth mentioning that H2R will have a broad portfolio, diversifying risk across a range of geographies.

Description
Energy companies that feel under pressure to repay loans and show growth may opt to sell more to higher-
income segments, negating some or all of the company’s proposed additional impact.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The use of impact-linked grants and loans, which will incorporate a measure of the depth of poverty of a
customer base, will be used to incentivize companies to target lower-income segments.The impact-indexed
loans will have KPIs to ensure customer retention is achieved responsibly and sustainably.
Additionally, Acumen will conduct thorough due diligence on each Hardest-to-Reach investment to ensure
that companies are capable of properly utilizing H2R funds. The IC will be instructed on ensuring that the
mission is a core component of each investment. Term sheets will stipulate the use of funds for each loan
or equity investment.
Selected Risk Factor 4: Distortion
Category Probability Impact
Other Medium Low
Description
The act of choosing a subset of companies to fund, some of which may operate in existing sub-Saharan
African markets, could distort the future market for off-grid solar, and crowd out less well-connected
companies. Relatedly, the volume of concessionary debt going towards energy companies could distort the
overall energy access debt market.
Mitigation Measure(s)
While there are existing companies operating in Hardest-to-Reach markets, there are not many of them,
and few if any that have reached a significant scale serving the most challenging reaches of the country.
By incentivizing companies to reach first-time customers, H2R is creating and nurturing new markets.
within weak-grid and off-grid areas, thus the risk of distorting an existing market remains low.. As evidence
from ODI suggests, the risk of crowding out other possible (private) sources of finance is less relevant in
low-income countries where financial markets are insufficiently developed, and investors are unlikely to
have access to international capital markets at affordable rates in the absence of the concessional
intervention. In addition, the concessionality provided to the companies is linked to the impacts achieved in
terms of first time energy access and poverty level of customers, which will likely ensure that the benefits of
concessionality pass down to the low income, first time energy access customers (in terms of increased
supply of entry-level products) and minimize a potential for market distortion.
