 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
 | Category |  |  | Probability |  |  | Impact | 
 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
Other |  |  | Medium |  |  | Low |  | 
 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
 | Description |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
The act of choosing a subset of companies to fund, some of which may operate in existing sub-Saharan
African markets, could distort the future market for off-grid solar, and crowd out less well-connected
companies. Relatedly, the volume of concessionary debt going towards energy companies could distort the
overall energy access debt market. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
 | Mitigation Measure(s) |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
While there are existing companies operating in Hardest-to-Reach markets, there are not many of them,
and few if any that have reached a significant scale serving the most challenging reaches of the country.
By incentivizing companies to reach first-time customers, H2R is creating and nurturing new markets.
within weak-grid and off-grid areas, thus the risk of distorting an existing market remains low.. As evidence
from ODI suggests, the risk of crowding out other possible (private) sources of finance is less relevant in
low-income countries where financial markets are insufficiently developed, and investors are unlikely to
have access to international capital markets at affordable rates in the absence of the concessional
intervention. In addition, the concessionality provided to the companies is linked to the impacts achieved in
terms of first time energy access and poverty level of customers, which will likely ensure that the benefits of
concessionality pass down to the low income, first time energy access customers (in terms of increased
supply of entry-level products) and minimize a potential for market distortion. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 151
F
Category Probability Impact
Operational and Technical Medium High
Description
When the program ends, the end of concessionary financing could mean that firms find Hardest-to-Reach
markets unsustainable to operate in or cease serving low-income segments within those markets.
Mitigation Measure(s)
Hardest-to-Reach is an integrated life-cycle financing to accompany companies to expand into new,
challenging markets and to support their sustainable growth over the longer term through supportive
patient capital and line of sight working capital financing which is linked to impact outcomes, which will
contribute to building robust markets in Hardest-to-Reach geographies. Over time, the success of H2R
investees can derisk these previously untested markets while also demonstrating the success pathway -
including through the use of blended finance. Combined this should make it easier for these companies to
access financing. In addition, H2R seeks to address the viability gaps faced by companies in terms of
capacity, strategy and enabling environment. Over the life of the two vehicles, two pools of technical
assistance capital will support ecosystem development to ensure that, through training, local capacity
building, and stakeholder coordination efforts - among other things - the sustainability of the intervention is
enhanced and impacts beyond the life of the fund continue in a self-sustaining way.
Selected Risk Factor 6: Due Diligence
Probability Impact
Category
Governance Low Medium
Description
Operating in certain countries and through certain on-lending structures (particularly onto smaller
distributors) poses a DD challenge, Where good market information is scarce, this increases the complexity
of conducting satisfactory due diligence and thus the risk of financing operationally, financially and/or
reputationally unsuitable companies.
Mitigation Measure(s)
In addition to careful due diligence and investment structuring, in-depth market studies inform the H2R
strategy at the country-level, as well as uncover macro risks. In the case of distributor finance via
manufacturers, the investment team will work closely with the manufacturer borrowers/on-lenders to
screen-out distributors that are not suitable for this facility for financial or ESG reasons.

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 152
F
Category Probability Impact
Forex Medium Medium
Description
Currency or Foreign Exchange risk (FX Risk) is a key inhibitor of capital inflows and deal progress in the
off-grid energy sector, particularly in least developed countries such as the ones that Hardest-to-Reach
aims to impact. Local companies face challenges when receiving loans in ‘hard currency’ while their
operations and sales are managed with local currency. Significant depreciation in local currency value
could make it very challenging for distributors to service their H2R debt.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The due diligence process will incorporate an assessment of country risk, including foreign exchange and
hard currency liquidity risk. Acumen is exploring the feasibility of local currency lending alongside hedging
partners.
Selected Risk Factor 8: Forced Labor
Category Probability Impact
Reputational Low Medium
Description
Raw materials for solar products and some solar products may come from geographies currently under
international scrutiny for forced labor practices. Several solar product manufacturers also operate in areas
under international scrutiny for forced labor practices. It is also estimated that there are 3.7 million forced
laborers in sub-Saharan Africa, largely in the informal economy (particularly in informal, artisanal cobalt
mining industries within several H2R target countries). There is therefore some risk of forced labor in the
value chain.
Mitigation Measure(s)
Acumen will include forced labor in its ESMS and will integrate it into its company due diligence, including
requesting disclosure of suppliers from potential portfolio companies, and conducting ongoing monitoring.
Acumen will mitigate forced labor through the use of screening tools, in its deal terms and as part of its
monitoring and evaluation process.

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 153
F
Governance Medium Low
Description
Some companies that receive H2R investment are early-stage startups, and may have inefficient
management or governance structure which may result in ineffective decision making and the funds
allowed to them may not be utilized properly. This risk could materialize due to separation of key-
executives or change in group share-holding structures. The materialization of this risk could result in
ineffective decision making at company’s level and the company might not achieve desired outcome from
the availed funds which will ultimately impact on their repayments. Projected H2R impact, including GHG
emissions, households accessing renewable energy, and retained employment, may fail to materialize.
This failure could result from a number of factors, including, but not limited to, ongoing effects of the
COVID-19 pandemic, customers’ inability to pay, and/or mismanagement of companies receiving H2R
investments.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The facility manager has a well-designed credit due diligence process which involves detailed review of
ownership, governance, management and board structure/effectiveness along-with interviews of senior
management. In case any weakness is identified, at the assessment level the borrowers are advised to
resolve these issues appropriately along-with these strong covenants are also incorporated to improve the
governance structure. Furthermore, any major change in ownership structure is also restricted in the legal
documentation. The screening process described in the ESMS is meant to ensure that H2R investments
are directed to companies with a viable, impactful business model. These measures, combined with the
monitoring and oversight described in Section E, should mitigate the risk of attenuated impact H2R expects
to have limited exposure to governance risks. Locally owned and managed early stage distributors,who
may have more governance risks than other investees in the H2R portfolio could be invested with the
support of relevant advisors with local market expertise. If H2R finds that a company has particular
governance risks, the manager may decide to create conditions subsequent to address these risks.
Selected Risk Factor 10: Sanctions and AML/KYC
Category Probability Impact
Sanctions Low Medium
Description
Hardest-to-Reach is investing in countries that are on the UN Sanctions List. Hardest-to-Reach seeks to
make investments in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Somalia. Investing in these countries
increases the likelihood of investing in companies or individuals that are on UN Sanctions Lists or other
sanctions lists. The materialization of this risk can have serious consequences such as blockage of funds
from investors, regulatory or criminal proceedings against the funds/investors, sanctions, and may also
cause monetary losses.

Mitigation Measure(s)
The Hardest-to-Reach team has conducted extensive market and political risk research across H2R
markets. The team has developed a strong level of knowledge of country-specific risks across H2R
markets.
As a result of this research, Acumen has developed a project-specific AML/KYC plan that details the
AML/KYC policies and procedure.
Each potential investee that has been IC approved is expected to undergo a thorough background check.
The diligence team will also seek to diligence key persons including their board, investors, senior
management, founders, and the C-suite. If any company is linked to money laundering or financing of
terrorism then they will not receive H2R funds.
In the DRC and Somalia, prior to investment, the H2R team will check UN Sanctions Lists, Terrorist
Exclusion Lists, The Office of Foreign Assets Control watchlist, and others to ensure that no key persons
are on the +100 watchlists. If people are identified on the lists, H2R will not proceed with the investment.
Selected Risk Factor 11: Excluded Activities
Category Probability Impact
Prohibited practices Low Medium
Description
Hardest-to-Reach is reaching new markets and investing in early-stage companies with limited track
records who may engage in prohibited practices. If regulatory entities or investors find that a company
engages in prohibited practices, the company or individual could face criminal charges, shutting down of
operations, or blockage of funds from investors. If H2R is found to invest in such a company, the
materialization of this risk can have serious consequences such as blockage of funds from investors,
regulatory or criminal proceedings against the funds/investors, sanctions and may also cause monetary
losses.
Mitigation Measure(s)
Hardest-to-Reach has developed an Exclusion List to screen out potential Investees engaging in any
prohibited practices. Potential Investees will be required to declare that they do not engage in any activity,
do not fund any activity, and do not support any activity on the Exclusion List. If a company does engage in
activity on the Exclusion List then they cannot receive H2R financing. H2R investees will also agree to a
binding legal agreement that prohibits engagement in Exclusion List activities.

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 155
F
Credit Medium High
Description
The imposition of ambitious, time-bound impact goals could create incentives to push the number of loans
at the expense of quality. This could have a deleterious effect on the credit risk management of energy
companies, reducing the stability of their cashflows and viability in the medium term. Companies could also
respond by adopting aggressive collections techniques at the risk of breaching relevant consumer rights
and legal protections. This could create overindebtedness among low-income households, and other
consumer protection-related concerns.
Mitigation Measure(s)
For PAYGo companies, business viability is dependent on more than sales volume. Cash flow only comes
from a pool of receivables if they are of sufficient quality. Assessing risk management capacity, monitoring
portfolio health, and incorporating collections rate into the index for impact-linked loans will likely be
essential. TA support is available for investees with portfolios showing signs of deterioration and the due
diligence process is designed to flag the types of weaknesses in governance and business processes that
make poorly managed growth more likely. Ensuring that companies subscribe and adhere to the GOGLA
Consumer Protection Principles is one practical mitigant. H2R due diligence process will seek to identify
any CP weakness/challenges faced by the potential investee. Investees will be supported to fulfill and grow
beyond the minimum standards of practice in their treatment of customers, in order to safeguard impacts
and respect the rights of consumers

out in the initial investment strategy. Operating in H2R contexts is high risk and materialization of this risk
could result in investee defaults and lower fund-level returns.

a 2x 1-year extension at the fund manager's discretion, to create flexibility around the timing of equity exits
and possible debt restructuring.

Description
H2R faces the risk of not being able to source investments and build pipelines of the target size. Local
distributors may not be investable and H2R could spend time, money, and energy on due diligence for
companies that do not meet H2R expectations. As H2R is a time bound program, any delays in deploying
capital would negatively impact potential returns and scaling impact.
Mitigation Measure(s) The goals of the MSF are to create strength in OGS distributors and to support

be viable MEF pipeline borrowers. In addition, part of the MSF strategy is to establish new entities, through
a JV structure, to initiate the growth of markets with few or no investable opportunities. H2R has developed
strong screening and eligibility criteria for a variety of the investing activities to ensure quality of investment
proposals.

engagement with stakeholders throughout project development and implementation. The H2R project team

Key Project Level Environmental and Social Risks
The project has four primary environmental and social risk concerns:
● E-waste
● Consumer Protection
● Forced Labor
● OGS Company ESG Readiness
E-waste
While there are many strong environmental benefits to Hardest-To-Reach, the project team recognizes
both environmental and climate risks for the project. One of Hardest-To-Reach’s primary environmental
concerns is solar e-waste. Off-grid businesses will be selling millions of products to first time buyers in the
H2R markets. These markets have weak and nascent waste management sectors. Moreover, many
African countries have weak regulatory requirements for e-waste. Last mile distributors may have weak or
immature e-waste policies, procedures, and procurement. Moreover, the e-waste markets in Hardest-to-
Reach countries are in a nascent stage with few players and little coverage.
Consumer Protection
There are two primary social risks for Hardest-To-Reach. First, pay-as-you-go (PAYGo), products sold on
credit, create risks for customers who can face issues such as over-indebtedness, poor credit, and defunct
products if they fall behind on their payments. PAYGo also allows many customers who could not afford to
pay for a solar home system up front the opportunity to access electricity with smaller recurring payments.
Additionally, the team has concerns around consumer privacy and protections for PAYGo and other solar
home system customers. While many companies are now GOGLA consumer protection signatories,
customers still face the risk of customer data being compromised, improperly stored, stolen, or sold to
malicious third parties. Infringing on customer data protections may open off-grid solar customers to stolen
identity, fraud, and other issues surrounding identity theft.
Forced Labor
Second, the H2R management team is concerned about forced labor in the solar supply chain. Human
rights investigators have found evidence of forced labor in some regions where there are solar
manufacturers. Advocacy groups warn that marginalized people may be facing mass detention in certain

=== PAGE 164 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 160
G
regions. Moreover, these marginalized people face dangerous working conditions that may be exacerbated
by ongoing global trends. Advocacy groups and human rights officials expect these global factors to create
downward pressure on manufacturers to increase forced labor practices under worsening conditions.
OGS Company ESG Readiness
The project team expects that Hardest-to-Reach will invest in companies with varying degrees of ESG
readiness. Larger and more established off-grid solar companies are expected to demonstrate maturity
across a number of ESG issues. Several larger pipeline companies have indicated that they have strong
ESMSs, consumer protection policies, and other environmental and social mitigants in place. Acumen’s
experience has demonstrated that early-stage SHS companies, especially last mile distributors, may not
have robust ESG policies and procedures, nor would they have strong organizational capacity to mitigate
ESG risks. These companies have a small footprint so their risks are marginal to the project success and
impact on beneficiaries.
The Hardest-to-Reach ESMS includes the ESIA, which has a more extensive report on project and
company level environmental and social risks and impacts.
Environmental and Social Risk Mitigants
To ensure the Hardest-to-Reach project achieves its mission and impact, the team has designed a
thorough ESMS aligned with GCF Policy, Acumen Policy, and industry best practices.
The ESMS shares the project development, management, and monitoring and reporting policies and
procedures. All investments will be screened against the project Exclusion List before being accepted for
due diligence.
The project team will diligence companies with a variety of ESG diligence tools including base-line
questionnaires, site visits, company evidence in the form of policies and procedures, desktop research, a
climate resilience assessment tool, and supplementary questionnaires.
The ESG findings will be memorialized in an ESG due diligence report and the investment memo. The
Investment Committee is expected to consider ESG factors in their deliberations. The ESG due diligence
report will also provide the information needed for developing the term sheet binding, time bound, ESG
Action Plan.
The project will offer Portfolio Companies technical assistance tailored to supporting company-specific
ESG, consumer protection, gender, and business readiness needs. This will include: needs diagnostics,
webinars, direct support, and policy and procedure guidance and resources.

Indigenous Peoples
The program intends to have a landing page on the AE website that will share information about the
program including the ESMS. We seek to provide guidance on how indigenous communities can request
support from the GCF independent Redress Mechanism and/or the GCF Secretariat’s indigenous peoples
focal point at any stage, including before a claim has been made. Additionally, the team seeks for H2R
investees to have indigenous peoples’ policies that will communicate how GCF can be reached. This is
especially important for investees that directly engage with indigenous communities.
Acumen, as the AE, and the H2R team has reached out to indigenous organizations to learn from, share
the project design, and ask for input. We have also asked NDAs to connect our team with indigenous
communities. We seek meaningful engagement with indigenous populations who may be impacted by the
project prior to first close. We intend to report to indigenous organizations about project activity and direct
them to OGS expanding in areas that have indigenous populations so that they can benefit from access to
affordable, clean, electricity opportunities.

G
Acumen has conducted a thorough and robust gender assessment for the Hardest-to-Reach project
aligned with the objectives of GCF’s Gender Policy, Acumen’s Gender Sensitivity Policy for GCF-funded
projects. The gender assessment informed the development of the Hardest-to-Reach Gender Lens
Investing Strategy and the Hardest-to-Reach Gender Action Plan. The H2R gender assessment and GAP
are detailed in Annex 8.
As part of a H2R pilot project, Acumen hired a lead consumer impact surveying business to survey
beneficiaries of the pilot project. The H2R team will need to learn from more beneficiaries, but the initial
findings demonstrated similar impacts for men and women. Both groups felt the need and importance of
using SHS products to attain electricity.
The team also conducted extensive stakeholder engagement across the Hardest-to-Reach markets
including speaking with companies, government entities, industry associations, NGOs, and civil society
organizations. The H2R team spoke with local gender experts and civil society organizations from multiple
H2R markets on local gender challenges and opportunities that informed our gender lens investing strategy
and gender work.
The H2R team worked to do project-level gender assessment that included 14 country assessments.
The team generated two country assessments for the remaining Hardest-to-Reach countries. The team
relied on desktop research, industry experts, gender experts, OGS companies, and survey data to inform
the gender assessments, GLI strategy, and Gender Action Plan.
Findings
Barriers to gender equality in OGS sector
The link between energy access and gender equality is well recognized. Energy poverty has a strong
gender dimension as the lack of access to energy inhibits women’s well-being, and their access to
economic opportunities, and it strongly affects women’s living conditions and time-use.
One of the key barriers in the market relates to lack of sex-disaggregated data for the OGS sector both at
the consumer and workforce levels.
Gender and social norms limit women’s access to technologies and their abilities to enter the workforce.
Companies have a limited understanding of the business case for gender inclusion in their businesses, and
of how to make their practices more inclusive. Several companies we spoke with shared that they are
beginning to build institutional capacity on gender and want to build inclusive policies and procedures into
their operations.

=== PAGE 167 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 163
G
Serving women with OGS technologies
Overall, evidence shows that women have less access to off-grid electricity than their male counterparts,
and they mostly use pico-solar products and lanterns or other lower-tier technologies.183 An analysis
conducted by Value for Women on 59 companies working in the energy sector found that only 23% of
companies collect sex-disaggregated data on customers, and half of them reported that they serve 46% of
customers who are women. In H2R country contexts, prevalent gender norms are likely to affect access to
off-grid solar technologies, influencing companies’ abilities to reach women. Discriminatory gender norms
inhibit women’s rights to own land and other assets, making it challenging for women to access credit and
purchase renewable energy technologies. PAYGo companies may reach a lower percentage of women
customers due to additional barriers related to mobile ownership and mobile money usage among women.
Women’s participation in OGS companies’ workforce
ESMAP and GOGLA recently surveyed 37 OGS companies from 20 different countries and found that on
average women constitute 41.7% of workers across all levels. In contrast, a previous GOGLA study
indicated that only 27% of women work in the OGS sector. An analysis completed by Value for Women
found that on average women represent 33% of the workforce of energy companies.
The country assessments indicate that several barriers limit women’s participation in the workforce and in
the economy more generally, with prevailing gender norms, gaps in education levels and discriminatory
policies and practices affecting women’s productive activities and economic empowerment in several
countries.
Hardest-to-Reach Gender Work
Hardest-to-Reach seeks to build OGS markets with a gender lens, and strong commitment to gender
equity. H2R is also committed to supporting companies to build their gender capacity to support their
operations and their customers. Additionally, H2R is committed to mitigating risks of sexual harassment,
abuse, and exploitation across the project, investees, and beneficiaries.
All companies will undergo a gender assessment to determine their gender strengths and weaknesses.
Opportunities for growth will be captured in a binding Gender Action Plan. All companies in the H2R
portfolio will have to create a GAP that will be monitored over the company engagement with H2R.
Companies must commit to strong anti-sexual harassment policies, non-discrimination policies, and their
best effort to collect sex-disaggregated data.
183 ESMAP (2022) Gender equality in the off-grid solar sector. A primer. The World Bank Group, Washington DC 2022

indictments, and convictions), and financial history (i.e., foreclosures, bankruptcies,
etc.).
ii) The different investing strategies the the Program will implore (Market Support
Facility and Market Expansion Facility), and requisite sectoral expertise and
operational infrastructure necessary for the distinct approaches.
1.2. Recording and Processing: Accounts payable will be reviewed and processed at the end
of each week. Each invoice is submitted to the Program’s accounting platform for review and
approval and must have an associated vendor record in the system. Before approving, the
appropriate finance employee will review all invoices, wires, checks and account coding.
1.3. Reconciling: The Program reconciles all bank, petty cash, and investment accounts
monthly, as follows:
a. Once available, the Finance Associate (or designate) reviews all relevant bank
statements
b. The Finance Associate (or designate) will complete the reconciliation within seven days
c. The following is the general outline to be used to reconcile accounts:
i) Comparison of bank statements and cash receipts, verifying dates and totals
deposited.
ii) Comparison of bank and/or wire transfer dates received against dates sent.

iii) Investigations of items rejected by the bank (i.e., returned checks or deposits).

2. Expense Reporting Procedures
2.1. Principles and Procedures:
a. The Finance Associate Director will be responsible for compiling monthly and year-to-
date expense reports. Expense reports are reconciled to the general ledger and accounting
records.
b. Quarterly financial reports, analyzing the Program’s financial position and the
effectiveness of its management, will be presented to its Limited Partners as required.
c. Records to be maintained include copies of contracts, invoices, changes to contracts or
budgets, proof of payments, and allocation tracking.
3. Expected Contractors
The Program may contract consultants for several purposes. Technical Assistance consultants will be
hired for expertise in ESG; Consumer Protection; Gender Equity; Business development (as it relates
to fundraising and financial systems management) for companies; Legal and Accountants/auditors.
The Program’s Market Support Facility (MSF) will focus on early-stage investments, employing equity,
equity-like, impact index loans, grants, and joint venture financing options. Launched in January 2023,
the MSF will run through to 2033. Although negotiations remain on-going, the Program has preliminarily
selected both a local market advisor and a separate small-ticket debt advisor. In each case, the firms
distinguished themselves from other providers through their unique value (i.e., their extensive
experience in both debt and equity lending to early stage off-grid energy companies across the
Program’s target geographies).
Conversely, the Program’s Market Expansion Facility (MEF) has both a separate investment vehicle
structure, strategy, and instrument size. The MEF will target later stage, more established companies
with larger ticket sizes, utilizing impact index loans (working capital), and receivables financing, and will
be structured as a pooled investment vehicle. With an expected launch in January 2024, the MEF will
run through to 2034. Given the difference in approach, in addition to the types of providers noted
above, the Program is considering contracting with certain service providers to support fund
management, such as an administrator and back office and support in risk assessments. While

G.4. Disclosure of funding proposal
Note: The Information Disclosure Policy (IDP) provides that the GCF will apply a presumption in favour of
disclosure for all information and documents relating to the GCF and its funding activities. Under the IDP,
project and programme funding proposals will be disclosed on the GCF website, simultaneous with the
submission to the Board, subject to the redaction of any information that may not be disclosed pursuant to
the IDP. Information provided in confidence is one of the exceptions, but this exception should not be
applied broadly to an entire document if the document contains specific, segregable portions that can be
disclosed without prejudice or harm.
Indicate below whether or not the funding proposal includes confidential information.
☐ No confidential information: The accredited entity confirms that the funding proposal, including its
annexes, may be disclosed in full by the GCF, as no information is being provided in confidence.
X With confidential information: The accredited entity declares that the funding proposal, including its
annexes, may not be disclosed in full by the GCF, as certain information is being provided in confidence.
Accordingly, the accredited entity is providing to the Secretariat the following two copies of the funding
proposal, including all annexes:
● full copy for internal use of the GCF in which the confidential portions are marked accordingly,
together with an explanatory note regarding the said portions and the corresponding reason for
confidentiality under the accredited entity’s disclosure policy, and
● redacted copy for disclosure on the GCF website.
The funding proposal can only be processed upon receipt of the two copies above, if containing
confidential information.

We refer to the programme titled “Hardest-to-Reach” in Angola, Benin, Burkina Faso, Burundi,
Central African Republic, Chad, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Lesotho,

strategies, and plans of the Democratic Republic of the Congo;

in the funding proposal is in conformity with relevant national laws and regulations.
We also confirm that our national process for ascertaining no-objection to the programme as
included in the funding proposal has been duly followed.

GCF/B.36/02/Add.06

Independent Technical Advisory Panel’s assessment of
FP211
Proposal name: Hardest-to-Reach
Accredited entity: Acumen Fund
Project/programme size: Medium
I. Assessment of the independent Technical Advisory Panel
1.1 Overview
1. The Hardest-to-Reach (H2R) programme is designed to supply off-grid solar (OGS)
energy to low-income populations in 16 least developed countries (LDCs) in sub-Saharan Africa.
It aims to develop an OGS ecosystem in countries with low electrification and high poverty
rates. The initiative supplies capital to OGS companies entering and expanding in these nascent
markets. Although the OGS market is thriving in many parts of Africa, there is reluctance among
companies to enter LDC markets and to engage with the poorest. These markets are considered
too risky by OGS companies, which prefer to focus their limited capacities on more profitable
and low-risk markets. The programme seeks to deliver clean first-time electricity access to over
54 million beneficiaries with high rates of poverty, where investors have not been willing to
enter at sufficient scale to meet the energy access needs of underserved segments.
2. The USD 250 million programme plans to establish two separate financing facilities with
different investment risk profiles. This is designed to help OGS companies expand in H2R
countries and extend their reach. The USD 50 million Market Support Facility (MSF) shall be
grant funded by philanthropies and donors and includes a USD 10 million reimbursable grant
from GCF. The MSF aims to support and improve the capacity of local players and regional
companies for market entry through grants, equity, debt, and technical assistance. For the USD
200 million Market Expansion Facility (MEF), Acumen intends to raise USD 145 million across
commercial investors and development finance institutions (DFIs), anchored by a USD 50
million junior equity tranche and a USD 5 million non-repayable grant capital from GCF. The
MEF aims to provide impact-linked concessionary loans to scale up companies’ operations and
settle in H2R countries. Interest rates shall be adjusted based on results achieved in terms of
first-time energy access and poverty level of the customers. The USD 65 million concessional
financing from GCF in the form of grant and junior equity is expected to mobilize private finance
to support OGS companies and build a sustainable OGS ecosystem in the challenging markets for
just energy systems transitions.
1.2 Impact potential Scale: High
3. The programme has both mitigation and adaptation impacts. The mitigation impact is
estimated at 5.1 megatonne of carbon dioxide equivalent (Mt CO eq) reduced over the lifespan
2
of the programme and, as adaptation outcome, the project expects to reach 54 million
beneficiaries of which 9 million are direct beneficiaries.
4. The mitigation outcome is achieved by providing OGS products to people to achieve
clean energy access (tier 1+). 120 MW of decentralized OGS energy generation capacity shall be
newly installed. Currently, the majority of rural households rely on kerosene and biomass as

=== PAGE 202 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.06
Page 198
their primary energy sources for lighting, cooking, heating, etc. In the baseline scenario, a large
portion of households do not have access to electricity due to lack of grids and low-income
levels, which limit a household’s ability to pay for electricity. The programme reduces the need
to rely on fossil fuels and biomass by replacing them with solar energy.
5. The greenhouse gas (GHG) mitigation impact was calculated using the United Nations
Framework Convention on Climate Change registered clean development mechanism
methodologies AMS-III.AR. (“Substituting fossil fuel-based lighting with LED/CFL lighting
systems”) and AMS-I.L. (“Electrification of rural communities using renewable energy”).
Assumptions for distribution of funds between solar home systems and lanterns, the number of
units to be financed per area, as well as the expected lifetime of products are presented by the
programme in a transparent manner and are considered to be reasonable. Black carbon
emissions have not been included by the programme in the calculations, which is conservative
especially as kerosene lamps have high potential black carbon emissions. The achievement of
the expected mitigation outcome is reliant on reaching the expected fund size and product
placement. Overall, the projected GHG emission reductions are deemed to have been calculated
in a conservative manner.
6. The expected adaptation outcome is 54 million direct and indirect beneficiaries. Indirect
beneficiaries are calculated by multiplying OGS sales by factor 5, which corresponds to the
average number of people per household in H2R countries. The 54 million beneficiaries are
people with first-time access to electricity. Rural electricity access in programme countries is 11
per cent on average.
7. The increase in resilience to climate change through the programme is based on the
following expected outcomes: (i) most vulnerable people and communities would still have
access to energy in the aftermath of displacement-inducing natural disasters caused by climate
change due to owning OGS products. It was calculated that 1.6 million people could benefit from
enhanced energy security through the programme based on the expected number of people to
be displaced due to climate hazards within the total projected number of H2R beneficiaries; (ii)
health, well-being, food and water security could be enhanced as OGS customers would be able
to more securely access information including extreme weather event and health warnings,
health information, and market data, such as for agricultural produce. OGS products linked with
additional devices, such as radios or mobile phones, allow access to climate-related information.
Seventy-five per cent of the total 72 million beneficiaries (of which 54 million are beneficiaries
with first-time electricity access and therefore counted as beneficiaries in the adaptation
outcome) are expected to access electricity power for the first time with an OGS product. This
results in a total of 54 million beneficiaries with improved access to information; and (iii) most
vulnerable people and communities’ benefit from increased and/or diversified income sources.
Energy access can contribute to increasing household income by increasing working hours
through access to light and increasing opportunities for home-based business. A 60 Decibels
energy benchmark study revealed that 10 per cent of OGS clients could diversify and increase
their income base.1 Based on the 54 million first-time customers of OGS, this results in 5.4
million direct beneficiaries profiting from increased and more diversified income sources. The
total number of 54 million beneficiaries is based on the maximum number of beneficiaries of the
three aforementioned impact areas. The programme thus has a potential impact on increasing
the climate resilience of around 15 per cent of the total population in the participating
countries.
8. The three core adaptation outcomes of the programme, while expected to be significant,
may be challenging to measure or report to GCF. While the programme’s logical framework
includes “User surveys to determine beneficiaries with improved and/or new climate-resilient
livelihood options”, no mention is made of tracking enhanced access to climate-relevant
1 60 Decibels. (2020). Why Off-Grid Energy Matters.

=== PAGE 203 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.06
Page 199
information through OGS-powered communication media. In terms of the assumptions made
that the OGS products installed will provide resilient energy access, through durability in the
face of extreme events and portability in the case of displacement, no mechanism has been built
in to monitor performance of the OGS products.
9. Overall, the independent Technical Advisory Panel (iTAP) considers that the
programme has a high adaptation and medium to high mitigation impact. Cumulatively, the
impact potential is considered to be high.
1.3 Paradigm shift potential Scale: Medium
10. The programme promotes the entrance of companies in the African energy sector into
off-grid markets, where investors have not been willing to enter up to the present. The blended
finance structure has the ability to crowd in investors that would otherwise find the markets too
nascent or risky through initiatives to de-risk these markets by providing new market entrants
with impact-linked concessional finance and targeted technical assistance. Last-mile
distributors have a crucial role to play in delivering OGS products, but capital is currently not
flowing into the space. The programme can thus achieve a transformational impact in reaching
clients and markets currently only marginally covered by private sector approaches.
11. Companies that thrive in these risky and nascent markets would be willing to increase
their business in these markets, thus resulting in positive multiplication effects. The programme
supports companies to build solid operational platforms in challenging markets, and to grow in
such markets, thereby scaling up their ventures and providing clean energy to a larger
population of unelectrified people.
12. Acumen intends to share the knowledge and evidence-based insights gained through the
programme. This can result in increased capital inflows and additional investments on the
ground. The programme’s demonstration of linking energy access and adaptation, as well as
showcasing that companies can also thrive in such difficult surroundings, should also unlock
funding for OGS ecosystems in more difficult markets. Demonstrating the viability of challenging
markets can unlock other investments from broader sources of capital, thereby sustaining the
growth of these markets in the long term and adding to a replication effect.
13. Scaling up the programme would depend to a large extent on the sustainability of
market efforts. Experiences with COVID-19 have shown that OGS companies struggled with high
levels of default among their customers. The Acumen project Participation in Energy Access
Relief Facility (FP148) outlined that energy access companies struggled with dramatically
reduced sales and collections, coupled with disrupted supply chains, limited cash reserves, and
tightening funding sources, which are crippling companies’ ability to fund operations. This
shows the fragile base of most companies in this market. While COVID-19 in conjunction with
other external factors can be considered extraordinary, the exposure of OGS companies to
external shocks remains high and the risk of defaults from their customers permanent. The
targeted poorer segments of society are especially exposed to numerous external shocks,
including climate-related ones, which can negatively affect their payment ability. For people
who are close to or below the poverty threshold, the payments for OGS equipment might be one
of the first to discontinue in case of existential needs.
14. The experience of many development activities is that successful interventions do not
replicate automatically. On-ground demonstration of successful intervention is a positive first
step but not sufficient for a high level of replication and transformational change. The
programme does require activities to include all relevant stakeholders and to actively manage
and spread the knowledge generated. This might not coincide with the goal of involved private
enterprises to avoid inflow of competition. Overall, the planned programme activities in the
area of knowledge management and outreach are not considered to be comprehensive enough

=== PAGE 204 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.06
Page 200
to result in a massive replication effect. However, this might well be taken up by international
development agencies and entities more familiar and experienced with outreach activities,
which could build upon the programme’s on-the-ground activities.
15. The programme’s focus is on working with private enterprises to make commercial
ventures in this market successful. The programme recognizes the importance of creating an
ecospace that is positive towards OGS, reducing barriers and creating incentives. This is largely
related to government policies and activities. While the programme does relate with the
involved governments, there is no clear and comprehensive engagement plan with the national
governments to improve the framework conditions.
16. Overall, iTAP considers that the programme has the potential to increase the appetite of
private companies and capital to also invest in more challenging markets and thus create a
paradigm shift. To have an even larger transformational impact, additional measures in the
realm of outreach, capacity-building, knowledge management, and stronger engagement with
governments will be required. However, this is not necessarily the core expertise of the parties
involved in the programme and it is highly probable that positive programme experiences
would be taken up by the international development community to “spread the word”. The
paradigm shift potential is considered to be medium.
1.4 Sustainable development potential Scale: Medium to High
17. The programme is aligned with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 7 (affordable,
reliable, modern and sustainable energy for all), SDG 3 (good health and well-being), SDG 4
(improved educational outcomes), SDGs 1 and 8 (economic savings and income generation), and
SDG 13 (climate action).
18. One factor that could limit sustainable development impacts, or even cause negative
impacts, is the local currency rate risk from MEF on-lending to OGS companies. The iTAP is
concerned about the financial sustainability of an MEF USD loan both from an OGS company and
an end-customer perspective. In the funding proposal, it is written that “Acumen is exploring
the feasibility of local currency lending alongside hedging partners” but, in discussions with
iTAP, Acumen wrote that “In the meantime, the H2R MEF would make loans in USD. The target
borrowers for H2R MEF would be expected to be sophisticated OGS companies with
multinational operations, aware of the impact of currency fluctuations on their borrowings.”
This essentially means that the OGS companies will pass those currency risks to the ultimate
hardest-to-reach consumers. Given current volatility in currency markets, such a pass-on can
potentially have devastating impact on the ability of those consumers to pay. Alternatively, if the
OGS companies are “forced” to keep that risk on their own balance sheet, it may jeopardize the
companies' financial viability. For the very sophisticated OGS companies who truly understand
the local currency risks in some of these markets, the MEF funding may not be even worth it.
19. In terms of benefits, OGS products can have positive impacts on people’s health and
safety. Traditional kerosene lanterns are harmful to people’s respiratory health because of
household pollutants, and can cause burns and fires. Indoor air pollution from kerosene
lanterns is related to particulate matter and carbon monoxide and disproportionately affects
women and children, who spend more time at home. According to a 60 Decibels study
conducted in 2020,2 48 per cent of OGS customers reported health improvements after
acquiring OGS products.
20. OGS systems can potentially help to preserve ecosystems and reduce deforestation by
substituting unsustainable biomass harvesting for energy usage with OGS systems.
2 60 Decibels. (2020). Why Off-Grid Energy Matters.

=== PAGE 205 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.06
Page 201
21. OGS products can enable people to generate income through their use, either directly
(e.g. expanding business hours or offering new services such as cell phone charging) or
indirectly (e.g. shifting tasks or activities to the evening because of better quality light). In the
case of biomass harvesting used in absence of OGS systems, it can also reduce workloads,
primarily of women and children, allowing more time to be dedicated to other activities. The
programme can also contribute towards increased financial inclusion and access to the formal
banking system through usage of the PAYGo financing structure to provide OGS products,
allowing people to build their credit histories.
22. The programme targets the creation of around 14,000 additional green jobs as a co-
benefit. An estimated 4,600 of these jobs could be a source of employment for women. However,
at least some of these jobs might not be additional ones but substitutes for jobs held before (e.g.
vendors of kerosene lanterns).
23. The programme will target the industry’s benchmark of having 32 per cent of its
customers as women and will aim to support women-led businesses. The programme also
intends to engage companies and the OGS ecosystem in developing more opportunities for
women to work. The programme will track gender-disaggregated data for multiple indicators,
allowing for the generation of knowledge on the engagement of women with energy products
and services useful throughout the OGS industry.
24. Overall, the sustainable development potential of the programme is considered medium
to high. It can make critical steps to improve the livelihoods of the poorest in a sustainable
manner. Tackling the currency risk could strongly improve the sustainability potential of the
programme.
1.5 Needs of the recipient Scale: High
25. Across the 16 African countries included, there are around 54 million beneficiaries that
do not have access to modern electricity services – representing roughly just under 10 per cent
of the total unelectrified population of sub-Saharan Africa. On average, 78 per cent of the
population in these countries lives below the lower-middle-income poverty line. They are
residing in acutely climate vulnerable contexts in terms of worsening heat stress, more frequent
droughts, more intense floods, and extreme weather events. Nearly half of the bottom twenty
countries listed in the Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN) climate vulnerability
index3 are programme countries. Regional vulnerability to the increasing climate hazards is
exacerbated by non-climate drivers such as high poverty levels, weak infrastructure systems,
lack of emergency response capabilities, and fragile grid electricity and telecommunications
networks.
26. At country and company level, limited investment can currently be attracted to the
market targeted by the programme. Eighty per cent of the capital raised by OGS companies
between 2012–2019 has flowed to larger and more established, first-generation companies
whose primary location and focus is East Africa, with Kenya attracting the lion’s share of the
capital. OGS start-ups also focused on entrenching their market position and attracting higher
margin customers, leaving out the rural, poorer markets of LDCs with a higher actual and
perceived risk.
27. International financing going to developing economies in support of clean energy
focuses within sub-Saharan Africa on now-proven markets, and risks leaving other countries
and regions behind. Political instability, macroeconomic uncertainty, policy and regulatory
issues, institutional weaknesses, and lack of transparency contribute to a less favourable
3 The ND-GAIN Country Index summarizes a country's vulnerability to climate change and other global challenges in
combination with its readiness to improve resilience. Higher index scores are given to less climate vulnerable countries.

=== PAGE 206 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.06
Page 202
investment climate in targeted countries. Underinvested geographies are in need of capital
willing to take risks in untested OGS markets. The International Energy Agency states that the
affordability of clean energy transitions will depend on reducing the cost and improving the
availability of capital.4
28. The programme’s market focus and instruments used incentivize investment in the
areas and countries with the most urgent financing needs. GCF funding is critical to enable and
mobilize private sector investment. GCF investment is in line with its core purpose of enabling
and catalysing investment in critical and risky areas with a high need and demand where
private capital would otherwise not flow. The iTAP therefore considers the needs of the
recipient as high.
1.6 Country ownership Scale: Medium
29. The prioritization of the energy sector in most nationally determined contributions
(NDCs) is likely to reflect both its relevance as a large emission source and the availability of
various cost-effective mitigation measures. All developing countries included mitigation
measures within the energy sector in their NDCs. The programme is also aligned with national
electrification strategies and national adaptation plans.
30. No-objection letters have been received from the 16 programme countries: Benin,
Burkina Faso, Burundi, Chad, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Guinea, Guinea Bissau,
Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, the Niger, Sierra Leone, Somalia, Togo, Uganda, and Zambia.
31. The programme has developed a stakeholder engagement plan and has also realized
initial stakeholder engagement meetings. The programme plans to engage with stakeholders,
especially national designated authorities, at regular intervals though iTAP notes that a range of
other public actors would also be important to engage, including ministries related to energy
and trade and industry, and regulatory agencies. To date, the programme has engaged with over
90 different stakeholders across 28 countries, representing a variety of stakeholder groups. In
early 2023, Open Capital Advisors, on behalf of the programme, carried out five in-country visits
to five key programme markets to meet with relevant stakeholders and gain market insights.
Senior members of the programme team joined Open Capital Advisors for three of the trips.
32. The country ownership is assessed by iTAP as medium. The programme aligns with the
countries' NDCs and national adaptation plans. However, on-ground stakeholder engagement in
the 16 countries has so far been limited. Stakeholder and country participation and involvement
is thus to a significant extent a planned and hitherto unrealized activity.
1.7 Efficiency and effectiveness Scale: High
33. The programme intends to leverage additional capital of factor 3 relative to the GCF
contribution for the overall MEF, and factor 4 including the MSF and the MEF. Government
agencies, foundations, DFIs, governments and even commercial investors have indicated
interest in layering their capital with first-loss grant capital. If primarily government agencies,
foundations and DFIs invest, the co-investment from the private sector will, however,
presumably be fairly limited.
34. The total investment amount shall exceed by factor 3 the initial project investment
amount, based on anticipated reinvestments.
4 International Energy Agency. (2021). Financing Clean Energy Transitions in Emerging and Developing Economies. Paris:
International Energy Agency.

=== PAGE 207 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.06
Page 203
35. The USD 250 million programme (for the MSF and the MEF) targets the provision of
entry level electricity access to 72 million people (of which 54 million access for the first-time
electricity) at a cost of around USD 3.5 per person, which is considered to be low-cost.
36. The estimated GCF cost per t CO 2 eq avoided, considering the 50 per cent assigned GCF
financing to mitigation, is around USD 6, which is considered low. The GCF funding generates
significant adaptation benefits by providing first-time energy access and strengthening the
climate resilience of 54 million people.
37. Acumen has successful and broad experience with similar initiatives, also with the GCF
(i.e. KawiSafi Ventures Fund FP005 and Participation in Energy Access Relief Facility FP148).
The capacity of Acumen to set up, oversee and manage such funds is deemed as high. The MSF
funds shall be transferred to a newly formed limited liability company, which will be a pass-
through entity wholly owned by the accredited entity (AE). The MEF is expected to be formed as
a general partnership with the AE which is expected to indirectly wholly own the general
partner.
38. The overall iTAP assessment concerning efficiency and effectiveness is high as the
programme can achieve significant mitigation and adaptation impact at a low cost while
crowding in potentially some, albeit limited, additional private finance.
II. Overall remarks from the independent Technical Advisory Panel
39. Based on the assessment above, iTAP endorses this funding proposal.
40. The iTAP notes that the programme is entering a potentially high-risk market and that,
in the learning stage, various ventures will probably fail. However, the approach proposed, and
the measures taken, as well as the experience of the AE in this type of venture, ensure that risks
are managed well while still striving to reach people underserved by traditional private sector
approaches. The role of GCF is to provide risk finance to push the borders beyond business as
usual and to reach people not covered by traditional approaches through an effective approach
with a high impact and replication potential. Therefore, the programme ticks all the boxes of the
investment criteria set forward by GCF.
41. The iTAP recommends that the AE strengthen the logical framework to be able to track
progress towards adaptation outcomes 3 and 4. The user surveys planned to track the number
of beneficiaries with enhanced climate-resilient livelihood options (outcome 5) can also include
questions to track enhanced access to climate-relevant information, or to communication media
as a proxy for that (outcome 4), as well as the durability/portability of the OGS systems in the
face of any extreme events experienced (outcome 3).
42. The iTAP recommends that the GCF concessionary capital be utilized to take local
currency basket options or other hedging products at the MEF fund level rather than push such
a risk onto OGS companies, or worse, onto end customers. The hedging products may be
expensive for the MEF, but they will certainly be expensive for the OGS companies and their end
customers who will bear that volatility (which must be borne by someone). Such a hedge may
ultimately also address concerns from potential limited partners on the financial sustainability
of MEF on-lending. Either way, the main goal of blended finance is to crowd in commercial
capital, but it is equally important to utilize concessional capital to pay for “insurance” products,
which minimize risk for the companies and customers operating in hardest-to-reach markets.

Reply to the Independent Technical Advisory Panel assessment
findings
Proposal name: Hardest-to-Reach
Accredited entity: Acumen Fund
Impact potential
Acumen is pleased to note that the impact potential is considered ‘high’. The commentary captures the
cross-cutting scope and we note the emphasis on the adaptation and resilience impacts (#6 and #7), for
which there is a pressing need in low income communities where this project will reach. As referenced,
the 54 million adaptation beneficiaries are people achieving first-time access to electricity (around 15 per
cent of the total population in the participating countries), and many will receive entry level solar home
systems, via a pay as you go plan, to match their ability to pay.
Monitoring the adaptation outcomes of the program is a core consideration of the program design.
Acumen’s experience of incorporating user surveys has shown their effectiveness in capturing a range of
impact dimensions, including climate resilience and adaptation metrics, and gender disaggregated
impact. Survey questions can reveal patterns of household access to climate-relevant information through
OGS-powered communication media, at baseline and endline, in terms of both objective and/or
quantitative [e.g., point(s) of access, frequency of access, information subject matter] and subjective
and/or qualitative [e.g., perceived ease of access, perceived usefulness of access] metrics. Tracking the
frequency of access to climate information, for example, is a specific and measurable indicator to inform
outcome 4, and we are considering additional monitoring methodologies to add depth to this picture, as
well as verification capacity. In terms of Outcome 3, resilient energy access, through durability in the face
of extreme events and portability in the case of displacement, in addition to event-responsive customer
surveys, in the proximate aftermath of extreme climate events, our discussions are ongoing with
providers of technologies able to capture and track location and usage data of off grid solar products that
will enable accurate monitoring of energy consumption patterns during and after a climate event.
Acumen recognizes the opportunity to apply innovative methods to monitor and verify climate resilience
impact, with a possible demonstration effect for the other energy programs, with broad positive impact
across the sector.
Paradigm shift potential
Acumen notes the iTAP’s balanced and helpful assessment of the program’s paradigm shift potential. As
highlighted in the commentary, H2R has the potential to play a pivotal role in attracting investment into
hard-to-reach markets where capital has not traditionally flowed, with the help of a blended finance
structure which effectively mitigates the real and perceived risks associated with investing in these
nascent markets. Overall, we are also positive about the multiplication effects that can be achieved
through this approach, including through the knowledge sharing component.
Acumen is paying close attention to the various risks which could undermine the impact of the program.
The sector’s lessons from the shock of the COVID pandemic should be seen as a source of resilience for the
sector in the medium and long-term. Off-grid solar companies faced challenges such as higher costs of
raw materials and decreased incomes among their predominantly rural and economically disadvantaged
customer base. As noted, there is still a need to address the fragility of OGS companies and the risks they
face from external shocks, particularly to protect customers, as well as H2R investments, and our ability
to achieve the desired volume of reinvestment. As mentioned, beyond H2R’s investments, a dedicated
technical assistance facility will support companies to build up their capacity and long-term viability. TA
areas include consumer protection, gender, enterprise development and ESG.
Acumen is aligned with the view that broad stakeholder engagement is needed to enhance the potential
for transformational impact. Acumen is a member of the REACH partnership, a newly formed group of
leading energy access practitioners and a knowledge sharing platform, with expertise in areas including
capacity building – including technical assistance – of all stakeholders (companies, financiers, and
governments) and policy and regulatory support to create enabling environment.

Sustainable development potential
The iTAP’s ‘medium-to-high’ rating of the program’s sustainable development impact is noted. As the
commentary suggests, there are interlinkages between clean energy access, economic development
(income generation/diversification, savings, job creation), educational outcomes, climate goals, and
health and wellbeing. The guidance to address currency risk is noted. Looking across the sector, we also
note that the viability of different local currency lending approaches is being explored and the H2R
approach will benefit from any lessons being shared.
Needs of the recipient
Acumen welcomes the iTAP’s positive assessment of the alignment between the H2R intervention and the
needs of the recipient. As outlined in the funding proposal, H2R has been designed in response to the
clear needs of the rural populations where energy access is lowest, addressing the urgent financing needs
of the identified countries, and enhancing climate resilience through energy access in least developed
countries and to some of the most climate vulnerable communities in the world.
Country ownership
Acumen notes the ‘moderate’ rating for the level of country ownership and in particular the guidance for
broad and in-country engagement. The program aligns with the countries' NDCs and national adaptation
plans, and there is alignment with government electrification targets. In-country engagement is ongoing
and Senior members of the program team are regularly in the region, enabling engagement across the
spectrum of stakeholders.
Efficiency and effectiveness
Acumen notes the iTAP’s positive assessment of the program’s efficiency and effectiveness, and in
particular Acumen’s track record establishing and overseeing programs of this nature. As highlighted,
with the support of the GCF funding, H2R can generate significant adaptation benefits by providing first-
time energy access and strengthening the climate resilience of 54 million people.
Overall remarks from the independent Technical Advisory Panel:
Acumen notes the overall positive remarks from the iTAP on this program, along with recognition of
Acumen’s track record, in particular to deliver the impact while managing the risks of the proposed
program.
Acumen also notes the clear mission alignment between H2R and GCF, to deliver a break from a business-
as-usual electrification trajectory and to reach people not covered by traditional approaches of
investment.
The guidance on the logframe is noted and aligned with the approach we are developing, as is the
feedback to address currency risk, potentially by taking local currency basket options or other hedging
products.

Introduction
This document provides an assessment of the barriers and opportunities for advancing gender
inclusion in Hardest to Reach (“H2R”) initiative countries. The assessment includes an overview
of the evidence on women’s access to clean energy technologies, women’s participation in the
off-grid solar (“OGS”) sector workforce, and the key barriers to advancing equality in the sector.
This document outlines key entry points for the H2R initiative, followed by detailed in-country
assessments for the sixteen target H2R countries.
Barriers to gender equality in the OGS sector
The link between energy access and gender equality is well recognized. Energy poverty has a
strong gender dimension as the lack of access to energy inhibits women’s well-being, and their
access to economic opportunities, and it strongly affects women’s living conditions and time-use.
Off-grid energy technologies have a direct benefit to women’s health, particularly in terms of
reduced risks of pulmonary and respiratory diseases. Women’s participation and leadership in the
OGS sector can help accelerate the transition to a low-carbon economy by promoting clean
energy use and addressing energy poverty, while also advancing women’s economic
empowerment. However, multiple barriers limit women’s ability to access OGS technologies and
to fully participate in OGS value chains as business leaders, employees and entrepreneurs.
One of the key barriers in the market relates to lack of sex-disaggregated data for the OGS
sector both at the consumer and workforce levels. The limited sex-disaggregated data
available about customer segments and demand for products leads to missed opportunities to
reach women customers and meet their needs. In addition, the lack of data on women-owned
enterprises and the potential for productive uses of energy prevents increasing the number of
women customers and the chance to design business strategies and projects that could transform
their economic opportunities.
Historical inequities of distribution and control of assets impact women’s ability to access
OGS products, and affordability is a well-recognized barrier to accessing OGS technologies (for
both women and men). In many countries, women face discriminatory property and tenure laws,
resulting in women’s lower access to financing, to mobile phones and mobile money.
Gender and social norms limit women’s access to technologies and their abilities to enter
the workforce. Intrahousehold decision-making and mobility constraints inhibit women’s ability
to be aware of energy products and to purchase them. Women may be discouraged from seeking
employment opportunities as sales agents and technicians because in some contexts these may
not be considered suitable opportunities for them, or because they are discouraged from
interacting with men due to social and gender norms.
Companies have a limited understanding of the business case for gender inclusion in their
businesses, and of how to make their practices more inclusive. OGS companies may not
strive to reach women customers or to hire women because they are unaware of the positive
3

=== PAGE 213 ===
Page 209
impacts on their business performance, and they may see this as an extra cost rather than a
strategy to meet profitability and business goals. Further, companies’ policies often do not
recognize gender equality as a priority and few companies have equal opportunities policies or
are intentional in addressing gender equality in their strategies to attract, recruit, and promote
women at all levels. Even when companies have an explicit gender strategy or they intentionally
strive to make their practices more inclusive, they face challenges in attracting women workers,
designing products and services for female customers and women entrepreneurs, and ultimately
attracting gender-lens investments.1
The sector lacks appropriate and dedicated training and mentorship opportunities for
women to enter and thrive in the workforce. Because of prevailing gender norms, women may
be excluded from educational opportunities and may not be considered suitable for employment
opportunities in technical roles, as well as sales and distribution roles. Further, male-dominated
workplaces are not attractive to women and pose additional risks to gender-based violence and
sexual harassment.
Serving women with OGS technologies
Overall, evidence shows that women have less access to off-grid electricity than their male
counterparts, and they mostly use pico-solar products and lanterns or other lower-tier
technologies.2 SHS customers are predominantly rural men living under the median poverty line
of $3.10.3 In a survey conducted on 35,000 customers of 49 OGS companies in 17 countries, 60
Decibels found that only 32% of customers are women.4
An analysis conducted by Value for Women on 59 companies working in the energy sector found
that only 23% of companies collect sex-disaggregated data on customers, and half of them
reported that they serve 46% of customers who are women. A small group of companies (6) also
collect data on end-users, and they reported serving 60% women among their end-users.5 In
another study, GOGLA (the global association for the off-grid solar energy industry) found that
women buy solar lanterns and smaller products mostly on a cash basis. In a survey conducted
with 37 OGS companies, ESMAP and GOGLA found that about 40% of companies collect sex-
disaggregated data on customers, and those who do report that 45% of their customers are
women.6 Another report indicates that the share of women in PAYGo solar customers is as low
as 25%.7 Based on the limited and fragmented available data, it can be concluded that, on

These studies indicate that the sector overall lacks sex-disaggregated data, resulting in a limited
understanding of gender-related barriers to access and limited knowledge on the impact that
these technologies have on women’s lives. The limited knowledge about customer segments and
women’s demand for OGS products leads to missed opportunities to reach women's customers.
In addition, men are the main purchasers of energy products, even when women are the primary
end-users; this results in skewed consumer data and products that do not always reflect the needs
or preferences of women.
In H2R country contexts, prevalent gender norms are likely to affect access to off-grid solar
technologies, influencing companies’ abilities to reach women. Discriminatory gender norms
inhibit women’s rights to own land and other assets in most countries, making it challenging for
women to access credit and purchase renewable energy technologies. PAYGo companies may
reach a lower percentage of women customers due to additional barriers related to mobile
ownership and mobile money usage among women (see Table 2). Overall, in Sub-Saharan Africa,
the gender gap in mobile ownership is 30%. This gap has grown from 22% in 2017 since
ownership of smartphones among men in the region has steadily outpaced that of women.
Further, the gender gap in mobile internet usage in the region stands at 37%.9 For the countries
for which sex-disaggregated data is available (e.g. Uganda and Zambia), the low rates of access
to electricity in H2R contexts are even more pronounced in female-headed households.

African Indigenous People, which can be defined as “nomadic and semi-nomadic pastoralists and
hunter/gatherers who live in situations of marginalization and discrimination,”28 are faced with
additional challenges in accessing resources and opportunities. In H2R countries, indigenous
communities are hunter-gatherers, pastoralists and nomadic populations often without state
recognition. They heavily rely on nature and land for their livelihood and are often located in
forests and conservations areas, facing eviction from their land. Further, African indigenous
people are generally poorer and lack access to education and health. Indigenous women face
additional challenges such as sexual violence (e.g. Pygmies in DRC). In West Africa, political
instability and conflicts disproportionately impact women and female-headed households. Women
and girls make up a large proportion of internally displaced populations, they are victims of
systemic attacks and kidnappings, and are forced into slavery.29
In the context of a changing climate, indigenous communities and minority groups whose lives
depend on the health of their natural environments are increasingly more vulnerable to shocks,
while their specific energy needs are often overlooked. Without addressing their needs, the
transition to clean energy is hindered in many SSA countries. Empowering Indigenous
populations, women, youth, and other traditionally marginalized people is an essential part of
protecting rights and creating jobs. In the context of H2R, OGS technologies can provide first
access to clean and reliable energy for communities that are usually not included in traditional
business models and energy programs. Their additional vulnerabilities (i.e. geographic
remoteness, lower access to information and resources, higher poverty rates, discrimination)
should be considered when assessing strategies for OGS product dissemination and when they
consider hiring in the communities they serve.
In conclusion, it is safe to assume that product reach to women and other vulnerable communities
in H2R markets will be slightly lower than average, or compared to countries where the OGS
sector is well established (e.g. Kenya). The H2R initiative provides an important opportunity to fill
some of the knowledge and data gaps on reaching women as OGS customers by requesting
investee companies to collect and track sex-disaggregated data on sales.
Women’s participation in OGS companies’ workforce
Data on women’s participation as employees and leaders in the sector is scarce and fragmented.
ESMAP and GOGLA recently surveyed 37 OGS companies from 20 different countries and found
that on average women constitute 41.7% of workers across all levels.30 In contrast, a previous

GOGLA study indicated that only 27% of women work in the OGS sector.31 An analysis completed

companies. Similarly, in the renewable energy sector in general women hold roughly 32% of
jobs.32 Another recent study based on 64 surveyed companies operating in SSA found that
women represent 37% of the decentralised RE workforce, and that they are more likely to be
employed in corporate support positions (administration, communications and sales).33 Only 13%
of women had higher-paying science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM)-related
jobs, and 16% held non-STEM, technical positions.
Based on the available market data, it can be concluded that globally women represent about
33% of the clean energy workforce across all levels and this figure can be used as a benchmark
for female workforce participation.

management positions.34 The key challenges affecting companies operating in these contexts
relate to workplace policies and practices, social norms and gender stereotypes and legal
barriers.
The country assessments indicate that several barriers limit women’s participation in the
workforce and in the economy more generally, with prevailing gender norms, gaps in education
levels and discriminatory policies and practices affecting women’s productive activities and
economic empowerment in several countries. Among H2R countries, only Uganda presents data
for Distributed Renewable Energy (“DRE”) labour force participation of women, with 27% of
women being employed in the sector. Lesotho reports an overall high representation of women in
private sector energy companies compared to regional and global averages (42%), however
these women are reportedly concentrated in administrative roles rather than technical or
managerial roles. For other countries, this data is not available but it is likely to be considerably
lower, especially in markets such as Togo, Guinea or DRC where gender norms prevent women
from undertaking many productive activities and where the OGS sector is still in its nascent
stages. The rates of secondary school enrolment remain low across SSA (36% on average), and
of the few women who do attend university, only a small segment completes a STEM degree,
which is needed for higher-paid and more senior jobs in OGS companies. Once women enter the
job market, they encounter discrimination, including the widespread misconception that women
are not suited for technical roles. Companies that intentionally recruit women for these positions
face pipeline-related challenges and need to address such gender and social norms.
Women entrepreneurship is also hindered by gender norms and discriminatory policy frameworks.
In most of the assessed countries, women are predominantly represented in the informal sector,
in some cases they do not have the same rights to register a business or open bank accounts,
and they largely lack access to formal financing.

The H2R initiative brings opportunities to mandate that companies collect and annually report a
sex-disaggregated staff footprint, with data on female versus male employment at all levels. Such
data can be also used to showcase the business case for the inclusion of women across all levels
of the OGS workforce.
Stakeholder Engagement
As part of the process of understanding the needs and perspectives of women in Hardest-to-
Reach geographies, we have engaged with over 25 individuals, notably via a Stakeholder
Consultation Forum with GCF Gender Monitors. The session had representation from over 11
sub-Saharan African countries, as well as from specialist gender lens off-grid solar organisations.
An example of the latter is Smiling Through Light (STL), a Sierra Leone-based social enterprise
which focuses on clean energy access by working with a network of local women to distribute and
sell solar products. STL focuses on the last mile which creates employment and income
opportunities in underserved areas.
