We also launched a customer survey for a pilot
investment in Benin where we listened to and
learned from 85 women about their experience
with OGS products. These women shared their
opinions on the value of the products, barriers to
purchase, and challenges with the products. Their
challenges and hopes mirrored what we heard
from gender experts, NGO leaders, and other
important stakeholders.
The following insights were gained from our
consultation and studies:
● The sector needs more support of
women leaders and entrepreneurs: The
view was expressed that, in order to
address the challenges and inequities
women face in energy access, it would be
impactful to have more women in leadership within the sector. This could be achieved by
investors backing more women-led businesses and by the provision of training to uplift
women in the workforce into positions of influence and leadership. Our gender lens
strategy is aligned with the 2X challenge to increase women participation in the OGS
sector. Additionally, we expect to provide training for women to be sales agents and
technicians in OGS as a part of our technical assistance.
● Awareness of off grid solar among women in some areas is still low: This is
particularly the case in very remote areas, where there are no distributors serving the
locale. According to our survey, women were slightly more likely to gain first time access
to electricity with OGS and have fewer OGS alternatives then men. As a result of our
consultations, conversations with gender experts and surveying of female OGS
customers, we are supporting several companies with technical assistance generating
gender-inclusive marketing strategies.
● Off grid solar products are very important as entry level electricity in rural areas:
Hardest-to-Reach initiative is delivering a product which women in rural areas will benefit
from, and will value if they are made aware of the various products and uses. 80% of
women in our survey shared their lives improved with access to electricity. 50% said that
their lives very much improved with their OGS product.
● There are grassroots women-led initiatives which are seeking NGO and donor
support: The consultation shone a light on some worthy initiatives which women are
engaged in at the grassroots level. While direct support of these is outside the scope of
the H2R initiative, we are hopeful the H2R’s uplift of the OGS sector can have a positive
knock-on effect, in particular by raising awareness of OGS.

=== PAGE 221 ===

Key entry points for the H2R initiative
1) Elevate women in the OGS sector as customers, employees and entrepreneurs. The
country assessments indicate gender gaps in access to energy and employment opportunities,
and a comprehensive programmatic approach is necessary to create opportunities for women at
all levels.
2) Do no harm from a gender perspective. This entails evaluating potential investee companies’
risk identification and mitigation with respect to negative impacts on women as part of its
Environmental, Social and Governance standards. H2R’s Environmental and Social Risk
Management Plan will establish gender-specific screening criteria.
3) Provide clean and affordable energy to women customers and women-headed
households. The country assessments and the global benchmarks indicate that women are
predominantly affected by energy poverty and that poor and vulnerable households are mostly
women-headed.35 The H2R initiative can impact women’s lives by requiring investees to collect
and track sex-disaggregated data on customers reached and by supporting companies to
implement strategies to better serve women, ultimately reducing gender gaps in access to clean
energy technologies.
4) Track investments in women-led businesses and in businesses that have gender-
forward business practices. Investors have a clear role to play in applying a gender lens to the
investment process and to inform investment decisions by intentionally examining the gender
balance of companies, their commitment to equality, and by measuring the progress of investees
in reaching women customers. The H2R initiative can encourage companies to recruit, retain and
advance women at all levels of the OGS value chain by integrating a gender lens in due diligence,
deal structuring and in post-investment support. Companies that are intentional in addressing
gender gaps in access to OGS technologies and opportunities can apply business practices that
build customer trust and loyalty, strengthen women’s capacity to enter and advance in the sector,
and at the same time reach women customers.
5) Positively impact organisational culture by supporting portfolio companies to adopt
and/or expand gender-inclusive policies and business practices. To increase the attraction,
retention, and advancement of women in the OGS workforce, companies need to have in place
inclusive workplace policies and practices. At a minimum, companies should be expected to have
anti-harassment, anti-discrimination, and wage parity policies, which are considered necessary
requirements to operate in H2R contexts where wage disparities persist and where gender norms
and gender-based violence (“GBV”) are inhibiting women’s economic empowerment. Other
policies and practices such as flexible working arrangements, parental leave policies, flexible
return to work after parental leave, etc. are necessary to create women-friendly workplaces and
to attract female talent. Further, companies can apply a gender lens to other areas of their
business, particularly in product design and market research and customer engagement areas
(sales, distribution, after-sales), as well as their supply chains. Such practices will enable
35
Energy Sector Management Assistance Program. 2022. Gender Equality in the Off-Grid Solar Sector. Washington, DC
12

=== PAGE 222 ===
Page 218
companies to understand women’s needs and to better serve women customers, ultimately
meeting sales targets and contributing to H2R’s program impact.
The H2R initiative will mandate companies to assess the level of gender inclusion in their
business, and support them in developing actions and strategies to become more inclusive. The
gender inclusion assessment carried out during due diligence and the GAP developed within 90
days of investment (see Gender Action Plan for details) will provide detailed information about
which policies companies are expected to develop or update, as well as the steps to increase
women’s participation in the workforce and strengthen the pipeline of women candidates.
Evidence shows that companies that undertake actions to close gender gaps and that integrate
intentionality in their strategies and business processes have been successful in attracting further
financing.36 Such an approach will contribute to H2R’s gender equality objectives and it will help
mobilize finance to enter these challenging contexts and to reach underserved markets.
6) Provide dedicated training and employment opportunities. At the ecosystem level, the
H2R initiative will address the lack of training and mentorship opportunities by supporting women-
dedicated training programs that aim at closing skills gaps. The H2R initiative should also focus
on establishing partnerships between training institutions, the private sector and recruitment
actors to increase awareness of job opportunities and to foster the creation of internships and
mentorship programs. The initiative can also enhance collaboration by convening stakeholders
such as gender lens investors, women’s associations, women entrepreneurs, and other key local
actors in engagement workshops to work together to improve the operating environment for
women in OGS markets.
7) Facilitate OGS sector transformation. Acumen has a track record of building ecosystems
with a gender lens. In H2R, Acumen will use insights to build the case for the benefits of investing
in hardest-to-reach markets and taking a gender lens to OGS sector facilitation. There is a
tremendous opportunity to gather insights on the strategies companies will adopt to close gender
gaps in the OGS sector, from reaching customers to hiring women in their workforce, and
disseminating lessons learned to the wider sector.
Country-level assessments
The assessment of the sixteen H2R countries identified context-specific challenges for advancing
women’s participation in the OGS sector. These countries present some of the lowest electricity
access rates and some of the highest poverty rates. Disparities between men and women persist
in the areas of economic opportunities, health, education, political participation, and
empowerment. Gender norms and customary laws shape women’s lives and their ability to access
assets and resources and to participate in economic activities.

preferences and affordability constraints will be mapped at the household and

Togo Entrepreneurs du Monde (EdM) is an initiative supported by the Economic Community
of West African States (ECOWAS) and the government of France, created in 1998,
that works with people living in fuel poverty by facilitating access to essential goods
and services for their families. Based in Togo since 2012, EdM runs the Mivo Energie
project that aims to combat global warming and deforestation in Togo by facilitating
access to clean, modern, and affordable energy products for vulnerable populations,
especially women.
Malawi FINCOOP is a financial cooperative that provides affordable financial services, serving
micro, small and medium entrepreneurs, farmers, and salaried employees. The
company’s Green Loan Programme targets low-income households across Malawi
using multiple channels such as Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs), civil
services, and technology partners. FINCOOP has tailored its payment terms to fit
women’s requirements through the deployment of payment methods such as Pay As
You Go models, cash, and group loans, and by offering longer repayment terms. From
2018 to 2020, more than 1212 female-headed households were able to access solar
products through this program.39
Lesotho Lesotho has launched a Women In Sustainable Energy Lesotho (WISE-L) initiative
that aims to promote gender equality and equity in the energy sector and create
opportunities for women.40
Burkina Faso ● The GEF-funded Africa Minigrids Program implemented by UNDP seeks to
demonstrate productive uses of electricity to reduce costs, increase the viability and
enable mini-grid development at scale. The primary targets and actors of the pilot
projects will be small-scale farmers (women and youth, mostly) who will benefit
directly from the electricity supplied by the solar mini-grids. The project started in
2022 and it is planned to end in 2026.41
● The GCF-funded Inclusive Green Financing Initiative (IGREENFIN I): Greening
Agricultural Banks & the Financial Sector to Foster Climate Resilient, Low Emission
Smallholder Agriculture in the Great Green Wall (GGW) countries42 program, is
implemented by the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) and
local organizations from the participant countries, including Burkina Faso. The
program seeks to provide concessional loans to foster the best adaptation and
mitigation practices for green businesses within the selected agricultural value
chains in each target country. Operated by local, national agricultural banks
(LNABs) – the Agricultural Bank of Burkina Faso– the facility will offer special lines
of financing for green business projects prepared by farmer’s organizations (FOs),
women and youth organizations, cooperatives, and MSMEs (including agribusiness
dealers and solar operators). Besides providing loans, the program includes a
Technical Assistance Facility (TAF) to address capacity, knowledge, and policy

Democratic Republic of Congo
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
The Democratic Republic of Congo is one of the biggest countries in Africa, with a population of around 92
million people – 50.1% of which are women – an annual population growth of 3.1%, with 33% of the total
population under the age of 15.
The Gender Development Index for the DRC is 0.885, placing women’s human development at about 83%
of that of men. According to the GDI scoring, the DRC belongs to the group of countries with the lowest
human development (countries with low equality in HDI achievements between women and men and
absolute deviation from gender parity of more than 10 percent). On the Gender Inequality Index (GII) which
measures disparities between men and women in the areas of economic opportunities, reproductive health,
and empowerment, the country is ranked among the highest in the world (151).
The DRC also scores low on human development, with women being in worse conditions compared to men
(0.449 HDI for women versus men 0.507), and DRC ranks 179th out of 191 countries on the Human
Development Index (2019).

Legal status of women
The DRC has ratified many UN Conventions relating to equity and inclusion, including the 1969 Convention
on Eradication of Racial Discrimination, the 1966 Convention on Civil and Political Rights, and the 1966
Convention on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR). Further, DRC has ratified the Convention
on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW). The 2006 Constitution prohibits
discrimination against women in its many forms and emphasizes gender parity in public institutions (Article
14). It also provides through Articles 5, 14, and 15 the foundations of legitimization of any policy of equality
and equity in the country. Under the Constitution, women and men have equal rights to work, education,
vote, justice, and political participation.

The DRC developed a National Gender Policy (2017-2021), which aims to achieve gender equality and
social empowerment through five strategic axes: (i) the consolidation of gender equality and the
empowerment of women; (ii) strengthening the role and place of women and girls in the economy and
employment; (iii) increased access of women and girls to decision-making spheres; (iv) fight against forms
of sexual violence; and (v) strengthening the institutional mechanism for implementation of the National
Gender Policy. Despite an overall favorable policy framework for gender equality, implementation of policies
remains a challenge, with a lack of appropriate budget, limited awareness, poor coordination, a limited
capacity of implementing agencies, as well as constraining societal gender norms.49
Political participation
The Constitution forbids discrimination against women (Article 14), but there is no law or policy that ensures
women’s just representation. The DRC demonstrates only 13% female representation in the National
Assembly, 10% of women elected at the provincial level, no female governors in the provinces, and just
under 14% women representatives as decision-making authorities for public administration.50 Gender
norms impact women’s political participation, and there is a strong notion that politics are for men and that
women often need to follow their husband’s opinions.
Social and cultural context
Men dominate both the political and social spheres, and they are the culturally and legally appointed heads
of the household, presenting them with decision-making power over most aspects of life. Women are
defined by their household or reproductive responsibilities, which include maintaining the physical and
moral well-being of their families. Men are perceived to be responsible for the financial health of their
families. According to the law, women are required to obey their husbands, and they cannot be head of the
household in the same way as men.51 Further, they do not have the same rights to remarry. Traditional
gender roles and social norms exist in both urban and rural areas; however, they appear to be more rigid
in rural settings.
Sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) has been a defining feature of the ongoing conflict in the country
and the DRC has one of the highest incidences of rape in the world, and there is no legislation addressing
domestic violence. Domestic violence is widespread and is generally accepted as a response to women’s
alleged failings in the household.52 In fact, sexual violence against women and girls has been prevalent,
especially by a partner or household member. UN Women reports that 51% of Congolese women
experience lifetime physical and/or sexual intimate partner violence, with 37% reporting violence in the last
12 months.53
Household decisions are dominated by men, and the lack of agency within the home and within
communities has a direct influence on women’s productive activities and their ability to access and control
resources. A survey conducted by the World Bank found that men take decisions over a woman’s income,
health, major household investments, and social visits. Gender norms mean that there is an expectation for
men to be the primary household breadwinner, and consequently they are expected to pay for major

purchases.
Indigenous women face additional challenges in DRC. Indigenous Pygmies are traditional hunter gatherers,
and thus remaining poor and marginalised with limited access to land rights. Women from these tribes are
often subjected to sexual violence by Bantu people, due to being considered ‘subhuman’.54 With DRC’s
forest cover being a vast 62% of the country’s land, conservation efforts have been made to protect this
“largest carbon sink of the world”, which include repossession of lands from them under the garb of
protecting these forests, which threatens the traditional way of life for these Pygmies and makes indigenous
women even more vulnerable due to displacement. Recently laws have been passed toward Promotion
and Protection of the Rights of the Indigenous Pygmy Peoples, granting them the right and access to free,
prior and informed consent before their land is exploited by government or industries.55
Health
A high maternal mortality rate is a major health issue in the DRC (740 per 100,000 live births); it is caused
by several factors such as lack of access to medical treatment, early marriage, and high birth rates.
Throughout the country, the average age at first birth is 19.9 years, and 37% of women aged 20-24 were
married before their eighteenth birthday, as compared to 6% of men in the same age group. Congolese
women suffer from poorer health compared to men, with women’s health being undermined by men’s
control over women’s bodies, low access to resources, and women’s lack of freedom to move.56
Education
One of the key drivers of inequality in the country is linked to gender disparities in education, directly
impacting women’s participation in the economy and wage earnings. Articles 43 and 44 of the Constitution
stipulate free obligatory education and the eradication of illiteracy. However, girls often drop out of school
due to early marriage and pregnancy, which leads to a gender gap in education.
The average Congolese woman will benefit from 5.3 years of formal schooling compared to 8.4 years for
men; as such, only 40% of women have attended secondary school compared to 69 % of men.57 Nationally,
an estimated 66% of Congolese women are literate compared to 89% of men.58 Among young women,
literacy is increasing; an estimated 80% of young women are literate compared to 91% of young men.
Traditionally, education for women and girls is less valued and households often prioritize education for
boys compared to girls.
Women’s economic participation and entrepreneurship
Sixty percent of the country’s population is under the age of 20, and this percentage will only expand, as
DRC is projected to attain a population of 120 million by 2030. More than 60% of women live under the

The labour force participation rate for women is 61.2% compared to 69.1% of men, and only 6.4% of women
work in wage employment, compared to 23.9% of men.60 Gender gaps persist across different economic
sectors, with large discrepancies in agricultural production (17.8% gap between men and women), in

wage or salaried workers compared to 25% of men.62 In the private sector, the wage gap is nearly 80%.
The underlying causes of such gaps include women’s higher burden of care work, which is the primary
factor behind women’s lower labour force participation. Lower educational attainment, skills, and
concentration in lower-paying sectors are instead the primary drivers of women’s lower-wage earnings. The
entrepreneurship gender gap indicates that businesswomen have lower levels of capital and lower numbers
of workers. The female share of employment in senior and middle management is 6% while only 11% of
firms have a female top manager (2013).
Further, across all sectors, lack of control over land, lack of agency in the household, prevalent gender-

empowerment.63
The first Family Code (1987) included legal restrictions to women’s mobility, workplace, marriage, and
assets, but the 2016 reform of the Code included the elimination of marital authorization for women’s access
to employment, bank accounts, and loans, directly impacting women’s ability to explore new economic
opportunities. While family laws have been updated, many have yet to be ratified. Specifically, Article 444
of the DRC Family Code (1987) provides that a husband is head of the household and the revised Family
Code (2016) still maintains this. However, of note in the revised version, is the elimination of the need for a
married woman to obtain her husband’s permission to open an individual bank account, or access financial
services such as credits or loans. As such, most married women’s decisions remain under the discretion of
their husbands, who retain control of all household, financial, and medical decisions in both statutory and
cultural law. Widowed, divorced, or single women face ostracization and most often must submit to the will
and authority of male family members.
The Women Business and the Law Index Score for the DRCF is 78.8 (2021). The overall score for the
Democratic Republic of the Congo is higher than the regional average observed across Sub-Saharan Africa
(71.5).
Gender and energy in DRC
Only 19% of the population have access to electricity. Gender norms restrict women’s access to resources
and assets, which directly impacts energy poverty. Because women often do not make decisions alone on
household spending, they are likely to have less access to energy products and technologies. Sex-
disaggregated data on access to energy as well as women’s participation in the sector is absent.

Uganda
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Uganda has a total population of 34.6 million, of which 51.21% are women. The country has one of the
world's youngest and fastest-growing populations with 55% of people under 18 years of age and a very
high fertility rate of 5.4.64
The Gender Development Index in Uganda is 0.927 and is ranked 166 out of 191 in Human Development
Index, placing the country among other ‘Group 3’ countries with a high absolute deviation from gender
parity, of 5–7.5%. This is largely driven by a gender gap in mean years of schooling and gross national
income per capita. 65 Uganda is ranked 131 in the Gender Inequality Index which measures disparities
between men and women in economic opportunities, reproductive health, and empowerment. 66

in Africa. This protocol specifies provisions for civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights as well as
the rights to development and peace, as well as reproductive and sexual rights for women.68,69
Uganda also compiled a Gender Policy in 1997 (revising it in 2007), The National Policy on the Elimination
of Gender-based Violence (2016) and the National Male Engagement Strategy, developed respectively
(2017) with a commitment to eliminate all forms of gender inequalities in the long-run.70,71 The policy is
meant to serve as a guiding framework for all levels of planning, resource allocation and implementation of
development programmes with a gender perspective. Under the National Gender Policy, Uganda has
identified 4 priority areas of focus including:
1. Gender and livelihoods; with the aim to redress three areas of inequality including gender
differences in livelihoods, time poverty, and access to and control over productive resources.
2. Promotion and protection of rights; by committing to eliminating gender differences in women’s
access to justice through the Judiciary Gender Policy and Strategy released in 2012.
3. Participation in decision-making and governance; wherein the country aims to overcome
obstacles to women's engagement in elective processes, limited capacity to participate effectively
in leadership and decision-making, low presence of women in technical positions.
4. Gender and Macro-economic Management; The government commits to women’s economic
empowerment by laying down strategies like gender budgeting, reforms in investment regulations
and domestic/local revenue generation systems and building the overall capacity of the national
government to include gender in macroeconomic policies.
The Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, under Article 21, prohibits gender discrimination generally and
under Article 31 sets the minimum age for marriage at 18 and provides for equal rights between men and
women during marriage and divorce. The Article 33 pertains specifically to the rights of women and requires
that the government provide opportunities to enhance the welfare of women and enable them to reach their
full potential, provide women equal rights to men in political, economic, and social activities, and. Article 33
also prohibits laws, customs, traditions, and cultures that are "against the dignity of women".72
While the above measures create a conducive policy environment in Uganda to address gender inequality,
restrictive socio-cultural practices continue to curtail women’s potential in the country. This has been further
exacerbated by COVID-19 during which increased incidences of violence against women have been
reported.73
Political participation
With women representing 34.9% of parliamentary seats in Uganda, the country ranks high in Africa with
regard to women’s political participation74. To ensure the representation of women in local governments
(LGs) (that have the powers enshrined under the LG Act, 1997 to make and implement development plans
based on locally determined priorities) the Ugandan government under the 1997 LG Act stipulates that
women should constitute a third of any local council. This affirmative action has led to women constituting

Social and cultural context
In Uganda, Women’s rights on land have been recognized in the Land Act (Cap 227) and Land Acquisition
Act (Cap 226) and the country aims to promote tenure security in women’s access to land under their IIIrd
National Development Plan. These have led to a sharp increase in both land and home ownership by
women and in joint ownership between the period 2013 to 2017, compared to male dominance in ownership
prior to 2012-13. However, the country continues to be a patriarchal and patrilinear society with women’s
domestic and household responsibilities impacting their effective participation in productive work. Further,
research has found that in Uganda, as women attain increased access to social networks and
empowerment, especially at the age group 30 to 39, they are often subjected to violence by their current or
former partners. 78 Almost 50% of women report experiencing some form of physical and/or sexual intimate
partner violence in their lifetime and about 30% reported experiencing it in the last 12 months. 79 Uganda
has developed a male involvement strategy, finalized in 2017 with the aim of engaging men and boys in
prevention and response to GBV.80
Health
Uganda has a maternal mortality ratio (MMR) of 375 per 100,000 live births (as of 2017) 81 which is
extremely high compared to the Sustainable Development Goal target of achieving no more than an MMR
of 70 by 2030. Even with the introduction of 14 different policy instruments over 15 years by the government,
to reduce MMR, the failures in referral policies, inadequacies in healthcare facilities and trained personnel
and transportation issues remained. 82 Unsafe abortions account for about 5% of maternal deaths in
Uganda. Abortion is illegal in Uganda and termination is allowed only in cases the pregnancy threatens the

Education
In Uganda, men are expected to complete 6.7 mean years of schooling compared to 4.9 years completed
by women.84 As of 2018, 83% of adult males are literate and 71% of adult females are literate. Interestingly,
however, among the young population, there is gender parity in literacy levels with 90% of women in the
age group of 15-24 being literate and 89% of men attaining literacy which shows an improving trend for the
next generation of the Ugandan population.85 However, the lower secondary completion rate is low among
both men (27.7%) and women (25.1%) in Uganda.86
Under its National Strategy for Girls Education (2015-2019) the country has created a policy implementation
Framework to promote girls’ education by aiming to harmonize education programs on Girls’ Education for
effective coordination, monitoring and evaluation, ensure adequate commitment to requisite human and
financial resources to promote girls’ education, institutionalize research on Girls’ Education to inform policy
development and build the capacity of education actors to address gender inequalities in education.87
Uganda has also been commended internationally by the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination
against Women for the strides made in the education sector, including a particular focus on building
infrastructure for the education of girls with special needs.88 Notably, Uganda has a Science Education
Policy (2004) under which physics, chemistry, and biology have been made compulsory in lower secondary
schools,89 and 75% of government sponsorships in tertiary institutions are for science-based courses.
However, only 25% of students opting for science-based courses at the university level are women, hence
they are unable to enjoy state-funded science education at this level. 90
Although the country has introduced key legislation to ensure improved education access for women the
country is still falling behind in effectively transitioning women into the world of work. There has been a
steep drop in labour force participation of women in the ages of 15-24, from 74.6% in 2013 to 54.2% in
2017. 91 While some of this decline can be explained by improved access to schooling, the share of inactivity
is also increasing among women with them being more likely than men to be both out of school and out of
a job due to familial responsibilities and lack of job opportunities. 92

As of 2019, the female Labour force participation rate for women in the age group 15 to 64 in Uganda is

In salaried employment, there are evident gender gaps in median monthly nominal wages earnt by men

across sectors. Women senior managers are concentrated in sectors like non-profits, education and
nursing, but have limited representation in financial service industries and IT sectors. 96
About 83% of Ugandan women are also engaged in unpaid care work, the most common forms being
cleaning, cooking, and other household tasks. While the least percentage of persons report engaging in
unpaid work for firewood collection, a disproportionately higher percentage of women report spending time
on this activity (42%) compared to men (22%).97
Gender and energy in Uganda
It is widely recognized that consistent and reliable access to energy is critical for both economic growth and
social transformation. Further, access to clean energy can improve health & well-being as well as
the status of time poverty among women by reducing the burden of collecting firewood. Over the past
decade, Uganda has increased its electricity generation capacity from 601MW in 2010 to 1839MW in
2020.98 However, in Uganda, biomass continues to be the predominant source of cooking fuel used by 94%
of the population with 72.8 % using firewood and 21.4% using charcoal. Further, firewood use is 3% higher
among female heads of households than men. 99 Overall 56% population has access to electricity, with the
majority of the households (27%) using solar kits for lighting, 19% using grid electricity, and 11% using solar
home systems. While 51.6% of women-headed households have electricity access in the country, 59%
men headed households have electricity access.100
There is high potential for women to be employed in the clean energy sector, as last mile agents generating
demand for electricity consumption, which continues to be a challenge in Uganda. At 100 kWh per capita,
Uganda currently has one of the lowest rates of electricity consumption per capita in the world.101 However,
currently, the participation rate of women in Distributed Renewable Energy is 28% of the total workforce in

Benin
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Benin has a population of 12.8 million people, with a young population of 42% below the age of 14. The
fertility rate in the country stands at 4.6 which is significantly high compared to other countries in the region.
104
The Gender Development Index in Benin is 0.880 and the country is placed with ‘Group 5’ countries with a
high absolute deviation from gender parity, of more than 10%. This is largely driven by a gender gap in
expected and mean years of schooling. 105 Benin has a Gender Inequality Index of 0.602 and is ranked
152, which measures disparities between men and women in economic opportunities, reproductive health,
and empowerment. 106

Legal status of women
Benin has ratified various UN conventions which aim towards ensuring equity and inclusion, including the
Elimination of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) in 1982, and the Convention on the Rights of the
Child (CRC) in 1990.108 In the African region, Benin has also ratified the Solemn Declaration of the Heads
of State on Gender Equality in Africa and committed to action under the Protocol to the African Charter on
Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa.109
The Constitution of Benin accords equal rights to all without distinction of origin, race, gender, religion,
political opinion, or social position under Article 26. Under its Code of Persons and the Family in the
Republic of Benin, the country also sets the legal age of marriage at 18 for both men and women. It

promulgates that men and women are guaranteed the same inheritance rights under the law. Further, Benin
has also established a policy framework to translate the legal commitment to action through its National
Gender Promotion Policy, National Policy for the Promotion of Women in Agriculture, and the National
Action Plan to Combat Gender-Based Violence. Benin, under its National Gender Promotion Policy
(consolidated in 2009), aims to achieve gender equality by 2025, however, the action plan to implement
strategies laid down under the policy was only articulated in 2015 and is yet to be reviewed and assessed
which raises questions on how successful the country’s progress is towards the envisioned goal of the
policy. 110 Other gender promotion systems in Benin include the establishment of Social Promotion Centers,
a National Commission for the Promotion of Women, a National Institute for the Promotion of Women, and
the Ministry of Social Affairs and Microfinance.111
Although the legal and policy institutionalization in Benin is robust, policy implementation is replete with
enforcement issues in the backdrop of heavily patriarchal social structures still prevalent in the country.
Political participation
Women in Benin remain underrepresented in political positions. In the 2019 legislative elections, only 6%
of National Assembly members were women. Similar to this trend, In the 2020 municipal elections, 4.3% of
councilors were women and there were 4 women mayors out of 77 elected representatives. Benin has now
deployed a new electoral code was deployed in 2021 which has reserved a minimum quota of 24 out of
109 seats for women, at the rate of one woman per electoral district.112 At the communal counselor level,
women had only 3.86 % representation in 2020.113
Social and cultural context
There is a continued problem of Gender Based violence experienced by women in Benin with 23.8% of
women experiencing it at least once in their lifetime.114
There is a wide regional disparity in women’s access to land across Benin. While women in central and
southern Benin have more control over land, for example; 20.7% in Couffo, and 17.8 % in Plateau, women
in other regions have significantly limited access like in Alibori, (10.9 %) & Atacora (12.2%).115
Health
Benin has a maternal mortality ratio (MMR) of 397 per 100,000 live births (as of 2017). 116 As per the Benin
Household Demographic and Health Survey analysis showed that while 89% of women reported going for
at least one antenatal care (ANC) visit, only half of these women initiated ANC in the first trimester and
completed 4 or more visits.117 This gap in the utilization rate of maternal health services, a study finds, is

Education
The literacy rate among women in Benin is 31% compared to 54% for men120 and 10% of females in primary
school-going age are out of school.121 However, interestingly, at the tertiary level, Benin has one of the
world’s highest percentages of women graduating from Engineering and ICT courses at 54.6% and 55.1%
respectively (as a percentage of total graduates in the sector).122 The country has a National Policy on
Literacy and Adult Education which was adopted in 2001 and aimed at reducing the rate of illiteracy among
men and women by half between 2001 and 2010123 however World Bank data suggests that between 2002
and 2012, the literacy rate actually dropped by 1%. 124 While enrollment of girls is high at the primary level,
even surpassing that of boys, there is an evident gender gap in secondary education enrollment which is
40.8% for men compared to 34.1% for women. 125 Benin has committed to a post-2015 Education Sector
Plan (2018-2030) to promote access and retention in education for girls by waiving school fees at the
secondary level for girls. The country has budgeted USD 6.4 million for the year 2019 for this fee waiver for
girls. Further, Benin has budgeted USD 306,023 between 2018 and 2021 to provide scholarships for
promoting girls’ enrollment in agricultural and industrial education. 126
However, to improve the enrollment and retention rate of women at the secondary level, Benin needs to
address structural gaps in its education system. The World Bank-supported Global Partnership for
Education Project identified challenges that cripple Benin’s education system currently including; high
administrative burden among staff, slow-moving and highly political decision-making processes that
interfere with managerial decisions, improper division of roles and poor coordination across Ministries,
rapidly changing leadership at the institutional level and the problem of high-absenteeism of teaching
staff.127

Women’s economic participation and entrepreneurship
Benin has seen a growing Labour Force Participation among women in the past 2 decades. While the
disparity between men's and women’s labor force participation (LFPR) in not high overall with about 69.3%
LFPR for women and 73.3% for men, the type of work conducted by women is largely informal. As per the
Enquête Harmonisée Sur le Conditions de Vie des Ménages survey in Benin, 95.5% of women workers
concentrated in the informal sector compared to 86% of men.129 Women and young people constitute the
majority of unemployed people, with 37,5% of 15-24 old being without a job, and 24,6% of them being
women.
While the high share of female graduates in Engineering and ICT fields should create a thriving
entrepreneurship environment in the country for women, as per data only 25.9% had female directors and
36.7% of businesses have women among their shareholders.130 However, the country has an above-
average estimated gross income per capita among women of 2,998$, compared to other Sub-Saharan
African nations.131 Women-led businesses are concentrated in service industries such as accommodation
and food as well as retail and wholesale, which unfortunately have seen been most impacted due to COVID.
Female-headed businesses in Benin remain unregistered with only 13% having certification compared to
21% of men-headed businesses having requisite registration.132
Gender and energy in Benin
According to ERI-ESI 2018, 63.4% of households use charcoal compared to 22% for gas and 12.2% for
wood, and energy use for cooking is predominantly biomass.133 About 41% of households have access to
electricity in Benin. 134 Only 35% of women have access to electricity, compared to 69% of men.135
The Energy Ministry in Benin has prepared a gender profile for the energy sector in 2020 and a 2021-2025
National Action Plan for the Policy for Gender Mainstreaming and Energy Access in Benin and
operationalized a Gender and Development Unit to ensure gender mainstreaming across the Ministry’s
projects.
ECREEE is implementing a project entitled: Promoting Agricultural Competitiveness through Solar Energy
(PAC-SOLAR) in Benin with the aim to enhance women’s access to renewable energy. As part of this
project, women have also women have been trained and charged with the job of cleaning the solar panels
regularly, and maintain solar PV installations.136
However, overall, women in Benin are unable to access training and finance to learn high-skill trades in the
energy sector and there continues to be a higher preference for employing and financing men in the energy

Zambia
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Zambia has a population of over 19 million,138 of which 50.5% are women, and where over 55% of the
population lives in rural areas – the majority of them being women.139
Zambia has a comparatively equal development index when compared with other Sub-Saharan African
countries, with a Gender Development Index of 0.965. The country is placed with ‘Group 2’ countries with
an absolute deviation from gender parity between 2.5 percent and 5 percent. This is a result of the country
achieving equality in SDG 4.4 of mean years of schooling with both girls and boys receiving 7.2 years of
schooling. 140 Zambia has a Gender Inequality Index of 0.540 and is ranked 138, which measures disparities
between men and women in economic opportunities, reproductive health, and empowerment. 141

Legal status of women
Zambia has a favorable policy framework to advance gender equality in the country. The Constitution
(Amendment) Act No. 2 of 2016 provides equal rights to women and men to freely participate in, determine
and build a sustainable political, legal, economic and social order. The Constitution also underlines national
values and principles which include equity, equality, and non-discrimination.142 Further, the country has
also enacted the Gender Equity and Equality Act, 2015, to strengthen the legal framework for the elimination
of all forms of discrimination against women and girls as committed under the Maputo Protocol; and put in

place affirmative action to eliminate all barriers which prevent women from participating meaningfully in all
spheres of life and create a conducive environment for such participation. The Act also provides that “an
employer shall not discriminate against a woman by dismissing or demoting 17 the woman on the basis of
sex, marriage, disability, pregnancy or maternity leave or subject the woman to any other disadvantage in
employment” further stipulating that women must be awarded maternity leave with pay without loss of

human rights with the revision of their penal code in 2005, 2010, and 2012 as per which punishments for
sexual violence have been made more severe.144
As a result of Zambia’s policy environment, the country has made strides across the board with respect to
women’s health status, labor force participation, and literacy rate as is highlighted in the following sections.
Political participation
Women’s participation in political and economic spheres in Zambia is low, however, it has continuously
risen. The proportion of parliamentary seats held by women increased from 14% in 2011 to 18.9% in
2018.145 However, recently women’s political representation has seen a decline in the most recent August
2021 election, with women now holding 13% of parliamentary seats and 21% of cabinet positions compared
to 17% and 40% of seats in the executive cabinet in 2016. This decline is a result of the recent limited skills
and resources available to women candidates required for political mobilization and the inability of leading
parties to fulfill mandatory quotas for the representation of women within their cadre. Further, the election
apparatus in the country has also been unable to curtail violence during polls, which dissuades women
candidates and also impedes voter turnout among women voters. 146
Social and cultural context
There are 73 ethnic groups in Zambia, categorized into three social systems which include matrilineal
patrilineal, and bilateral social structures. However, overall, Zambian society is based on patriarchal values
and is highly conservative. Zambia has a dual legal system consisting of civil law and customary law, with
customary law favoring men over women with respect to land access and marriage.147 However, data
suggest that Zambia has a very low gender disparity in ownership of a house with 35% of women owning
a house either alone or jointly and 38% of men having home ownership rights alone or jointly.148
The country presents high rates of GBV, with more than one-third (36%) of women age 15-49 having
experienced physical violence at least once since age 15, and 14% have experienced sexual violence.149

The MMR in the country is much lesser than in other Sub-Saharan African countries. Maternal mortality

2018 and 84% of deliveries by women took place at health institutions. Further, 97% of women who

provider.150 The Zambian government under the Gender Equity and Equality Act, also protects and
promotes women’s sexual and reproductive health for girls, and reinforces women's right over family
planning. The country has also added Comprehensive Sexuality Education to the school curriculum and
there has been an increased focus on youth in sexual education and service provision through training
programs for healthcare providers and peer educators in adolescent-friendly sexual reproductive health

Education
As per World Bank estimates, about 83% of adult women in the country are literate and this estimate has
been steadily rising over the past 2 decades.153 This is a result of the country’s holistic Girls Education and
Women’s Empowerment and Livelihoods (GEWEL) project to support girls from vulnerable households with
school requisites and fees to enable them to complete secondary education. The project aims to increase
access to secondary education for 25,000 adolescent girls coming from extremely poor households.154
However, higher education is very low in the country, with the DHS estimating that only about 6% of women
and 8% of men attain higher education.155 However, in an effort to increase women’s access to tertiary
education, the country has now reserved 30% of state-offered bursaries to support women. Further, to
encourage women’s admission in STEM fields at the tertiary level, the country has reduced the cut-off score
for girls for entry into these courses.156

percentage of the working-age population (15 years old or older) at 52.8% compared to males at 47.2%.157
However, men constitute 62% of formal employment, while women only 38% and 73% of women contribute
to unpaid family labor.158 The largest proportion of women works in agriculture, followed by sales
professions. Within the agricultural sector, women represent only 19% of formal employees while men make

Gender and energy in Zambia
Zambia have experienced a high rate of deforestation, posing an increasing challenge to women and girls
who are primarily responsible for fuelwood collection and need to travel long distances to collect firewood
for household energy. Estimates suggest that women in Zambia spend on average 800 hours a year in
fuelwood collection.162 Overall, only 32.8% population of Zambia has access to electricity.163 However,
compared to other Southern African countries, Zambia has one of the highest shares of modern renewables
in energy consumption at 27.6 in 2017%. However, this share has seen a slight decline from 29.4%.164
The Ministry of Energy conducted a Gender Assessment of the Energy Sector in Zambia in 2018 and is in
the process of developing a Gender Mainstreaming Strategy and Action Plan.165 Zambia’s Energy
Regulatory Board (ERB) has also committed to participate in the Women in Energy Regulation Internship
Program, organized by the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC) with funding

Mozambique
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Mozambique is an East African nation that has a population of 33.1 million people, with a young and
adolescent population of 34% between the age group of 10 to the age of 24 years. The fertility rate in the
country stands at 4.6. 167
The Gender Development Index in Mozambique is 0.922 and the country is placed with ‘Group 4’ countries
with a medium to low equality in HDI achievements between women and men (absolute deviation of 7.5–
10 percent). This is primarily driven by a gender gap in expected and mean years of schooling of 2.4 years
among females and 4.1 years among males. 168 Mozambique has a Gender Inequality Index of 0.537 and
is ranked 136, which measures disparities between men and women in economic opportunities,
reproductive health, and empowerment. 169

Legal status of women
Mozambique has ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women

themselves for their land use and the 2005 Amended Commercial Code under which women can engage

also has a Gender Policy which was approved in 2018 and its corresponding Implementation Strategy was
operationalized in the National Action Plan for the Advancement of Women (PNAM 2018-2024). The PNAM
“aims at re-enforcing the promotion of gender equality in all spheres of development of the country, adopting
a transversal approach to gender dimension, becoming an instrument of inter-sectoral coordination, to
ensure gender equality and empowerment of women”.173 However, there is limited punishment rape within
marriage under the country’s penal code (only 2 to 6 years) whereas it is 2 to 8 years outside of marriage.
While the legal framework of the country creates a mechanism for gender-equal laws to be implemented,
the process of enforcing laws is rife with challenges, especially in rural areas, and limited awareness among
women of their rights under the Mozambique Constitution and associated laws.174
Political participation
Mozambique has a comparatively high representation of women in politics and has a smaller gender gap,
compared to even some developed countries, with 42.4% parliamentarians being women and 57.6%
men.175 The government has a policy mandating 30% participation of women in local councils and
associations. However, the country is far from achieving the target of 50% representation as committed
under the 2008 SADC Protocol on Gender and Development. Currently, the country is performing poorly in
creating a conducive environment for women to participate in the leadership and decision-making bodies
of political parties in the country. Even at the municipal level, women leaders have limited representation
with only six women elected as Mayors and 8 as Presidents of the Municipal Assemblies, among 53
municipalities in 2018’s assembly elections.176 However, under the Gender Policy and its Implementation
Strategy, Area 2 on Governance the country has categorically tried to focus on introducing legislative
measures to ensure the equitable inclusion of women in top positions in the electoral lists of the political
parties and groups of citizens and in decision-making bodies. A study by USAID suggests that women
(especially younger women) face a lot of party resistance when entering political life and public decision-
making.177
Social and cultural context
While legally, men and women are accorded equal rights, the Mozambiquan society is patriarchal and
gender-unequal customs and social order continue to be reinforced across family, community, and
institutional systems. 21% of women in the country have experienced intimate partner violence in their
lifetime.178 However, studies suggest that there is severe underreporting of violence due to the perception
that it is a private matter, with survivors being unaware of formal mechanisms to report and seek help and
most survivors reaching out to community leaders and families.179

a limited progression of women to secondary and university levels of education.187 As a result, only 31% of
girls transition to secondary school, and only 2% complete university.188

at the quality and intensity of employment, with women working predominantly in the informal and
subsistence sectors as self-employed or unpaid workers and working lesser hours in productive
employment compared to men.191 While 31% of men are unpaid workers, this figure is much higher, at 44%

Gender and energy in Mozambique
Currently 30.6% of the population in Mozambique has access to electricity.196 About 80% of the energy use
is from biomass197 which places a disproportionate burden on women to collect firewood. To expand the
country’s electrification, Mozambique launched Mozambique’s National Energy for All Programme in 2018
which targets full access to electricity by 2030.198
The share of modern renewables in Mozambique’s final energy consumption has significantly increased
between 2014 and 2017 from 18.7% to 30%. Vast gas reserves have been discovered in the Rovuma Basin
of Mozambique, which will enable the country to become one of the top 10 suppliers of liquefied natural
gas. However, the power, gas, and mining sectors combined have not been able to generate much
employment in the extractive industry, creating no more than 1.1% of jobs in 2018.199
In the country, there are existing initiatives and organizations that focus on expanding women’s
representation and building the capacity of women who are engaged in the energy sector, For instance,
1. The Mozambique Women Of Energy is a platform for women in the energy sector who identify
areas of action for gender equality in this sector
2. BRILHO programme, an SNV - Netherlands Development Organisation program in partnership with
TechnoServe aims to increase the number of women with access to modern energy solutions in
off-grid communities and enhance the inclusion and empowerment of women in the sector as
collaborators and leading businesses. They do this through technical training of companies on
gender-forward company policies and practices

Sierra Leone
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Sierra Leone is a country in West Africa, on the Atlantic Ocean. The country has a population of 8.3 million
people, with a young and adolescent population of 33% between the age group of 10 to the age of 24 years.
The fertility rate in the country stands at 3.9 which is somewhat lower compared to some of the other West
African nations.200
The Gender Development Index in Sierra Leone is 0.893 and the country is placed among ‘Group 5’
countries with a high absolute deviation from gender parity, of more than 10%. This is primarily driven by a
gender gap in mean years of schooling; with 3.5 years among females and 5.8 years among males. 201
Sierra Leone has a Gender Inequality Index of 0.633 and is ranked 162, which measures disparities
between men and women in economic opportunities, reproductive health, and empowerment. 202

“..every person in Sierra Leone is entitled to the fundamental human rights and freedoms of the individual,
that is to say, has the right, whatever his race, tribe, place of origin, political opinion, color, creed or sex..”205
The country has laid a solid legal foundation for gender equality with the recent Gender Equality and
Women's Empowerment (GEWE) policy released in 2021, which is a consolidation of the country’s existing
National Policy on the Advancement of Women and the National Policy on Gender Mainstreaming adopted
in 2000. Apart from this, the country has three other Gender Justice Acts; including the Child Rights Act;
the Anti-Human Traffic Act; the Sexual Offences Act 2012 (amended in 2019). The GEWE has the following
broad objectives; which it aims to meet through a multisectoral approach206
1. Achieve gender equity and equality in all sectors and enable women to take their rightful position
in national development, political leadership, and decision-making;
2. Ensure satisfactory quality of life for women and girls and eliminate the feminization of poverty;
3. Eliminate all forms of GBV and discrimination
Taking cognizance of the need to educate and sensitize men, the country also released a Male Involvement
Strategy for the Prevention of SGBV in Sierra Leone; aiming to encourage the participation of men and
boys as change agents and allies in changing power relations to champion women’s and girls’ rights.207
However, a study has indicated that the donor-funded (UNFPA) objective and intended approach to male
engagement in the country have not necessarily translated to project design and implementation by local
organizations. And while the involvement of men towards maternal care is reaping dividends, the training
aimed at empowering men to engage in women’s empowerment, may in fact run a risk of reinforcing
patriarchal structures that dictate that men are responsible for ‘protecting women’, taking the agency away
from women.208
Political participation
In Sierra Leone, the position of women's political representation remains dismal with only 12.3% of women
MPs being women.209 Under the Gender Equality and Women’s Empowerment Policy, Sierra Leone’s
cabinet committed to ensuring women's active participation in political leadership and decision-making at
all levels by setting aside 30% of elective and public offices for women.210 To enforce compliance with this
quota system; the country has also amended the Political Parties Act, to replace the Political Parties
Registration Commission with the Political Parties Regulation Commission, enhancing their statutory
powers to penalize parties that fail to comply with quota provisions.211 However, despite these measures,
women candidates face multiple barriers that impede their participation in public political life including
violent hostility, intimidation, limited fund availability, low literacy, and confidence.212 Further, customary

laws are also in contrast to statutory laws especially at the local levels, with women not being recognized

Social and cultural context
The presence of customary laws in Sierra Leone undermines women’s position as owners of land tenure.
Since the majority of ethnicities are patrilinear, women are not entitled to land. And while it is a criminal
offense to evict widowed women from their land, there continues to be ignorance about the legal rights of
women to land tenure and reported dispossession of land among widows or divorced women.214 In Sierra
Leone, 53% of women have experienced Physical and/or Sexual Intimate Partner Violence in their
lifetime.215
Gender-based violence remains a critical area of concern in Sierra Leone, with the President declaring a
State of Emergency on rape and sexual violence in February 2019 which led to the amendment of the
Sexual Offences Act of 2012 by Parliament in 2019.216 As per the amended Sexual Offences Act, the
maximum penalty for rape and sexual penetration of a child has been increased from fifteen years to life
imprisonment; and provisions have been made for the introduction of prosecution for aggravated sexual
assault under this Act.217
Health
Sierra Leone has one of the world’s highest maternal mortality ratios of 1,120 per 100,000 live births as per
the UN database, just behind Chad and South Sudan.218 The country’s infrastructure withstood stresses
under the country’s civil war and Ebola epidemic and the public health infrastructure continues to face
challenges of inadequate health practitioner staff, low skills among health workers, limited availability of
medical equipment and supplies, as well as delayed referrals from lower level facilities. Further, while
almost all pregnant women make 1 ANC visit, only half of these women underdo HIV testing during ANC
visits.219 Women’s agency to decide their age of marriage and use contraception for family planning is also
limited in Sierra Leone. 29.6% of girls are married before the age of 18, 21% of women aged 15-19 had a
birth or were pregnant (in 2019) and 25% of married women report an unmet need of family planning, which
has not changed between 2013 and 2019. Women also have poor nutritional status with 47% of women
aged 15-49 being anemic. 220
Education
Literacy rate among women aged 15 and above is only 40% in Sierra Leone. Regionally this is lower than
other African countries and also much lower compared to the literacy rate among adult boys which stands
at 55%, as per World Bank data.221 The gap is even wider as per the country’s Demographic and Health
survey, with 42% literacy among women compared with 62% among men. Data from 2015 indicates that

A UNESCO study cites that in 2017 almost a third of girls who dropped out of school did so because of

catering, and hairdressing) compared to men in manufacturing and construction related training. To
encourage STEM education, the Government has established a grant-in-aid policy for providing
scholarships to all students studying these subjects.225
Women’s economic participation and entrepreneurship
While World Bank estimates point to similar LFPR among men (58%) and women (59%) aged 15 to 64226,
the country’s DHS points to a disparity with men more likely to be employed than women (72% versus
69%).227 Although the trends around women’s tertiary and technical education are encouraging, these don’t
necessarily translate to women’s transition to gainful employment opportunities, where existing disparities
and discrimination undermine young women’s competitive position compared to men. In 2018 for instance,
the Employment-to-Population Ratio for young women with tertiary education is 10 percentage points lower
than young men’s, and the gap widens to 12 percentage points in higher education. Tertiary educated
women who are NEET (not in employment, education, or training) is 24% compared to 17% men.
However, any form of vocational education significantly increases women’s ability to start looking for work,
much more effectively than men; with young female NEETs who received any formal vocational training
relatively much less subject to idleness (defined by a state where they are not even looking for work) (58%)
than their male counterparts (74%).228
Sectorally, women are majorly concentrated in agriculture (54%) and sales (37%) jobs, and are less likely,
compared to men, to be in skilled manual work (4% versus 9%) or in managerial/technical/professional
roles (3% versus 14%). Women’s position as workers remains dismal, as an extremely high percentage of
women in agricultural work (69%) are unpaid and 31% of women in non-agricultural work remain unpaid.229

While there are no recent estimates of women entrepreneurs in Sierra Leone, an IFC study from 2015
estimated 2.1 million women entrepreneurs engaged in micro-enterprises. However, these women
entrepreneurs face myriad barriers to accessing finance for their businesses and primarily access finance
from personal sources such as gifts or personal savings or rely on informal community-based fund
mobilization for petty cash, through the Self-Rotating Saving and Loan Scheme locally known as osusu.230
Gender and energy in Sierra Leone
Electrification rates in Sierra Leone are low compared to other countries in the region. Only a small portion
of the population in Sierra Leone has access to electricity, estimated to be between 26.2% (World Bank,
2020)231 and 23% (DHS, 2020). About 64.4% of cooking fuel comes from wood, and 32.6% is charcoal,
putting women at a high risk of smoke inhalation and respiratory diseases.232
Sierra Leone is a part of ECOWAS and is implementing their policies for gender mainstreaming in Energy
Access. Under ECOWAS, The Ministry of Energy is responsible for supervising the Barefoot Solar
Engineering Training Centre, established to undertake rural electrification projects and to provide solar
training to illiterate women.233 The country also has a Barefoot Women Solar Engineers Association of
Sierra Leone, started by women trained at Barefoot college India on the installation and maintenance of
solar PV systems, and installation of solar pumps. While these women are not formally educated, they have
been able to play a critical role in last-mile access to energy for households in 32 towns and villages.234
The Barefoot women have also provided solar connections to 60 community clinics in northern Sierra
Leone, which earlier lacked continuous electricity, putting lives at risk, especially making childbirth risky at
these clinics. With solar panels, Barefoot women have been able to ensure cheap, clean, and stable
connections thus making institutional deliveries at these facilities much safer for women.235 Between 2014
to 2017, 50 solar women technicians were trained under this program and solar PV systems were installed
in 3,500 Households.236
Among off-grid energy providers operating in Sierra Leone, the women-led company Smiling Through Light
founded by Mariamma Kamara is leading the way in deploying women to provide clean energy access
through the distribution and sale of solar products, focusing on the last mile. The company has a 100%
female sales agent force and 80% of the entire organization including leadership is made up of women.
Smiling Through Light has trained 1000 individuals in Sierra Leone on clean energy access using a
storytelling approach and provided solar lamps to 400 school children in off-grid communities under their
‘One Child, One Lamp’ campaign.237

Guinea
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Guinea is a country in West Africa with vast nature reserves. The country has a population of 13.9 million
people, with a young and adolescent population of 34% between the age group of 10 to the age of 24 years.
The fertility rate in the country, at 4.4, is very high compared to some other countries in the West African
region.238
The Gender Development Index in Guinea is 0.850 and the government is placed with ‘Group 5’ countries
with a high absolute deviation from gender parity, of more than 10%. While the country does not have a
very high difference between men’s and women’s income, the high deviation is potentially a result of high
gender gap in mean years of schooling with 1.3 years among females and 3.2 years among males. 239
Guinea has a Gender Inequality Index of 0.621 and is ranked 157, which measures disparities between
men and women in economic opportunities, reproductive health, and empowerment. 240

Legal status of women
Guinea, similar to many other Sub-Saharan and West African countries recognizes customary law along
with statutory laws. This, in some areas of social and cultural life, impedes women’s ability to exercise their
agency as equal citizens, especially in the inheritance of wealth and land, where while statutory law grants
women 1/8th of wealth and equal rights to land, customary law prevents women from claiming these.242 In
the international arena, Guinea has committed to gender equality through ratification of various UN and
regional conventions, such as; the Convention on the Elimination of all forms of Discrimination Against

The Constitution of Guinea was amended in 2001 to put in place a regulatory environment that is non-
discriminatory and supports gender equality.244 Further, in 2020, the constitution was amended to specify
the age of marriage for girls at 18, and include “physical integrity” as part of their rights.245 However, various
Civil Codes reinforce men’s familial authority by recognizing them as the sole head of the household, with
sole guardianship of children and Guinean women cannot transfer citizenship to children through marriage
to men outside the country.246 However, certain limiting legal restrictions curtail women’s full participation
in the Guinean economy, such as women having to seek their husband’s approval to pursue a trade or
profession of their choice.247
Political participation
As per the Global Gender Gap report, there are 29.6% women in parliament in Guinea compared to 70.4%
men.248 A recent report from 2021 by the country’s first woman Economy and Finance Minister suggests
that Guinea has close to 31% of ministerial portfolios being held by women as of 2021, which is about 9%
higher than the average from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) countries and
there has been a 57% increase in the number of women in politics between 2010 and 2021. The report
however notes that while more women have joined public life, their representation in decision-making
positions is still very low, with only 25 women hold holding directorial positions, compared to 67% having
intermediary positions such as division and section heads.249 While Guinea has Gender Focal Points
designated in all Ministries to undertake gender-responsive planning and budgeting, research suggests that
GFPs (often women in low-level positions) do not have clear mandates and find it difficult to navigate and
assert their authority in male-dominated ministerial networks.250
Further, many studies point to the ineffective civil registration system in Guinea, due to which women are
unable to register for identification proofs, curtailing their ability to participate in public and political
life.251,252Further, mobility restrictions and safety concerns during political demonstrations, spousal
permissions required, time poverty, and low education rates all limit women’s ability to effectively contribute

to political life in Guinea.253 However, recently the country has adopted a significant legal mandate, which

Social and cultural context
Customary and religious practices in Guinea severely limit women’s ability to realize their rights as citizens
of Guinea. Within marriage and families, women’s position is undermined under traditional and customary
law. Child marriage is also rampant in the country with 46.5% of girls married off before the age of 18.255
Even though polygamy is prohibited under statutory law,256 among married women in age 15 to 49, 42% of
women are in polygamous unions.257 Guinea also has one of the world’s highest rates of female genital
mutilation (FGM) with 94.5% of women in age 15-49 reporting that they have experienced FGM,258
traditionally regarded as an important socio-cultural rite of passage for initiation of girls into adulthood and
marriage which is ceremoniously celebrated. On the other hand, patriarchal norms dictate that women must
be chaste before marriage, and forced marriage (especially for widows) is common. At the community level,
there is judicial inaction on FGM, leading to the continued practice of FGM. And while there have been
increased awareness drives to educate people on legal sanctions imposed under the law on FGM, this has
only led to people forgoing celebratory rituals to conduct FGM more privately. 259,260
Health
The state of reproductive agency among women is poor in Guinea. The high rate of FGM highlighted in the
previous section is also coupled with inadequate poor maternal care women receive. While at 576, Guinea
has a lower MMR than some other countries in the region, Guinea has a long way to go to reach the SDG
target of less than 70 by 2030. Close to 28% of all female deaths in the country are maternal deaths.261
This could be due to a variety of factors, such as high rates of anemia among women, 46% of women in
the 15-49 age group are anemic, limited usage of and access to modern contraception, with 36% of
unmarried sexually active women stating that their contraception needs are unmet and 22% of all women
reporting unmet family planning needs.262
Education
Guinea has the lowest mean years of schooling among girls in the world at 1.3 years as per Gender
Development Index.263 As per the country’s DHS, there is a wide gender gap in education between young

Women’s economic participation and entrepreneurship
As per the country’s DHS, the Labour force participation rate among women is 66% while among men it is
81%. Agriculture, animal husbandry, and fishing or hunting are the main sectors of employment for both
men and women. Interestingly however, unlike a lot of other Sub-Saharan African nations, 64% of women
in Guinea are self-employed in agriculture instead of working as family members on farms. However, only
29% of women working in agriculture were remunerated in cash.268 Women’s agricultural work is 8
percentage points less productive than men's in Guinea due to disparity in land ownership and men being
much more likely to use farm inputs such as fertilizer, irrigation, and high-quality seeds.269 Among women,
there has been a steep decline in the proportion of those employed in agriculture, from 52% to 37%. There
has been a transition of women from agriculture to sales professions, with 32% of women working in sales
and services.270
Culturally, entrepreneurship is not seen as a respectable work avenue for women in Guinea.271 Regionally,
Guinea is much behind average in terms of female entrepreneurship with only 9% of firms having female
founders, compared to 29% in the Sub-Saharan African region, as per the 2016 World Bank Enterprise
Survey for Guinea (conducted for formal enterprises, and excluding microenterprises, where women are
largely concentrated). Further, about 25% of enterprises in the country had no female employees.272
As per Global Findex women are behind men by 13% points in bank account ownership, with 24% of women
having accounts, compared to 37% of men. Similarly, in terms of mobile money account holding, women

Gender and energy in Guinea
Currently, only 44% of households in Guinea have access to electricity, and only 5% of the population has
access to clean cooking technologies.275 In Guinea, cooking is predominantly done outside the home and
60% of households use wood for cooking.276
Among notable initiatives in the country, the Women’s Fund for Gender Equality (FGE) developed a training
program on renewable energy technologies to promote sustainable livelihoods for women and in
partnership with a local grantee organization Partenariat - Recherches - Environnement - Médias (PREM),
trained 300 women in Guinea’s Tristao Islands how to plant, grow, harvest, and sell products made from
moringa plants using solar polytunnel dryers. This resulted in 25,000 moringa trees being planted and
greenhouse gas emissions being reduced by 40 tonnes as a result of solar drying technology, between
2013 to 2016.277, 278
Currently, there is an ongoing Research Project on Energy Transition for Women’s Economic
Empowerment through the Horticultural Value Chain in Guinea, to understand and address mechanisms
for use of solar irrigation systems in the horticultural value chain, for irrigation, processing, and preservation.
The project which aims to improve the profitability and working time of rural women by 2025, is also building
the capacity of women to use solar technologies and access finance. The program is being implemented
by the Initiative prospective agricole et rurale (IPAR) in collaboration with the Centre d’étude et de
coopération internationale (CECI) and is funded by the International Development Research Centre
(IDRC).279

Burundi
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Burundi is a country in East Africa, south of the Equator. The country has a population of 12.6 million people
and one of Africa's highest population densities. Burundi has a young and adolescent population of 32%
between the age group of 10 to 24. The fertility rate in the country stands at 5.1.280
The Gender Development Index in Burundi is 0.935, and the country is placed with 'Group 3' countries with
medium equality in HDI achievements between women and men, with an absolute deviation between 5%
and 7.5%. Although there is a gender gap in mean years of schooling, with 2.5 years among females and
3.9 years among males, there is a relatively low difference between women and men in the estimated gross
national income per capita, compared to other East African countries ($668 for women and $797 for
men).281 Burundi has a Gender Inequality Index of 0.505 and is ranked 127; the index measures disparities
between men and women in economic opportunities, reproductive health, and empowerment. 282

Legal status of women
Several national and international policy instruments are in place in Burundi to advance gender equality.
Burundi ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW)
in 1992 and the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) in 1990.284 As a member of the African Union

Burundi's regional regulatory framework. The GEWE strategy focuses on four key pillars, namely:
