● Leadership, voice, and visibility285
The Burundian government also adopted the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child
on the Sale of Children, Child Prostitution, and Child Pornography in November 2007, reinforcing the legal
protections from sexual violence and exploitation for women and girls.286
Within the sub-region, the Pact on Peace and Security in the Great Lakes region was adopted during the
International Conference on the Great Lakes region in 2006, which established measures to address
violence against women and children through its Protocol on the Prevention and Suppression of Sexual
Violence Against Women and Children.287
Regarding the national legislation, the Constitution of the Republic of Burundi (2005, Art 13) recognizes
gender equality stating that ‘All Burundians are born equal in merit and dignity. All citizens enjoy the same
rights and are entitled to the same protection by the Law. No Burundian shall be excluded from the social,
economic, or political life of the nation by reason of race, language, religion, sex, or ethnic origin”.288’ The
Public Administration Statute (2006) prohibits discrimination in recruitment, pay or dismissals based on sex,
in line with the Labour Code.289 Recently (2020 – 2021), Burundi mandated equal remuneration for work of
equal value.290
Political participation
The 2005 Constitution sets a quota of 30% to ensure the participation of women in decision-making bodies
such as the National Assembly and government (Art. 129 and 164) to address women’s
underrepresentation in public life.291 This milestone was achieved through the leaders of women’s
associations' advocacy at the time of the Arusha Agreement.292 293 According to the 2022 Global Gender
Gap report, women hold 38.2% of the seats in Parliament and 37.5% of the ministerial positions.294 Burundi
had its first women Prime Ministry, Sylvie Kinig in 1994.
Social and cultural context
Burundi is characterized as a patriarchal society where women have very little decision-making power
compared with men. These norms determine power dynamics between men and women from an early age
and are reflected in the high rates of physical and economic exploitation of women.295 Women’s primary
responsibility in Burundi is considered to be the care of the household, which results in carrying out a
disproportionate amount of the burden of domestic work, leaving them with little time to accomplish anything

Women’s rights over land are governed by customary law, which discriminates against women. In the
context of a patriarchal culture such as the Burundian, “women do not inherit the land, they are only
usufructuaries and their right to use it depends on the goodwill of their parents, brothers and sometimes
their in-laws.298 This is particularly problematic for women because it leaves them unprotected in times of
hardship or when they are abandoned or widowed. 299
GBV is a pervasive problem in Burundi. Nearly close to half of the women in the country (46.7%) have
suffered intimate partner physical and/or sexual violence.300 Domestic violence “is a mainstream
expectation within family life and something which is seen as a necessity and, to a certain extent, as a good
thing. It reflects the woman’s status as being inferior”.301 Economic violence is also common in Burundi. It
is exerted by prohibiting victims from accessing or using household assets, the crops harvested by them
and, controlling their access to health care, employment, and excluding them from the household
expenditures decision-making.302
Health
Women of reproductive age (15-49 years) often face barriers with respect to their sexual and reproductive
health and rights: in 2017, 39.6% of women had their need for family planning satisfied with modern
methods.303 The adolescent birth rate is 58.2 per 1,000 women aged 15-19 as of 2015, down from 84.5 per
1,000 in 2011. HIV/AIDS is also a problem that disproportionately affects women in Burundi. There are
85,000 people in Burundi living with HIV, from which 45,000 are adult women and 30,000 are adult men.304
Education
Gender norms in Burundi limit women's access to continued education, resulting in a higher rate of illiteracy
in women. 305 While 68% of women aged 15 and above are literate, 81% of their male counterparts are
literate. 306 Families educate girls emphasizing the productive and reproductive roles that women must
assume. Girls are also expected to look after their younger siblings and help with domestic and agricultural
work.307 This unequal division of labour in the household burdens young women, limiting their time to study,
while young men have time for studying and gaining vocational skills. Girls are far more likely to be
withdrawn from schools and retained at home. Some reasons for girls' premature withdrawal from school

Women’s economic participation and entrepreneurship
Women in Burundi play an active role in the agricultural sector, which provides 90% of the country’s food
production.309 They constitute 55% of the agricultural labour and carry out 70% of farm work. Despite
women producing most of the food crops used for family consumption, they often do not have the decision-
making power over the use of the harvest.310
Women are highly involved in informal sectors, particularly in rural areas, which generally require low
qualifications, rather than in the trade and commerce sector, which are better paid.311 Further, Burundian
women are expected to carry out a disproportionate amount of the burden of household work, limiting their
opportunities to find employment or start a business.
Regarding laws that promote or hinder women's entrepreneurship, there are no differences between the
opportunities women and men have to start a business since both can sign a contract, register a business
and open a bank account on unequal terms. However, Burundian law still does not prohibit discrimination
in access to credit based on gender, hindering women’s ability to pursue entrepreneurial activities.312
Gender and energy in Burundi
Only 11.7% of the population in Burundi has access to electricity313, a rate four times lower than the average
in Sub-Saharan Africa of 48.2%,314, and access to clean and modern energy in Burundi remains extremely
low.315 Almost all cooking relies on traditional fuels (99% of the households), and around 90% of rural
households depend on conventional three-stone stoves.316
Gender norms and gender dynamics play an important role in purchasing energy-related products and
appliances within households. Women are often the primary users of energy appliances, and the use of
fuels and technologies may directly impact their health. However, they may not be able to decide to buy
cleaner energy technologies since many of them do not have control over their earnings and household
purchases.317
Some of the gender-focused programs implemented in the region include the Lumière program,
implemented by local NGO FVS-Amade in partnership with UNICEF. Active since 2015, FVS-Amade works
with Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs) to serve the last mile consumers with clean energy

Togo
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Togo is a country in western Africa. The country has a population of 8.7 million people, with a young and
adolescent population of 32% between the age group of 10 to the age of 24 years. The fertility rate in the
country stands at 4.1.322
The Gender Development Index in Togo is 0.849, and the country is placed in ‘Group 5’, countries with low
equality in HDI achievements between women and men, with a high absolute deviation from gender parity
of more than 10%. This is primarily driven by a gender gap in mean years of schooling, with 3.4 years
among females and 6.8 years among males. Togo has a Gender Inequality Index of 0.580 and is ranked
149; the index measures disparities between men and women in economic opportunities, reproductive
health, and empowerment.323

Legal status of women
In the international arena, Togo ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination
against Women (CEDAW) in 1983 but has not yet ratified the Optional Protocol on violence against women.
The country also ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) in 1990,325 the Beijing Platform
for Action in 1995,326 and the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights
of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol) in 2005.327 Togo incorporated the principle of gender equality in
the Constitution in 1992, which states: “All human beings are equal in dignity and in right. The man and the
woman are equal before the law. No one may be favoured or disadvantaged for the reason of their familial,

Following the recommendations of CEDAW, Togo enacted the reforms in 2012 and 2014 to the Persons
and Family Code, making significant progress towards gender equality. Before the reform, the Family Code
restricted women's rights by not granting a woman an equal right to choose where to live, to get a job
without her husband's permission, and to be named head of household.329 However, despite these
progresses, the Women, Business and the Law (WBL) 2022 report notes a setback for Togo in terms of
gender equality with the enactment of a new Labor Code in 2021, that no longer broadly prohibits the
dismissal of pregnant workers leading to a decrease in its WBL score from 84.4 in 2021 to 81.9 in 2022.330
Political participation
Over the years, the participation of women in politics has increased, with women occupying high-level
government positions, including the Prime Minister’s Office, the National Assembly, and the Ministry of
Defense.331 However, women remain under-represented at the upper levels of power and decision-making:
in the Executive, the Legislature, and the Judiciary and the control of information. Women hold only 18.7%
of the National Assembly seats and 31% of the ministerial positions.332 Togo currently has a women Prime
Minister, Victoire Tomegah Dogbé, who has held the position since September 28, 2020, and is the first
woman holding the position.
Social and cultural context
Despite the progress made in recent years in Togo on the legal status of women and their political
participation, culture, religion, and strong traditions still allow discriminatory practices against women. While
the practice of child marriage has declined in recent years, this practice still occurs in some regions of the
country. According to the latest Global Gender Gap report, Togo has an early marriage rate of 13.8% of
women.333 This practice is partly due to cultural factors such as the dowry that can be an economic
motivation for low-income families to get girls married off early or for strengthening bonds between
families.334 Both the Children’s Code and the Personal and Family Code set the minimum age of marriage
at 18 years, and the Law on Reproductive Health 2007 prohibits forced marriage (Art. 11, 2007).335
The Civil Law in Togo establishes that marriages can be monogamous or polygamous (Personal and Family
Code, Art.42).336 Women still face discrimination regarding family laws in Togo, for instance, women have
to wait 300 days to remarry, unlike men that do not have to wait. Further, there is no legislation specifically
addressing domestic violence in Togo.337 Widows also face discrimination and violence in Togo. Despite
existing specific protections under the civil law for widows that prohibit degrading mourning rites, such as
tests to make a woman prove she didn’t kill her husband, deny her access to food and any income-

In terms of inheritance, women are not entitled to inherit from their husbands or fathers under customary
law in Togo. However, civil law provides both women and men equal rights to inheritance (Personal and
Family Code), although it also stipulates that these rights may be waived if the spouses opt for customary
rules in matters of succession (Art. 404).339 Further, civil law grants equal rights and access to land among
women and men, but customary law often excludes women or limits their access to land.340 In fact,
traditional practices relating to land ownership vary across ethnic groups. In some cases, women can only
purchase land through a man, while in other areas, women are excluded from ownership altogether.341
Gender-Based Violence (GBV) is another problem that hinders gender equality. In Togo, 22.1% of ever-
partnered women have suffered intimate partner physical and/or sexual.342 Some of the Togolese
government’s efforts to reduce the risk of GBV include the adoption of the Politique Nationale de l’Equité
et de l’Egalité de Genre du Togo in 2011, a policy to establish an institutional, sociocultural, legal, and an
economic environment favorable to the achievement of gender equity and equality in Togo; and to address
forms of violence against women.343 FGM is also prohibited in the country since 1998 through Act No. 98-
016, which is also considered a harmful practice and prohibited in the Law on Reproductive Health 2007
and the Child Code 2007.344
Despite the existence of a legal framework for FGM, there is still a lot of work to be done in terms of
education and sensitization. A government study found that more than 20% of the population believes that
it is acceptable and justifiable for a man to be violent against his wife.345
Health
Togo’s national health policy, adopted in 1996 and revised in 1997 includes improving women’s and
children’s access to primary health care by providing improved geographical coverage as one of its key
objectives.346 Togo started taking into account the reproductive health component, and the gender
dimension was mainstreamed in it, following the recommendations of the International Conference on
Population and Development held in Cairo in 1994.347
Despite having equal rights to use contraception, women of reproductive age (15-49 years) in Togo face
barriers to accessing sexual and reproductive health information and services. In 2017, only 29.6% of
women made informed decisions regarding sexual relations and about 39.6% of women had their need for

Education
One of Togo’s most significant challenges in terms of education is reducing the existing gender gaps. Only
55% of women aged 15 and above are literate, compared to 80% of men.352 Many women reportedly drop
out of school due to pregnancy, and there is a prioritizing of boys’ education over girls.353 According to
UNESCO, the lower secondary completion gap between boys and girls is 10.7, more significant than the
gap in the Sub-Saharan Africa aggregate, which is 4.7.354
The Togolese government has made progress in reducing the gender gaps through the implementation of
initiatives focused on girls’ education, some of these include:
● Togo joined the Global Partnership for Education in 2010 and received support to implement
multilevel interventions tackling school-level and institutional obstacles and harmful social norms
affecting girls throughout their education to strengthen their school enrollment.355
○ Under this initiative, Togo received a 7 million COVID-19 grant from the World Bank, one
of its key objectives included supporting girls with targeted back-to-school campaigns
through sensitization programs on early marriage, gender-based violence, early
pregnancies, and the importance of continuing to learn.356
● The country has also developed an education strategy for 2014 to 2025 to “develop a quality basic
education to achieve universal primary education by 2022.”357

women’s labor force participation rate was 55.5%, compared to 59.4% for men.358 However, women are

In the past decades, Togo has made significant progress in supporting women’s entrepreneurship and
economic participation. The country has enacted reforms under all eight indicators in the WBL index
(Mobility, Togo has made significant progress since 1970 —the first year covered by the Women, Business,
and the Law (WBL) index. The country has enacted reforms under all eight indicators in the index (Mobility,
Workplace, Pay, Marriage, Parenthood, Entrepreneurship, Assets, and Pension). One of the most
significant reforms was the enactment of the 2006 Labor Code that prohibited the dismissal of pregnant
workers, mandated equal pay for the same work, and prohibited gender discrimination in employment.360

Under civil law in Togo, women and men are granted equal access and participation in all spheres of life,
including economic life.363 This right allows women and men to open individual bank accounts and access
formal financial services such as a line of credit or financial loan, regardless of marital status.364 But there
are gender gaps in access to financial services and products because of barriers that women typically face,
such as lack of collateral. Married under the marriage community of property regime are prohibited from
providing such guarantees without their husbands’ consent.365
Regarding leadership and entrepreneurship, according to the Global Gender Gap 2022 report, only 11.4%
of the firms in Togo have female top managers, and 10.7% have a majority of women ownership. The same
report highlights that Togo has the highest share of women in senior roles, with 70.1%. Further, the
percentage of women business owners has increased in the last two decades, from 22% in 2014 to 32%
in 2020.366
Women in Togo spend disproportionately more time on unpaid care work than men, which negatively
impacts the time they can spend pursuing formal economic activities. As of 2016, women entrepreneurs in
Togo spent 19.3 hours per week on care work compared to 8.8 for male entrepreneurs.367
Gender and energy in Togo
Only half (54%) of the Togolese population has access to electricity.368 The country has a relatively
diversified energy mix, and more than 13% of its final energy consumption comes from renewable supplies
of energy, mainly hydropower.369 In Togo, as in other countries of West Africa, women are the most
vulnerable and affected by energy poverty and its effects. They are the most exposed to health risks related
to the use of polluting fuels they are responsible for cooking. This burden also limits their participation in
other activities, especially income-generating activities, causing a vicious circle by not having the means or

Among notable initiatives in the sector, Entrepreneurs du Monde (EdM) is an initiative supported by the
Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the government of France, created in 1998,
that works with people living in fuel poverty by facilitating access to essential goods and services for their
families. Based in Togo since 2012, EdM runs the Mivo Energie project that aims to combat global warming
and deforestation in Togo by facilitating access to clean, modern, and affordable energy products for
vulnerable populations, especially women.371
Under the CIZO programme, the Government of Togo (GoT) has granted licenses to two companies to
provide solar home systems in the country.372 Bboxx is an off-grid solar energy provider, with operations
across Sub-Saharan Africa, that manufactures and provides installation and maintenance services for solar
home systems and cooking solutions through a Pay-As-You-Go (PAYG) model.373 Recently Bboxx secured
an €11m loan from the Off-Grid Energy Access Fund (“OGEF”) to provide 1.5m Togolese people with clean
energy and support smallholder farmers in Togo to access solar-powered irrigation.374 One of the key pillars
of the company is Female Empowerment through the provision of affordable and safe alternatives to
traditional fuels through an affordable PAYG model. The company is also known to collect sex-
disaggregated data from customers and analyze their repayment rates.375 In other countries such as
Nigeria, Bboxx is also working with local partners to train women entrepreneurs in building businesses and
bringing clean energy to their communities, also leveraging local women's workforce across their
distribution networks to reach target regions. 376

Malawi
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Malawi is a South-East African country bordering Mozambique, Zambia and Tanzania. The country has a
total population of 20.2 million people, with a demographic dividend skewed toward the young and
adolescent population (between the age group of 10 to the age of 24 years), who make up 34% of the
population. The fertility rate in the country stands at 3.9 which is very high compared to regional averages.377
The Gender Development Index in Malawi is 0.968 and the country is placed among ‘Group 2’ countries
with an absolute deviation from gender parity between 2.5 percent and 5 percent. The disparity in mean
years of schooling for females (4.1 years) and males (4.7 years) is lower compared to other countries in
the region.378 Malawi has a Gender Inequality Index of 0.554 and is ranked 142, which measures disparities
between men and women in economic opportunities, reproductive health, and empowerment.379

Legal status of women
Malawi’s constitution of 1994, upholds gender equality, prohibiting gender-based discrimination under
Article 20 and accords women the same rights as men to enter contracts, maintain property, retain
citizenship and custody of children. Further, the Constitution principally outlines gender considerations for
national policy development and adoption of legislation to obtain gender equality through “(i) full
participation of women in all spheres of Malawians society on the basis of equality with men; (ii) the
implementation of the principles of non-discrimination and such other measures as may be required; and
(iii) the implementation of policies to address social issues such as domestic violence, security of the
person, lack of maternity benefits, economic exploitation and rights to property”. 381 The country has also
demonstrated its commitment to furthering gender equality by ratifying international treaties such as the

Convention on the Elimination of all forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) in 1987 and the
CRC - Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1991.382 Further, Malawi is also a signatory to The Protocol
to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (2005), The Beijing
Declaration and Platform for Action (BPfA), and the Southern African Development Community (SADC)
Protocol on Gender and Development.
The country has adopted the Gender Equality Act as a Law in 2013 with the aim to “promote gender
equality, equal integration, influence, empowerment, dignity, and opportunities, for men and women in all
functions of society, to prohibit and provide redress for sex discrimination, harmful practices and sexual
harassment, to provide for public awareness on the promotion of gender equality, and to provide for
connected matters” with a focus on Human Rights, Employment, Education, Sexual and Reproductive
Health and Civic Awareness.383
Malawi’s Ministry of Gender, Children, and Social Welfare consolidated a National Gender Policy in 2015,
with the goal to reduce gender inequalities in priority areas including; education and training; health;
agriculture, food security, and nutrition; natural resources, environment, and climate change management;
economic development; governance and human rights. The following objectives have been identified by
the policy:
1. To advocate for increased access, retention, and completion to quality education for girls and boys.
2. To ensure women, men, boys, and girls' sexual and reproductive health rights, and HIV AIDS status
are improved.
3. To strengthen gender mainstreaming in all sectors of the economy.
4. To reduce poverty among women and other vulnerable groups (Orphans, widows, PLHA, persons
with disabilities, and the elderly) through economic empowerment.
5. To promote women’s participation in decision-making positions in both politics and public life. vi.
To reduce gender-based violence.
6. To strengthen the capacity of the National Gender Machinery.
The policy commitment is complemented by a Monitoring and Evaluation Plan and has been developed in
alignment with various other national policies such as the country’s larger Growth and Development
Strategy, Reproductive Health Policy, Education Policy, Agricultural and Environmental policies as well as
the National Youth Policy.384
Political participation
Malawi boasts of electing the second African female president, Joyce Banda (from 2012- 2014). However,
the country still lags behind in women’s political participation.385 As per the Global Gender Gap report, 23%
of the parliament is composed of women, compared to 71% of men. The gap widens for ministerial
leadership, with 17.39% of women and 82.61% of men holding ministerial positions.386

Studies have suggested that Malawian voters view women as less credible leaders than men, expecting
women to conform to gender norms, however, women are also held to a much higher standard than men
parliamentarians. There is also a relegation of women to fixed roles within the party ranks, commonly, the
‘women’s wings’ which do not have a clear mandate within political parties. Further, women candidates
face discrimination, negative campaigning, and increasing expenses during campaigning, which causes
high turnover among women candidates. 387 The country is yet to take affirmative action on women’s
participation in politics, with no legislative quotas for women’s representation.388
Social and cultural context
Malawi’s social life is dictated by customary law which is patriarchal in tradition. While the country has areas
with matrilinear communities, social norms across these still continue to favor men. Women also have
limited access to productive resources like agricultural plots, and women-managed agricultural plots are
also smaller than that of men (by 12%) with 25% low productivity as a result of limited access to farm
inputs.389 The incidence of violence against women is very high in Malawi with 37.5 % of women having
experienced physical and/or sexual intimate partner violence in their lifetime.390 This figure has continuously
risen between 2004 to 2016 from 15% to 33%.391 This continues even as the country’s National Plan of
Action to combat Gender-Based Violence (GBV) provides an overarching framework to prevent GBV and
the Domestic Violence Act (2006) underlines the penalization of violent offenses against women.392 The
country also has one of the world’s highest rates of child marriage, with 42% of girls married before the age
of 18, and 9% being married below the age of 15.393 To tackle the pervasive issue of child marriage, the
country has developed a National Strategy to Eliminate Child Marriage, which aims to reduce the
prevalence of child marriage in Malawi by 20% by 2023. The implementation of the strategy is to be
coordinated by a multi-sectoral task force and through the establishment of community child protection
committees, community victim support units (CVSUs), Community-Based Child Care Centres (CBCCs) and
Children’s Corners (CCs).394

The maternal mortality rate in Malawi stands at 349 per 100,000 live births.395 The country has seen great
progress in expanding women’s access to institutional care, and as per the country’s last DHS, Malawi has
a very high rate of institutional deliveries, increasing significantly from m 55% in 1992 to 91% in 2015-16.
Although only half (51%) of women had at least 4 ANC check ups in their last pregnancy.396 Further, as per
the country’s fifth Integrated Household Survey (IHS5), 68% of women were assisted by nurses or midwives
while 28% were assisted by doctors or clinical officers.397 There is also high access to family planning
methods among women, with a lower unmet need reported among all women (13%) as compared to other
countries in the region.398 A majority of married Malawian women users of family planning methods report
making a joint decision regarding family planning methods along with their husbands. However, there has
been no increase in the median age at first birth, since 1992, which is currently hovering at 18.9 years.399
The incidence of HIV among women in Malawi is high at 27.5%, and along with complications arising during
pregnancy, they are the leading cause of death among girls of age 15-19 in Malawi.400
Education
Malawi has a universal primary education policy that is free for all.401 As per the Integrated Household
Survey, 62.6% of females are literate.402 The high incidence of child marriage among Malawians also
reflects attitudes toward girls’ education. Among dropouts from secondary school, 32% of females
mentioned marriage being the primary reason they had to drop out.403 There is a gender gap of 6.87
percent in the secondary education enrollment rate in Malawi as per the Global Gender Gap report
(2022).404 Access to higher education beyond secondary schooling is limited in Malawi among both men
and women (above the age of 15), with only 1.2% of women having tertiary education qualifications, and
men having a somewhat higher rate of tertiary education at 2.7%.405
The country has developed a long-term National Educational sector Investment plan to improve enrollment
and quality of education in the country and a particular objective to increase equity in secondary education
with a particular focus on girls. To enhance girls’ education attainment, the country has introduced
affirmative action by mandating 50-50 selection criteria in secondary schools, construction of girls' hostels,
provision of bursaries, and provision of health, nutrition, physical education, and sports. In Technical,
Entrepreneurial, and Vocational Education and Training, a code of conduct has been introduced to combat
gender-based violence (GBV).406
The Ministry of Labour, Youth, Sports, and Manpower Development (MoLYSMD) has also released The
Malawi TEVET Policy, and the first priority area under this policy is to increase access and equity in Malawi’s
TEVET system and increase current levels of enrolment of female students and vulnerable students

Women’s economic participation and entrepreneurship
While Malawi has a comparatively high Female Labour Force Participation in the sub-region, their
conditions of work are far from ideal. As per the country’s Fifth Integrated Household Survey (2019-20),
91.8% of women in Malawi between the ages 15-64 are engaged in income-generating activities. The
highest proportion of women (81.7%) in Malwai have engaged in agriculture or fishing activities and wage
work is the least common with only 6.6% of women engaged in it. Wage work is conducted by men more
commonly (10.6%), and casual work employs a larger proportion of working women (58%) than men
(47%).408 Unpaid work is also more common among women, with the 2015-16 DHS revealing that 59% of
women are not paid for their work compared to 26% of men.409 There is also a gender pay gap in Lawali,
with women earning only 64 cents per dollar paid to men.410 The Integrated Household Survey also finds
that across the board, women wage earners work fewer hours, and spend more time on non-market
activities such as household chores.411
As per the Global Gender Gap report, only 14.2% of firms in the country have female top managers, and
only 11.4% of firms have female majority ownership.412 While women entrepreneurship is proportionately
high in Malawi, they are relegated to non-IT sectors and access to resources and inputs are key barriers
limiting their productivity. As per IHS 5, the most common form of non-farm enterprise in Malawi is in the
Wholesale and retail trade; Accommodation, and food service sectors. A higher percentage of enterprises
in his sector is operated by female-headed households (71%) compared to men (58%). On the other hand,
in the Transportation and storage; Information and communication sector, men hold a higher proportion of
enterprises (10.8%) compared to women (4.5%).413 A word bank analysis also found that women business
managers’ sales are about 65% less than those of male managers, however, the difference reduces to 45%
when controlled for household and enterprise-level factors which indicated that return on resources is the
major reason for the gender gap. Further, the analysis found that while men are more likely to use saved-
up agricultural income as start-up capital, women rely on gifts from friends or family.414

Lesotho
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Lesotho is a landlocked country in Southern Africa. The country has a total population of 2.2 million people,
with a young and adolescent population (in the age group 10-24) of 29%. The fertility rate in the country
stands at 3 per woman, which is lower compared to other countries in the continent.419
The Gender Development Index in Lesotho is 0.985 and the country is placed among ‘Group 1’ countries
with high equality in HDI achievements between women and men (an absolute deviation of less than 2.5
percent). Lesotho is the only country among those categorized as ‘low Human Development Indexed
countries’ that falls in Group 1 of GDI and has higher mean years of schooling for females (6.6 years) than
males (6.0 years).420 Lesotho has a Gender Inequality Index of 0.557 and is ranked 144, which measures
disparities between men and women in economic opportunities, reproductive health, and empowerment.

Legal status of women
Lesotho achieved democracy in 1993 and the country’s constitution’s Bill of Rights enshrines non-
discrimination and equality with respect to legislation, governance, sustainable development
considerations, and democratic institutions of the State.423 The country, like many others in the region, has
a pluralistic legal system, recognizing customary law, Roman-Dutch Law (Common/Civil Law) along with
Statutory Law. While the Statutory law under the Constitution forms the supreme law of the land and
provides equal rights to men and women, customary and common laws often relegate women to minority
status. Internationally and regionally, Lesotho is a signatory to key conventions upholding women’s rights
including The Beijing Declaration and its Platform for Action (in 1995), and the Convention on the
Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) in 1995. To empower women, and

of Married Persons Act, which entitles both men and women to the same rights and obligations regarding
their marital duties, Land Act, and Companies Act which reinforces women’s rights to own property and
control productive assets.424
The country has a strong gender focus as part of its National Strategy Development Plan, and aims to
mainstream gender across the 4 focus areas of the Plan including inclusive and sustainable economic
growth and job creation, human capital strengthening, enabling infrastructure building as well as
governance and accountability system strengthening.425
The country also has an ambitious Gender and Development Policy outlining 12 gender objectives to be
implemented through a rights-based, multi-sectoral approach. These objectives range from providing legal
protection, political representation, and quality education access for women, to addressing issues related
to gender and climate change as well as gender-based violence, providing food security, health, and
sanitation access, and aiding women’s involvement in peacebuilding and media & ICT. Lesotho has also
charted out a robust mechanism for the implementation of this policy with cross-cutting strategies including
effective research, coordination, capacity building of the governing machinery, and Gender Responsive
Budgeting and financing.426
The World Bank’s Women, Business, and Law index score Lesotho 78.1 out of 100. The country scores
particularly low in the ‘Parenthood’ indicator since the country is yet to institute legislation mandating
maternity leave for women. Further, the country does not have any provisions for criminal prosecution or
civil penalties against sexual harassment faced by women in the workplace.427
Political participation
With a strongly articulated policy objective around gender and governance, Lesotho demonstrates a high
commitment to ensuring women’s political participation. However, women still remain underrepresented in
both national and local level political positions, with only 26.4% of women in the National Assembly and
24.2% in the Senate.428 The Global Gender Gap report also highlights a gap between women and men’s
representation in ministerial positions with women holding only 22% of positions.429
Lesotho has introduced affirmative action with a 30% quota for women at the local council level and a
‘zebra-list’ model for the 40 proportional representation (PR) seats in the National Assembly where women
must be listed alternatively with men, in submitted PR lists, thus granting 40 out of 120 seats in the National
Assembly to women. However, regardless of these actions, there has been a steady decline in the political
representation of women, falling from 58% to 40% between 2005 and 2017 in local councils, and from 27%
in 2012 to 25% in 2015 in the National Assembly.430

Social and cultural context
The progressive nature of Lesotho’s institutional framework to address gender inequalities is evident in key
legal Amendments made by the country presented in the previous section, however, the country is still
patriarchal, and Law of Inheritance Act 26 of 1873 has not reversed the Basotho customary law where the
male child becomes the principal heir of his father’s property.431 Further, Gender Based Violence and Child
Marriage are still pervasive in the country. As per the country’s Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS)
from 2018, 19.4% of girls between the ages 20-49 were married before the age of 18 and 2.1% were
married before the age of 15.432 To reduce child marriages in the country, Lesotho launched a nationwide
campaign on Child Marriage in 2016, to raise awareness of the impact of early marriages on girls,
reinforcing the need to eradicate it.433 The Gender and Development Policy (2018-2030) has committed to
zero tolerance towards all forms of violence against women and the country’s Sexual Offence Act (2003)
also recognizes marital rape as an offense.434 Further, the country is also in the process of developing
Counter Domestic Violence legislation that criminalizes different types of violence, with the support of
UNFPA.435 Although even within this framework, some reports indicate that as many as 86% of women
experience GBV in their lifetime.436
Health
Lesotho has faced multiple catastrophic droughts including the El Nino, which have led to crop failures,
food shortages, violence, malnutrition, and displacement.437 These climate shocks often have a
disproportionately adverse impact on women’s health as they disrupt care received by women. Data
suggests that while the country expanded access to essential healthcare for women, quality provision of
care remains a challenge. The maternal mortality rate in Lesotho stands at 544 per 100,000 live births.438
While the rate of institutional deliveries in the country is high (89.4%) and so is the rate of antenatal care
(ANC) received by pregnant women, with 91% of women receiving at least ANC check ups at least once.439
The country still has a high rate of maternal deaths due to inadequate, inappropriate care received or
negligence at the health facility level.440 Similarly, with respect to reproductive and sexual healthcare,
compared to other countries in the region, Lesotho has a low rate of unmet need for family planning, with

only 11% of married women reporting unmet needs.441 However, cervical cancer is the most common cause
of death among women aged 40-49, due to late detection and treatment initiation.442
Lesotho also has one of the world’s highest prevalence rates of HIV among women with 30.4% of women
infected with HIV compared to 20.8% of men. This is due to unequal power relations as well as GBV, with
a significantly higher prevalence in women who had been forced into sexual relationships (39.3%).443 In
2018, the country also set an ambitious target to end HIV/AIDS by 2030 under their National HIV & AIDS
Strategic Plan 2018/19 – 2022/23 which focuses on innovation in interventions and delivery models, multi-
sectoral coordination, and adoption of results-based planning language and accountability frameworks. The
strategy has a strengthened focus on gender, with objectives around the reduction of Sexual and Gender-
Based Violence, along with a reduction in gender inequalities and reducing cultural and normative barriers
for women.444
Education
Lesotho has an overall high literacy rate among women compared with other countries in the region, and
has a higher literacy rate among women than men. As per the country’s 2018 MICS, 92% of women are
literate with 56.2% having attended secondary education and 13.2% of women having attended higher
education. Comparatively, only 76% of men are literate, with only 43% having attended secondary
education and 12.2% having attended higher education.445 However, at the tertiary education level, there
is a gendered divide in STEM education, with the proportion of female students to male students being
0.4% in the faculty of Agriculture, Science, and Technology at the National University of Lesotho.446
The country has a progressive education policy, under the Education Act (2010) which provides for free
and compulsory primary education for girls and boys. The policy also underlines that girls who become
pregnant while in school must be integrated back into schooling post after the delivery of their child.447 The
country’s Gender and Development policy also recognizes the gendered dimension to choice of disciplines,
with girls dominating ‘soft disciplines’, such as humanities, education, law, social sciences, crafts, and
nutrition while the ‘hard disciplines’ such as sciences' have more male students. To correct this imbalance,
the policy categorically commits to establishing mechanisms “to encourage women, girls, and other
vulnerable groups to study Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) subjects”.448 The
Technical, Vocational Education and Training courses in Lesotho are government-sponsored to enable girls
to complete these trainings.449

Women’s economic participation and entrepreneurship
As per Lesotho’s 2019 Labour Force Survey, the country has a female labor force participation rate (LFPR)
of 45.3%, which is lower than other countries in the region and about 10 percentage points lower than LFPR
of men (55%). The survey also highlights that most women are engaged in household-related activities as
employers for undifferentiated goods and services-producing activities of the households for their own
usage (25%) followed by the manufacturing sector (18%). Comparatively a high percentage of men were
engaged in agriculture, forestry, and fishery-related activities (17.4%) and constriction (16%). Further, the
mean earnings for women are much lower than men, i.e. Maloti 3,377.22 and Malori 4,672.92
respectively.450
As per the Global Gender Gap report 2022, there is also a wide gender gap with regards to the
representation of women as legislators, senior officials, and managers, with only 33.7% women and 66.2%
men as well as professional and technical workers, where women make up 39% workers.451
To encourage women’s participation in the labour force, Lesotho underlines very ambitious policy goals
under the Gender and Development policy, including (but not limited to) the expansion of women’s control
over productive resources, including land, information, technology, safe water, energy and finance,
harmonization of legislation and policy to provide better protection and working conditions for women,
putting in place public procurement quotas to source directly from women businesses, as well as advocating
a 30% quota for women in decision making positions in the private sector.452
The country also has a Science and Technology policy from 2008, which aims to achieve high participation
of women in Science and technology-related work, including teaching, learning research, and development.
Further, the policy places special focus on women entrepreneurs by providing them access to training,
technical assistance, marketing, and export development support, as well as increased access to
technology-based incubation.453 However, the successes of this policy are yet to be evaluated.
Gender and energy in Lesotho
In Lesotho, the majority of households do not have access to electricity. As per the MICS, only 43.8% of
people have access.454 The Department of Energy along with the UNDP, have collaborated on a gender
mainstreaming framework under the Sustainable Energy 4 All project with the following objectives:455
1. To build an inclusive energy sector with institutions free of discrimination and inequality
2. To build the capacity of women entrepreneurs to participate in the energy sector supply value chain
3. To facilitate the integration of gender during the implementation of electrification projects.
The energy policy (2015-2025) recognises gender mainstreaming as one of its guiding principles and states
that gender equality is an integral part of the formulation and implementation of energy programmes and
activities.456

Burkina Faso
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Burkina Faso is a landlocked country in West Africa. It has a population of 22.1 million people, with a young
and adolescent population of 33% between the age group of 10 to the age of 24 years. The fertility rate in
the country stands at 4.9.459
The Gender Development Index in Burkina Faso is 0.903, and the country is placed with ‘Group 4’ countries
with medium to low equality in HDI achievements between women and men (absolute deviation of 7.5 to
10 percent). This is partly due to the country’s significant gender gap in women’s and men’s estimated
gross national income per capita, which is $921.460 Burkina Faso has a Gender Inequality Index of 0.621
and is ranked 157, which measures disparities between men and women in economic opportunities,
reproductive health, and empowerment.461

Legal status of women
At the international level, Burkina Faso ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of
Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) in 1987, including the Optional Protocol on violence against
women, and the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in
Africa (the Maputo Protocol) in 2006.463 The country also ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child
(CRC) in 1990,464 and signed the Beijing Platform for Action Conference recommendations and conclusions
and committed to implementing them.465

At the national level, the 1991 Constitution (Art. 1) prohibits any discrimination on the basis of sex, stating
that all citizens are equal.466 In 1997 was created a Minister dedicated to women and gender issues
(currently the Ministry of Women, National Solidarity, Family and Humanitarian Action). Burkina Faso
adopted a National Gender Policy in 2009, which specific objectives are:
● Promote equal rights and equal opportunities in terms of access to and control over basic social
services.
● Promote participatory economic development, access, and distribution of more equitable resources
and incomes.
● Develop equal participation of men and women in decision-making spheres at all levels.
● Promote the institutionalization of gender in all areas.
● Promote a dynamic partnership for gender and development.
● Develop information and awareness-raising mechanisms aimed at all actors for a change in
behavior and mentality in favor of equity and equality in relations between men and women.467
In terms of laws and regulations that affect women’s economic opportunity in Burkina Faso, the country got
a score of 82.5 out of 100 in the Women Business and the Law’s 2022 index. This score is higher than the
regional average observed across Sub-Saharan Africa (71.5).468 However, when it comes to restrictions on
freedom of mobility, men have had the preference to choose where the family will reside
(Code des Personnes et de la Famille, Art. 294). In addition, the current legislation affects women's
employment and income by not having laws that enforce equal pay for work of equal value and paid parental
leave. The existence of a law that prohibits women from working in an industrial job in the same way as
men (Code des Personnes et de la Famille, Arts. 246 and 393) also limits women's opportunities.
Political participation
Despite the quotas of 30% of women for legislative and local elections, implemented in 2009 to promote
women’s representation in the political sphere,469 women's representation in the Assemblée Nationale is
still low, with women holding only 17% of the seats. The original Law on Quotas from 2009 established
financial sanctions (losing 50% of public funding) for non-compliance with the 30% quota, but these were
removed in 2020. However, if a party reaches or exceeds the 30 percent quota, it receives additional funding
as prescribed by the regulations related to public funding of political parties (Law on Quotas, Article 5 &
6).470 Burkina Faso has one of the lowest scores in the Global Gender Gap's Political Empowerment
subindex, just before Nigeria, and it ranks 138 out of 146 globally.471
Social and cultural context
Discriminatory practices towards women in Burkina Faso still prevail, due to the variations in social
relationships between men and women in the different ethnic groups, as each one has its customs and
culture, as well as the social and economic conditions of women in urban and rural areas, and women are
generally regarded as having a lower status than men.472 Often, society and the authorities disregard the

Family and Penal Codes favoring the customary law, which perpetuates practices that discriminate against
women.473
Despite the Burkinabe criminal and civil law establishing that forced marriage is illegal,474 early marriage is
still prevalent in Burkina Faso. Half of the women aged 20–24 (51.6%) were married or in a union before
age 18.475 This is in part because many families force their daughters into marriage due to poverty. Dowry
motivates families to arrange marriages for their daughters as soon as they reach puberty.476 Polygamy is
legal under the Family Code.477 A large part of the population is married under a polygamous regime (i.e.
38% of unions).478 Levirate is forbidden under the Criminal Code (Art. 376). However, under customary law,
widows are obliged to marry a brother of their deceased husband.479
Regarding inheritance, widows and girls have equal legal rights to inherit property under articles 742-744
of the Family Code. However, the customary law grants no right of inheritance to widows or minor children,
so they cannot inherit land either.480 Although civil law does not discriminate against women, women's
access to land, particularly concerning rural land, has always been challenging.481 Only 32% of married
women have access to land, and in most cases, they share it with others. Further, only 8.2% of women own
land alone.482 The poor access of women to land is a recurring problem due to customary laws, in which
the land is generally the family's property and only reserves rights of use to the woman, and the fact that
inheritance is the primary means of accessing land.483
In Burkina Faso, the percentage of women who have experienced intimate partner violence (11.5) is less
than the world average of 27%.484 However, gender-based violence (GBV) continues to manifest in many
ways, such as female genital mutilation (FGM), which is still common in Burkina Faso, despite its ban in
1996. 76% of Burkinabe women have had the procedure done.485 The country is one of the few in the region
to have prosecuted perpetrators under legislation banning FGM (Penal Code Art. 513-7, 513-8, 513-9).486
Health
While legislation is in place that grants the right to women’s reproductive health, more than half of the
Burkinabe women (54%), are excluded from the decision-making process relating to their own health.487
The national family planning policy, adopted in 2004, guarantees access to contraception to all women.
However, women face challenges accessing contraception mainly due to the disapproval of husbands and
problems with access, information, or cost.488 There is a higher incidence of HIV/AIDS among women than
men because they are still highly exposed to infection due to practices such as early or forced marriage,

While legislation is in place that grants the right to women’s reproductive health, more than half of the
Burkinabe women (54%), are excluded from the decision-making process relating to their own health.487
The national family planning policy, adopted in 2004, guarantees access to contraception to all women.
However, women face challenges accessing contraception mainly due to the disapproval of husbands and
problems with access, information, or cost.488 There is a higher incidence of HIV/AIDS among women than
men because they are still highly exposed to infection due to practices such as early or forced marriage,

the unwillingness of their partners to wear condoms, levirate marriage, and polygamy.489 It is estimated
that there are 51,000 women aged 15 and over living with HIV compared to 31,000 men.490
Social norms tend to exclude women from the family planning decision-making process. Although most of
the people think that the decisions must be made by both partners jointly; between a quarter and a third of
the people say that women do not have to take part in the use of contraceptives, birth spacing, and the
number of children since this is the husband's decision.491 Induced abortion is legally restricted in Burkina
Faso. It is estimated that 23 women abort per 1000 women ages 15–49 in 2020.492 Most of the time, they
are performed using non-recommended methods by untrained providers, causing a greater risk of
complications for women.493
Education
In terms of education, the literacy rate is higher in men 49.2% compared to 31% in women.494 The primary
completion rate is higher in girls (57.3%) than in boys (67.7%), but this situation is reversed in secondary,
where the completion rate for girls is 18.4% and 21.6% for boys, and this gap is even wider in rural areas.
495 Only 20.59% of women graduate with STEM degrees in Burkina Faso compared to 79.41% of men.496
The Directorate for the Promotion of Girls’ Education (DPEF) was established within the Ministry of Basic
Education and Literacy (MEBA) to promote activities to reduce gender-based inequalities. The DPEF also
leads activities to raise awareness to keep girls in school.497
Women’s economic participation and entrepreneurship
60% of Burkinabe women (% of women ages 15-64) participate in the labor force participation compared
to 76% of men (% of men ages 15-64).498 Women’s participation in the informal sector is high in Burkina
Faso, with 95% of the women working in the informal sector.499
Regarding entrepreneurship, there are no legal restrictions for women. Under civil law, women can access
credits, sign contracts, register a business, and open a bank account like men.500 However, formal financial
institutions consider women as "high-risk" applicants as they often do not have financial or material
security.501 This situation puts women at a disadvantage regarding access to bank loans, which can hinder
women's entrepreneurship. While there are no legal restrictions on Burkinabe women’s access to bank

Gender and energy in Burkina Faso
Burkina Faso's energy access rate is 19%, one of the lowest in the West African sub-region.503 The
expansion of off-grid electrification faces critical barriers, including inadequate policy and regulatory
frameworks, lack of access to finance, lack of local technical capacity, and high cost of new connections,
among others.504 These barriers may make it more difficult for women to access off-grid electrification due
to gender gaps in education, access to finance, land tenure, and cultural norms that prevail in the country.
The Africa Minigrids Program supported by UNDP and financed by the GEF, seeks to demonstrate
productive uses of electricity to reduce costs, increase the viability and enable mini-grid development at
scale. The primary targets and actors of the pilot projects are small-scale farmers (women and youth,
mostly) who will benefit directly from the electricity supplied by the solar mini-grids. The project started in
2022 and it is planned to end in 2026.505
Among other initiatives, the GCF-funded Inclusive Green Financing Initiative (IGREENFIN I): Greening
Agricultural Banks & the Financial Sector to Foster Climate Resilient, Low Emission Smallholder Agriculture
in the Great Green Wall (GGW) countries506 program is implemented by the International Fund for
Agricultural Development (IFAD) and local organizations from the participant countries, including Burkina
Faso. The program seeks to provide concessional loans to foster the best adaptation and mitigation
practices for green businesses within the selected agricultural value chains in each target country. Operated
by local, national agricultural banks (LNABs) – the Agricultural Bank of Burkina Faso– the facility will offer
special lines of financing for green business projects prepared by farmer’s organizations (FOs), women and
youth organizations, cooperatives, and MSMEs (including agribusiness dealers and solar operators).
Besides providing loans, the program includes a Technical Assistance Facility (TAF) aimed at addressing
capacity, knowledge, and policy gaps hindering the uptake of green business projects in the selected
countries. It will target LNABs, central banks, and clients (FOs, MSMEs, and cooperatives), with a special
emphasis on women and youth.507

Guinea-Bissau
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Guinea-Bissau is a coastal country in West Africa. has a population of 2.1 million people, with a young and
adolescent population of 32% between the age group of 10 to the age of 24 years. The fertility rate in the
country stands at 4.2.508
The Gender Development Index in Guinea-Bissau is 0.867, and the country is placed in ‘Group 5’, countries
with low equality in HDI achievements between women and men, with a high absolute deviation from gender
parity of more than 10%. The country particularly has a wide gender gap in mean years of schooling, with
2.4 years among girls and 4.9 years among men. Guinea-Bissau has a Gender Inequality Index of 0.627
and is ranked 159; the index measures disparities between men and women in economic opportunities,
reproductive health, and empowerment.509

Legal status of women
Internationally and regionally, Guinea-Bissau has made several commitments to equal rights for women.
The country ratified the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination
against Women (CEDAW) in 1981, as well as the Protocol to the Charter of Human Rights and Peoples on
the Rights of Women in Africa.511 Further, the country’s “Social Protection Framework Law”, Law 4/2007,
defines the conditions for the protection of women workers in the formal market, including maternity leave
provisions. However, It does not contain specific protection regulations for the informal labor market.512

Legislation exists in the country to protect women from violence, however, the implementation of these has
been weak with pervasive violence against women, as is examined in the next section. The Law on
Domestic Violence (Law Nbr. 6/2014 of 4 February) aims to combat cases of physical, psychological,
property, and sexual violence. The country also has a Law to combat Female Genital Mutilation (Law Nbr.
14/2011 of 06 June) which aims to prevent and combat FGM, the practice is still prevalent, as expanded in
the next section.513 While the country’s Land Law guarantees the right to private use of land without
discrimination, the Constitution does not have any specific provisions to protect women’s right to use land,
and their land tenure, as a result, is often insecure. Men continue to control and manage agricultural and
household land, while women live under the looming threat of having their land taken away.514
As per the Women, Business and Law index, the country has a score of 42.5 out of 100, with the poorest
performance in the workplace, pay, and entrepreneurship indicators, under Lei No. 2 of 1986, Art. 155(4)
of the country’s legislation, no provisions were found to grant women equal rights to an industrial job, same
as men, or equal pay. Under the country’s Civil Code, Art. 1680, women do not have the same right to
register a business or open a bank account. The country also does not have any legislation, criminal
penalties, or civil remedies for sexual harassment in employment, nor does it have maternity or paternity
benefits in place for working women.515
The country had developed a National Policy for Gender Equality and Equity, aimed at addressing gender
inequalities and combating discriminatory practices, however, this policy has not been adopted into
implementation yet. 516 With technical support from UNDP, the country’s National People’s Assembly is
currently in the process of revising the constitution with the integration of a gender lens.517
Social and cultural context
Guinea-Bissau is ethnically diverse with numerous sub-groups, with all these having a patriarchal social
structure (except the Bijagó group of the Bijagos Archipelago) and customary law aligned with traditional
gender roles.518 Social life among these ethnic groups is characteristically male-dominated, under the
culture of matchundaadi. The Matchundaadi culture is based on hierarchical control that men are
guaranteed over women, placing them in decision-making roles, and institutionalizing exalted men above
the law.519 Polygamy is a common form of marriage, with 39.2% of women in the age group 15-49 being in
polygamous unions,520 with men exerting their dominance over multiple women under such unions, where
men must prove their masculinity by producing more children.521 Gender-based violence, including Female
Genital Mutilation or “Fanadu di mulher” is a critical aspect of the matchundaadi culture, and is considered

Political participation
Guinea-Bissau has experienced political instability for decades. The political system is semi-presidential.
The country took affirmative action in 2018, by introducing legislation demonstrating its commitment to
uplifting women’s position in political decision-making. The country’s Parity Law establishes that there must
be a minimum of 36% of women in party lists for elective positions in the National Parliament and in local
municipal elections.528 The law also underlines sanctions in case of non-compliance. In 2019, only 8 of 21
parties that participated in the election complied with the Parity Law.529 election saw an increase in the
number of women members of parliament, from 7,8% (1999) to 13,7% however, the country’s government
has indicated their commitment women’s political participation by conferring 11 of the 31 ministerial
portfolios to women and a total of 35% female participation in the Executive of Guinea-Bissau.530
Health
Years of political instability and unrest have impacted women’s well-being in Guinea-Bissau. The country’s
deep-rooted customs that legitimize violence against women, forced marriages, and early initiation into
reproductive labor, have adversely impacted women's health. As per the MICS (2020), 27% of women in
the age group 20-24 reported that they had their first pregnancy before the age of 18. Further, women have
to travel far to access health facilities, which combined with poor road infrastructure makes the situation

Education
In a country, where about half of the households spent more than 65% of their incomes on food, education
becomes a non-essential expense.536 While the country’s Basic Law of the Educational System (2011)
despite many gaps in its implementation, guarantees universal, free, and compulsory education up to the
6th year,537 there is a long way to go in achieving gender parity in education at the secondary and above
levels. As per the country’s MICS (2020) literacy rate among girls (aged 15-49) is 32.6%, and Guinea-
Bisseau has a twenty percentage point literacy gap between boys and girls. While the difference at the
primary schooling level is not that stark, at the secondary school level there are only 11.7% females
compared to 20.5% boys. Guinea-Bissau has only a small percentage of boys and girls who attain technical
and higher education, with 2% of women having a technical education and 4% of men with technical
education, and 2.1% of women with a university education compared to 4.8% of men.538
The country has an education sector plan (2017- 2025) that promotes schooling and encourages the
retention of women in the first two basic cycles of education.539 However, quality of education and
infrastructure is a looming issue in the country, with most schools, not having basics such as instructor's
manuals, and other teaching materials; and the students not having access to pencils, paper, schoolbooks,
etc.540

Guinea-Bissau’s economy is predominantly based around agriculture, with cashew farming being the
primary source of income and employment for most of the country’s poor.541 As per the country’s Integrated
Regional Survey on Employment and Informal Sector (2019), 96% of women in Guinea-Bissau work in the
informal sector. Women in Guinea-Bissau are relegated to informal work and they compose the vast
majority of self-employed people at home; street vendors and domestic workers.542 As per the ERI-ESI
survey, 51.9% of women are in vulnerable employment as part-time, family workers, or self-employed,
compared with 33.4% of men. On the other hand, women are almost non-existent in high productivity
informal non-agrarian sector work such as civil construction work, transport activities, larger commercial
establishments, and far distance and regional trade.543‘Idleness’ among disillusioned youth is also higher
among women, with 31.8% of women in the age group 15-24, not in the education system or in employment,
compared to 18.8% of men. Further, only 9.7% of women have formal remunerated work in the agriculture
sector, while 27.5% of men have salaried work in the formal agriculture sector.544
Gender and energy in Guinea-Bissau
Currently, access to electricity among Guinea-Bissau’s population is low. As per the MICS (2020), 18% of
households have electricity access through a connection to a public grid and 17.7% of households have
electricity through a non-public network connection.545 Due to limited access to modern energy sources,
women have to spend a lot of time collecting wood and exposing themselves to harmful biomass fumes.
Notably, women are engaged in various biomass-intensive processing industries including charcoal
production, fish smoking, and street-food vending, and hence are important agents of change in the shift
towards cleaner energy use in the country.546
The country has released a National Action Plan for Gender Mainstreaming in Access to Energy and The
Guinea-Bissau Ministry of Natural Resources and Energy developed a National Action Plan (NAP), with a
specific focus on mainstreaming gender into national development plans. The NAP aims to create an
institutional framework for gender mainstreaming in access to energy followed by an intervention
framework. The plan highlights the need to train women and young people and raise awareness around
gender mainstreaming in energy, to enable a diverse and inclusive labor market in the energy sector. The
NAP also aims to periodically measure the progress of its implementation and assess effectiveness.547
UNDP is currently implementing a project aimed at promoting better access to modern energy services
through sustainable mini-grids and low-carbon bioenergy technologies among Guinea-Bissau’s forest-
dependent communities. As part of the project learnings, it was found that there is tremendous scope for
clean off-grid renewable energy to create entrepreneurship opportunities for women, especially in the food
processing and fishing sector (which is the second largest subsistence activity in Guinea-Bissau) and as

Niger
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Niger is a West African country with vast desert terrain. The country has a population of 26.1 million people,
with a young and adolescent population of 33% between the age group of 10 to the age of 24 years.550 The
country has one of the world’s highest fertility rates of 6.6 per woman.551
The Gender Development Index in Niger is 0.835, and the country is placed in ‘Group 5’ countries with low
equality in HDI achievements between women and men, with a high absolute deviation from gender parity
of more than 10%. The country has a high gender gap in mean years of schooling, with 1.7 years among
girls and 2.8 years among boys, and in gross national income per capita. Niger has a Gender Inequality
Index of 0.611 and is ranked 153; the index measures disparities between men and women in economic
opportunities, reproductive health, and empowerment.552

Legal status of women
The Constitution of Niger which was adopted in 2010 upholds equal rights for men and women and
guarantees the same rights and duties for women and men in Articles 8 and 10. Further, Article 22 explicitly
mandates the State to take measures to combat gender violence and take measures to ensure the full
participation of women in public institutions, and in national development, through the country’s policies.
The country’s quota law defines minimum representation percentages for women in public affairs and the
commercial and labor codes prohibit gender-based discrimination in hiring, work allocation, wages, and
promotion practices.554
However, Niger is one of the few countries in the region, which has not yet ratified the African Charter on
Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women.555 The country ratified the Convention on the
Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) in 1999, however, Niger has
expressed reservations about its implementation.556,557
Further, the country’s legal and regulatory system accords supremacy to customary law over statutory law.
For instance, the Civil Code, denotes men as heads of the household with marital authority over wives, the
Family Code recognized customary systems around matrimony and property, and the Rural Code fails to
provide promote and protect women’s ownership rights over land.558,559
The country has articulated its gender commitment in some key country policies and strategy documents
including the Sustainable Development and Inclusive Growth Strategy (SDDCI, Niger 2035), the
National Gender Policy, the National Women’s Economic Empowerment Strategy, National GBV
Prevention and Response Strategy, and the Gender and Islam Strategy.560 The country’s Gender
Policy has adopted 4 key lenses to reach its equality goals including; (i) improvement of the socio-cultural
environment in relation to demography, peace, and security; (ii) strengthening of the institutional and legal
framework to fight against gender-based violence and to enable equitable participation of men and women
in the management of power; (iii) economic empowerment and inclusive growth in relation to sustainable
management of the environment, disaster risk management, migration, and humanitarian emergencies; (iv)
strengthening of institutional mechanisms and organizational frameworks for coordination, monitoring-
evaluation, and partnership. The country also has a National Observatory for Gender Promotion under the

Prime Minister's office with a mandate to monitor, and promote gender equity and equality.561 Apart from

gender mainstreaming in policy-making and programmatic decision-making at ministerial and institutional

Social and cultural context
The prevalence of Gender Based Violence in Niger is at 28.4%.563 Women displaced in some regions of
the country, due to extremist Islamic groups’ armed incursions face a high threat of violence in resettlement
or refugee camps. Niger revised the Penal Code in 2003 to make provisions for certain forms of violence
against women, particularly sexual harassment, female genital mutilation, slavery, pimping, incitement to
debauchery, and rape however the country is yet to take holistic, adequate, and concrete steps to prevent,
punish and manage cases of gender-based violence (GBV) and child marriage.564 Niger also has the world’s
highest incidence of child marriage (76%), with close to 4.8 million child brides of which 2 million were
married before the age of 15. To combat this, In 2021, the government issued a decree institutionalizing
communal and village committees as formal child protection committees.565 This further impacts girls’ ability
to remain in school and complete their education. Polygamy is widely practiced in the country, and high
fertility is often a tool for women to command the respect of their husbands.566
Political participation
Niger has implemented quotas to enable the effective participation of women in decision-making by passing
Law No. 2000-008 in 2000, and further revising the quotas in 2019 up to 25% for elective positions and
30% for appointive positions.567 As per the latest Inter-Parliamentary Union data, in Niger’s National
Assembly, 30.72% of MPs are women, as per their December 2020 election.568 In the central
administration, out of 1,764 decision-making positions only 26% i.e. 466 are held by women, and at
the deconcentrated level (regional and departmental services of the Ministries), out of a total
of 1,007 decision-making positions, 8% are held by women. At the decentralized level, there are 17
women councilors out of a total of 104 councilors in City Councils however there are no female City
Council Chairperson. In Regional Councils, 34 women were elected out of a total of 260 councilors (13%).569
There is a wide gender gap in Niger’s ministerial representation, with only 15.79% women ministers
compared to 84.21% men.570 The country has supported the establishment of the Niger Chapter of the

Health
The high fertility rate in Niger has adverse impacts on women’s health and well-being. Niger has a maternal
mortality rate of 509 as per the Gender Inequality Index.572 The country also has very poor coverage of
ANC and PNC checkups, with only 27.8% of women having 4 or more ANC visits in 2016-18 and 39.4% of
women receiving post-natal care. In 2017 institutional births were also limited (38.2%) and only 36.8% of
births were attended by skilled health professionals. Anemia among women is also highly prevalent with
46% of women being anemic.573 The uptake of contraception in Niger is low due to religious beliefs under
Islamic law and women’s fears about seeking reproductive health services from male healthcare workers.574
Further, 18% of married women have an unmet need for family planning and only 50% of their demand is
met with modern contraceptive methods.575
Education
As per the World Bank data, Niger has a very low female literacy rate of 29%.576 Further, girls in rural areas
have low enrollment rates in schools. In 2016-17, the Gross Enrollment Rate for girls in primary school was
72% and only 59% of girls completed schooling in rural areas. This further declined at the secondary
schooling and higher education level with only 31% and 2% of girls enrolling respectively.577 Women face
access constraints due to inadequate financial resources available for their education, as well as early
marriage. Within schools, poor infrastructure, gender-based violence, and sanitation further exacerbate
these constraints for girls. To promote equality and gender parity in education, the country has developed
a National Strategy for Accelerating Girls and Women’s Education and Training (SNAEFFF).
Under this policy, through presidential decrees, the government in Niger has been working towards setting
up literacy and ‘second chance’ education programs for girls who have dropped out of schools by providing
assistance to parents, food rations, scholarships, and deliberation of a decentralization policy for secondary
education so that community schools can be set up and attended by girls and women.578 Considerig early
marriage and early pregnancy often leads to girls dropping out of schools, integrating women back into the
schooling system is a key challenge being faced, with these girls often ostracised by their communities for
falling pregnant. In 2019, the government of Niger adopted an order directing schools to allow married
and/or pregnant girls to return back to schools, continue their studies, and return after they have
delivered/have given birth.579
For promoting vocational and technical education, the country has developed a Gender Strategy in
Vocational and Technical Education and established 103 community-level training centers and 11

Women’s economic participation and entrepreneurship
Female labor force participation rate (LFPR) in Niger stands at 61.73%, and the country has a gender
disparity of 22.5 percentage points between men and women, with LFPR of 84.27% among men.581 The
high fertility rate, constricting societal norms, and women’s roles in managing their households are some
reasons they are unable to participate effectively in the labor force. As per the country’s Employment survey
from 2016, women work an average of 28 hours a week compared to men who work 43 hours. Agriculture
is the dominant sector, and most women work as informal agricultural workers. World Bank estimates that
about 91% of women are in vulnerable employment as of 2017.582 However, there is a wide disparity in
agricultural productivity of plots managed by women compared to men, with 19% less production per
hectare, which is due to land ownership issues, limited access to and issues in supervising hired farm
labour, and the quantity and quality of fertilizer used.583 In formal employment, public officers have a lower
representation of women civil servants, especially as senior staff, while at the junior level, there are 73% of
women in the Ministry of Public Service.584 A high proportion of women youth (77.1%) are also ‘idle’ and
not in education, employment, or training.585 Within wage employment, there is an estimated 29% gender
gap in earnings between men and women in similar roles, due to disparity in educational attainment and
concentration of women in low-productivity sectors.
Entrepreneurship in the informal sector is a crucial phenomenon among women in Niger, and 23% of
women aged 16-64 own an enterprise in the country. However, there is a vast gender gap of 61% in profits
accrued by women-owned businesses versus men-owned. This is due to factors such as the limited
availability of labor to help run the enterprise, literacy, and numeracy gaps, and informality of enterprise
registration. Textile manufacturing followed by wholesale retail trade and motor vehicle repairs are two main
sectors with the high disparity in profits, 82% and 68% respectively.586
Gender and energy in Niger
Currently, there are only 16.6% of households in Niger with access to electricity. The main source of fuel in
the country is wood. This causes a lot of time burden on women who are primarily the ones responsible for
firewood collection. Butane gas is another alternative source of energy in the country, however, the use is
expensive for poorer Nigeriens.587 In urban 38.2% of women-headed households have access to grid
