Chad
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Chad is a Central African country, with a population of around 17 million people – 49.8% of which are
women – an annual population growth of 3.2%, with 48% of the total population under the age of 15.
The Gender Development Index for Chad is 0.77. According to the GDI scoring, Chad belongs to the group
of countries with the lowest human development (countries with low equality in HDI achievements between
women and men and absolute deviation from gender parity of more than 10 percent). On the Gender
Inequality Index (GII) which measures disparities between men and women in the areas of economic
opportunities, reproductive health, and empowerment, the country is ranked among the highest in the world
(165).
Chad also scores low on human development, with women being in worse conditions compared to men
(0.339 HDI for women versus men 0.441), and Chad ranks 190th out of 191 countries on the Human
Development Index (2019).

human rights or to ECOSOC for women's rights violations.590 Women in Chad also have full voting rights.

in reflecting women’s legal rights in practice. Chad has a strong constitutional framework for equality which

includes the State’s obligation to eliminate all forms of discrimination against women, and has made some
progress towards achieving women’s right to equality. For example, Chad has taken the necessary
legislative measures to ban female genital mutilation and child marriage.591 Unfortunately, enforcement of
these laws is inadequate. Women and girls continue to face the prospect of lives of gender-based violence.
There are signs of positive steps. In 2022, the Ministry of National Education and Civic Promotion (MENPC)
of the Republic of Chad, a member of the Gender at the Center Initiative (GCI), sought international support
to provide technical capacity-building towards integration of gender equality issues into education policies.
In addition, the Government of Chad is preparing its Partnership Pact, a sector-wide document that will
articulate a priority gender-sensitive reform that a handful of donors and non-governmental organizations
will support over the next five years.592
Political participation
In Chad, women represent more than 50% of the total population and are potentially a decisive electorate.
A law on representative parity exists, though there is currently less than a 50% representation of women in
seats of national and local governments.593 As in other countries in the continent, gender norms impact
women’s political participation, and women’s groups within the country have called on the government to
guarantee parity in nominative and elective functions in the Republic of Chad and at regional level.594
Despite the challenges, 32.3% of seats in Chadian Parliament are held by women, which is higher than the
sub-Saharan Africa average of 25.7%.595
Social and cultural context
The social and cultural context of women is shaped by factors such as religion, traditional beliefs, and
societal norms. Despite legal protections, women in Chad often face discrimination in various domains,
including education, employment, and inheritance rights. Harmful practices like child marriage and female
genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) persist, particularly in rural areas, despite being prohibited by law.
Religion, predominantly Islam, significantly influences the social and cultural context of women's rights in
Chad. Conservative interpretations and cultural traditions may curtail women's autonomy in areas such as
marriage, divorce, and inheritance.In addition, Chad is a country where land ownership is often governed
by customary laws and practices that may vary among different ethnic groups and regions, and women's
access to and ownership of land can be influenced by social, cultural, and legal factors.
Traditional gender roles and norms also play a significant role, with women often expected to conform to
traditional roles as wives, mothers, and caregivers, constraining their opportunities for education and
employment. Women in Chad have made progress in advocating for their rights, with active women's rights
organizations and civil society groups working towards gender equality and women's empowerment. The

Chadian government has also taken steps to promote gender equality through policy reforms and legal
protections, although challenges persist in implementation and enforcement.
Health
A high maternal mortality rate is a major health issue in Chad. 1,140 women die per 100,000 live births,
which is more than double the sub-Saharan African average, although it has improved from 1,420 in
2000.596 The high maternal mortality rate is caused by several factors such as lack of access to medical
treatment, early marriage, and high birth rates. Chad also has a high adolescent fertility rate of 138.3 births
per 1,000 women aged 15-19. This is higher than the sub-Saharan average of 100.9.597
Throughout the country, the average age at first birth is 18.1 years. Furthermore, 24% of women aged 20-
24 were married before their fifteenth birthday, and 60% of women aged 20-24 were married before their
eighteenth birthday,598 compared with 8% of men in the same age group.
Chadian women suffer from poorer health compared to men, with only 31% of pregnant women receiving
adequate prenatal healthcare,599 and 34% of women being subjected to female genital mutilation.600
Moreover, women of reproductive age (15-49 years) often face barriers with respect to their sexual and
reproductive health and rights: despite progress, in 2019, only 17.5% of women had their need for family
planning satisfied with modern methods,601 and 30% of married women had an unmet need for
contraception.602 Furthermore, severe legal restrictions on abortion lead women to have abortions
performed clandestinely, usually in unhealthy conditions.603
Education
The education situation for girls in Chad faces numerous challenges, including limited access to quality
education, low enrollment rates, high dropout rates, early marriage and pregnancy, gender-based violence,
cultural and social norms, and poverty. These challenges often result in lower levels of educational
attainment for girls compared to boys, which can have long-term consequences for their empowerment,
well-being, and economic opportunities.
The average Chadian woman will benefit from 1.5 years of formal schooling compared to 3.7 years for
men.604 Furthermore, only 8% of women have attended secondary school compared to 24% of men.605
Adult literacy in Chad is also lower among women than among men, with 18.2% of women being literate
and 35.4% of men being literate. The gap in adult literacy between men and women is 17.2, which is larger
than the gap of the sub-Saharan Africa aggregate of 13.606

Traditionally, education for women and girls is less valued and households often prioritize education for
boys compared to girls. However, the Government of Chad has committed to mainstreaming gender
equality in its public education policies, which is an encouraging step in promoting education for girls and
women in Chad.607
Women’s economic participation and entrepreneurship
The labor force participation rate among females is 48.4% and among males is 70.8%, giving Chad a higher
labor force participation gap than the rest of sub-Saharan Africa. Factors such as early marriage, early
pregnancy, cultural norms that prioritize male education, and lack of access to quality education and
vocational training may hinder women's ability to enter the workforce. Furthermore, social norms and
traditional gender roles in Chad often dictate that women primarily engage in household and caregiving
responsibilities, while men are expected to be the breadwinners. This can limit women's ability to participate
in economic activities outside of their homes, and women may face discrimination, biases, and stereotypes
in the workplace or as entrepreneurs.
In Chad, 75% of employed people work in agriculture,608 which includes subsistence farming, fishing, and
animal husbandry. Women play a critical role in food production and contribute to the rural economy by
cultivating crops, raising livestock, and engaging in other agricultural activities to sustain their households
and communities. They also participate in the informal sector, which includes jobs in informal markets, petty
trade, and small-scale enterprises. Despite their important contribution, 98.8% of female workers are in
vulnerable employment, compared to 86.6% of men, both of which are higher than the sub-Saharan African
average. These are workers who are the least likely to have formal work arrangements, social protection,
and safety nets to guard against economic shocks; thus they are more likely to fall into poverty, posing
challenges to women’s economic well-being and empowerment.609 As such, 41% of the employed female
population lives below the poverty line compared to 39% of men.610
There are also gender gaps in the formal sector. It is estimated that only 1% of female workers are salaried
workers, compared to 13% of male workers,611 and women constitute less than 18% of professional and
technical workers.612 There is also an entrepreneurship gap, with only 9% of firms having majority female
ownership and only 12% of firms with female top managers.613 Furthermore, female entrepreneurs may
face challenges such as limited access to finance, markets, and business development services due to
gender-based discrimination.
The principle of non-discrimination on the ground of sex, age or nationality prevails within Chad’s Labour
Code (1996) with regards to employment, notably recruitment, hiring, terms and conditions, promotions,
training, assignments and termination. The Labour Code also guarantees paid maternity leave of 14 weeks,
during which mothers are entitled to the totality of their wages, with a further 6 months of unpaid parental
leave. However, women are mostly involved in the informal sector and precarious jobs and thus remain
excluded from the legal protection of the formal sector. Furthermore, even women within the formal sector
face gender bias. The Labour Code prohibits women from entering certain professions which could

Women’s economic empowerment is also threatened through challenges in accessing land, financial

Gender and energy in Chad
Only 11% of the population have access to electricity in Chad. Women in Chad, particularly those in rural
areas, often face additional challenges in accessing energy services due to factors such as poverty, social
norms, lack of infrastructure, and limited access to financial resources. These challenges can
disproportionately impact women's ability to access and benefit from modern energy services, such as
electricity for lighting, cooking, and productive uses. Sex-disaggregated data on access to energy as well
as women’s participation in the sector is absent.
In 2022, the World Bank approved the $295M Chad Energy Access Scale Up Project (PAAET) which aims
to increase access to electricity and clean cooking solutions via expansion of the main power grid and mini-
grids, standalone solar systems, deployment of improved stoves, and natural resource management.617
The project will include targeted interventions to improve access to electricity for female-headed
households, including in refugee camps, and female-led enterprises, promote women entrepreneurship,
and build awareness relevant to women and girls around energy services.618

Somalia
Overview of gender equality and gender gaps in the country
Somalia is an East African country, with a population of around 17 million people – 49.9% of which are
women – an annual population growth of 3.1%, with 47% of the total population under the age of 15.619
There is a scarcity of socioeconomic data in Somalia, including on gender, because of years of political
instability and civil war. This has led to lack of institutions and systems needed to collect, analyze, and
disseminate reliable data, limited capacity of the Government to undertake comprehensive data collection,
an inability for researchers and organizations to access certain regions for data collection, and significant
displacement and migration of Somali people which which complicates data collection and tracking of social
and economic indicators. As such, Somalia does not have a Human Development Index, Gender Inequality
Index nor a Gender Development Index.620
It’s likely that Somalia would belong to the group with the lowest human development group for all three
indices, and that gender inequality and deviation from gender parity is high.

Legal status of women
Women in Somalia face difficulties in accessing justice due to cultural restrictions, differing interpretations
of judicial regimes, and the absence of women within the judicial system. As of 2021, there are only two
female judges out of a total of 295 and 14 female prosecutors out of a total of 65, highlighting the need for
gender parity in the judicial system.622

Somalia has a Ministry of Women and Human Rights Development, mandated to advance the promotion
and protection of gender equality and human rights, including the rights of women, children and other
vulnerable groups. Increased awareness of the rights of women and girls has been driven by this ministry
alongside international rights groups. The Federal Government of Somalia launched the Somali National
Action Plan (NAP) in September 2022.623 Its purpose is to lay out and guide implementation of the Somali
Women's Charter and UN Security Council Resolution 1325 (UNSCR 1325). The inclusion and participation
of Somali women in peacebuilding and decision-making at all levels is the primary goal of the NAP, where
these ideals are recognized as a crucial foundation for effective governance, long-term peace, and
development.
Despite progress in the formal recognition of women’s legal status, the United Nations has reported that
cultural factors and customary law can be more accepting of inequities or victimization of women and
girls.624 For example, while no laws limit the participation of women or members of historically marginalized
groups in the political process (and they do participate), cultural factors have limited their participation.625
There is some hope the National Action Plan will be able to have a broad impact on women’s lived
experience in Somalia, including their legal standing. Conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence,
access to justice, inclusion in constitutional review processes, state building and peacebuilding, national
reconciliation and transitional justice mechanisms, prevention of violent extremism, as well as climate
change, humanitarian emergencies, and COVID-19, are all identified as relevant themes/action areas for
women’s wellbeing and equity, and are to be addressed by the national action plan.626
Political participation
In Somalia, women account for 50.15% of the population.627 In 2016, Somalia reached a milestone with
nearly a quarter of parliamentary seats occupied by women. In January 2021, a quota was announced for
a third of parliamentary seats to be reserved for female lawmakers. There has since been limited progress
in female representation in the national legislative bodies - the 329 seats in Somalia's lower and upper
houses of parliament - despite the quota. After the parliamentary elections in 2021-2022, women’s
representation fell to 20% in the House of the People, which is lower than the 2016 figure of 24%.628 There
were some gains made with 26% seats for women in the Upper House in 11th Parliament, in comparison
to 24% in 10th Parliament. Given the clan system at the foundation of Somalia’s politics, which is male-
dominated, Somali women largely remain excluded from key political and decision-making processes.629
Social and cultural context
Traditional customs, religious doctrines and societal expectations are among the various factors that
contribute to the social and cultural environment that Somali women experience. Women and girls across
the country face significant challenges, as gender inequality is pervasive. Somalia ranks as the fourth-
lowest country in the world for gender equality, with high rates of maternal and infant mortality, as well as

Health
A high maternal mortality rate is a major health issue in Somalia. 829 women die per 100,000 live births,
which is higher than the sub-Saharan African average.633 The high maternal mortality rate is caused by
several factors such as limited access to healthcare, poor healthcare infrastructure, socio-cultural factors

complications in childbirth which can lead to maternal mortality. What’s more, abortion in Somalia has been
criminalized, except to save the life of the mother,636 and a cesarean is performed only if the husband
and/or the mother-in-law give permission.637 Women are more malnourished than men and are less food
secure.638

The education situation for girls in Somalia is characterized by various challenges and disparities, such as
long distances to school, safety concerns, and lack of female teachers. Although there have been some
improvements in recent years, girls' education in the country continues to face obstacles. Socio-cultural
norms in Somalia often favor boys' education over girls', leading to gender disparities in access to

higher labor force participation gap than the rest of sub-Saharan Africa.644 An overwhelming majority of the
women are self-employed and work in agriculture-related activities. Very few women take up economic
activity that records high profits through exports and imports. For example, in the livestock and fishing
export industries, women are hardly represented. Female farmers also have less access to agricultural
resources, capital and information than their male counterparts.645

higher than the sub-Saharan African average.646 These are workers who are the least likely to have formal
work arrangements, social protection, and safety nets to guard against economic shocks; thus they are
more likely to fall into poverty, posing challenges to women’s economic well-being and empowerment.

and middle management in 2019, which falls in the second quintile of all countries for which there are
data.648
Women are also less likely to be able to access capital. In 2014, 33.7% of women and 43.6% of men in
Somalia had an account with a financial institution or with a mobile-money-service provider, both of which
are lower than the sub-Saharan average.649 The few institutions that provide financial services have
demanding conditions and procedures to access funding, such as strict requirements for collateral
securities (for example, land title), which few rural women own as compared to men.650

Gender and energy in Somalia
Energy access in Somalia is limited, particularly in rural areas, and women are disproportionately affected
by the lack of reliable and affordable energy sources. National energy access in Somalia is 18% and less
than 5% in rural areas.651 The lack of electricity affects women in various ways, such as limiting their access
to information, communication, and education, as well as constraining their economic opportunities. Sex-
disaggregated data on access to energy as well as women’s participation in the sector is absent.
Several programs and initiatives, led by international organizations, non-governmental organizations, and
the Somali government, aim to improve women's access to energy in Somalia. These initiatives focus on
promoting renewable energy technologies, building capacity, and fostering gender equality in the energy
sector. For instance, the Sustainable Charcoal Reduction and Alternative Livelihoods (SCREAL) project
aims to reduce dependency on charcoal by promoting sustainable energy alternatives, including fuel-
efficient stoves, and creating alternative livelihood opportunities, particularly for women and youth.652 The
Africa Minigrids Program (AMP) aims to bring new development opportunities to rural communities and to
increase access to electricity for 67K people, half of whom will be women.653

Conclusions and recommendation for the Gender Action Plan
This assessment provides an overview of the status of gender equality in the sixteen H2R countries. The
H2R initiative has the opportunity to address some of the underlying causes of gender inequality in the
countries by enhancing access for women to clean energy technologies and job opportunities in the
sector. In particular, the following objectives are relevant:
H2R’s Gender Objectives:
1. Elevate women in the OGS sector as customers, employees and entrepreneurs
2. Do no harm from a gender perspective
3. Provide poorest and most vulnerable women and Women Headed Households with clean energy
4. Invest in women-led businesses and businesses with gender-forward business practices
5. Positively impact organizational culture for women employees through the influencing portfolio
companies to adopt and/or expand gender business practices
The H2R Gender Assessment informs the development of the Gender Action Plan through the identification
of key barriers and entry points for the H2R initiative. In particular, the country-level assessments identified
barriers for engaging women as employees and leaders in these contexts, with prevalent negative gender
norms, incomplete education attainment, and limited access and control of assets influencing women’s
participation in the economy and in productive activities. Elevating women as customers, employees, and
business leaders in the OGS will require a comprehensive approach both within the investment process
and in the allocation of capital.
H2R’s Gender Action Plan will achieve its objectives through 4 components. The first is to apply a gender
lens across its investment processes to mitigate gender biases and identify hidden opportunities. This
involves integrating gender considerations at each step of the decision-making process to produce a
portfolio of investments positioned to meet H2R’s gender objectives. Second, H2R will offer post-
investment gender-focused TA to investees to incentivize companies to adopt, expand, and/or
implement gender-forward business practices. Post-investment TA support will focus on the development
and implementation of company Gender Action Plans (GAP) and on providing training to level set any gaps
in gender awareness at the investee level. Third, H2R will work to build opportunities for women in the
broader ecosystem through a dedicated training and employment facility to drive employment access and
readiness in OGS markets. Finally, H2R will catalyze OGS ecosystems in H2R markets by crowding in a
variety of stakeholders and sharing lessons. H2R will invest in insights, data aggregation, and OGS
ecosystem development to build a robust community of actors working together towards common goals.
These components are further detailed in the GAP.
101

--- Table 1 on Page 310 ---
The H2R Gender Assessment informs the development of the Gender Action Plan through the identification
of key barriers and entry points for the H2R initiative. In particular, the country-level assessments identified
barriers for engaging women as employees and leaders in these contexts, with prevalent negative gender
norms, incomplete education attainment, and limited access and control of assets influencing women’s
participation in the economy and in productive activities. Elevating women as customers, employees, and
business leaders in the OGS will require a comprehensive approach both within the investment process
and in the allocation of capital.
H2R’s Gender Action Plan will achieve its objectives through 4 components. The first is to apply a gender
lens across its investment processes to mitigate gender biases and identify hidden opportunities. This
involves integrating gender considerations at each step of the decision-making process to produce a
portfolio of investments positioned to meet H2R’s gender objectives. Second, H2R will offer post-
investment gender-focused TA to investees to incentivize companies to adopt, expand, and/or
implement gender-forward business practices. Post-investment TA support will focus on the development
and implementation of company Gender Action Plans (GAP) and on providing training to level set any gaps
in gender awareness at the investee level. Third, H2R will work to build opportunities for women in the
broader ecosystem through a dedicated training and employment facility to drive employment access and
readiness in OGS markets. Finally, H2R will catalyze OGS ecosystems in H2R markets by crowding in a
variety of stakeholders and sharing lessons. H2R will invest in insights, data aggregation, and OGS
ecosystem development to build a robust community of actors working together towards common goals.

=== PAGE 311 ===
Page 307
H2R Gender Action Plan
Impact Statement: If the appropriate investment capital and TA is provided to OGS companies, then they will be able to deliver clean
energy access to women customers and women-headed households and to increase diversity in their workforce, increasing
companies’ growth opportunities and contributing to women economic empowerment because they will be adequately incentivized
and capacitated to operate in ‘Hardest-to-Reach’ (H2R) contexts.
Outcome statement:
● Access to clean and decentralized energy to 34,047,623 women (47% of 72,441,750 total beneficiaries)
● Sustainable and inclusive growth of OGS businesses
● Reduction in 5.1 m tCO2eq to preserve and improve women’s health
● Increased resilience of women and girls via improved health, safety and wellbeing
● Reduced vulnerability of women
Output statement:
● Funding and technical assistance lead to increased capacity of OGS companies to serve low-income women customers and
to hire and retain women employees, as well as creating gender inclusive workplaces.
H2R’s Gender Objectives:
1. Elevate women in the OGS sector as customers, employees and entrepreneurs
2. Do no harm from a gender perspective
3. Provide poorest and most vulnerable women and Women Headed Households with clean energy
4. Invest in women-led businesses and businesses with gender-forward business practices
5. Positively impact organizational culture for women employees through the influencing portfolio companies to adopt and/or
expand gender business practices
